Adopted house rules are posted in an accessible format in a common area and given to each individual and guardian on admission and after any change. Rules are reviewed with the individuals at least annually.
No staff member may create, enforce or apply an unwritten rule. Staff who see a rule that restricts an individual's rights bring it to the Residence Supervisor immediately.

Any staff member or team member who believes an individual-specific restriction is needed submits a written request to the Residence Supervisor and Executive Director describing the risk or need, the data supporting it and the people consulted.

Before any restriction is approved, the planning team documents the specific assessed need, the positive interventions and less restrictive alternatives already tried (and why they were not enough), the exact limit proposed, how it relates proportionally to the need, how data will be collected and a time limit for review.

The team explains the proposed restriction to the individual and guardian in an understandable way, and records whether the individual and guardian consent. The agency also records that the restriction will cause no harm to the individual. Written informed consent is placed in the record (IR-08).

The Executive Director refers the proposal to the Human Rights Committee (IR-03) before implementation and records the Committee's recommendation. A restriction without committee review and a signed consent is not started.

If the restriction is approved, the Residence Supervisor writes it into the individual's plan (PCS-02) and trains every staff member who works with the individual on exactly how to apply it before they apply it.
Staff collect data on each use of the restriction and on the behavior or need it addresses, and record it as written in the plan. The Residence Supervisor reviews the data monthly.

The team reviews each restriction at least every 90 days and at the end of the time limit. It is discontinued unless the team documents continued need, renewed consent and renewed Human Rights Committee review. Restrictions are lifted as soon as the need ends.

An individual or guardian who disagrees with a house rule or restriction may ask for review by the Residence Supervisor, then by the Executive Director, and may file a grievance under IR-04, with help from an advocate of the individual's choosing. The agency does not retaliate.
No rights are restricted as punishment, for staff convenience, or as a substitute for services and supports. Restrictions are never applied to a whole group because of one individual's needs.

Emergency use of restraint or other restrictive interventions, and the planned behavioral interventions in an approved behavior support plan, follow BSP-01 and BSP-02. Any use outside the approved plan is reported under BSP-04 and reviewed by the Human Rights Committee.

The Executive Director reports the number and status of active restrictions, and any restriction review overdue, to the governing authority at least quarterly and includes them in the CQI plan (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approve house rules, refer restrictions to the HRC, ensure reviews occur and report on restrictions.
Hold house meetings, post rules, document restrictions and data, train staff and lift restrictions when the need ends.
Assess the need, try alternatives, obtain consent and set the review schedule.
Review each proposed restriction and recommend approval, change or rejection.
Apply only approved rules and restrictions as written, collect data and report concerns.

documentation: House meeting minutes and posted house rules
Written restriction requests and team assessments
Documentation of alternatives tried
Informed consent
Human Rights Committee review and recommendation
Plan language and staff training records
Data on each use and 90-day reviews
Grievances and outcomes
Quarterly governing authority reports

policies.title: Human Rights Committee
policies.applies_to: Licensee/Executive Director, Human Rights Committee members, Residence Supervisors and planning teams of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure an independent committee reviews practices that may affect individuals' rights, so that rights are protected and restrictions are justified.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses a Human Rights Committee (HRC) in accordance with N.J.A.C. 10:41A, as required of the licensee by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1. The HRC reviews proposed rights restrictions, behavior support plans that restrict rights, use of restrictive interventions and other matters affecting rights. It meets regularly, keeps a roster and minutes, and its recommendations are followed or answered in writing by the Executive Director. Composition, meeting frequency and quorum follow the requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:41A, which the Executive Director verifies at each annual manual review (GOV-03).

definitions.definition: The committee established under N.J.A.C. 10:41A to review matters that may restrict or affect the rights of individuals served.
A situation in which a committee member is directly involved in the care, supervision or finances of the individual whose case is under review, or has a personal interest in the outcome.
The minimum number of members who must be present for the HRC to act, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:41A and recorded in the committee's charter.

procedures: The Executive Director establishes the HRC, or arranges the agency's participation in a committee, in accordance with N.J.A.C. 10:41A. The Executive Director records the basis for the arrangement in the HRC charter.

The Executive Director appoints members in writing, maintains a current roster showing each member's name, role and term, and updates it whenever membership changes. Each member signs a confidentiality and conflict-of-interest statement on joining and each year.
The HRC charter states the committee's purpose, membership, quorum, meeting schedule, how requests are submitted and how decisions are made. The Executive Director reviews the charter yearly.

The HRC meets on the schedule set in the charter and additionally when a time-sensitive request is received. The Executive Director sets agendas and gives members the materials at least five business days before the meeting, unless the request is urgent.
A member leaves the room and does not vote on any matter in which he or she has a conflict of interest. The minutes record the recusal.

The Residence Supervisor submits to the HRC each proposed restriction (IR-02), each behavior support plan that includes rights limits (BSP-01), and each emergency use of a restrictive intervention (BSP-02), with supporting data, consent and the less restrictive alternatives tried.
The individual and guardian are told of the meeting and invited to attend, to speak, or to send a representative or advocate. Staff help the individual prepare and get to the meeting.

The HRC reviews the submission, asks questions of the team, and records a recommendation: approve, approve with changes, request more information or reject. Recommendations include time frames for the next review.

The Executive Director responds in writing to each recommendation within five business days. If the agency does not follow a recommendation, the Executive Director documents the reasons and informs the HRC at its next meeting.
No restriction subject to HRC review is put into effect until the HRC has reviewed it, except in a documented emergency, which is reviewed by the HRC at its next meeting or sooner.
The HRC reviews the status of all active restrictions at least as often as required by N.J.A.C. 10:41A and at the periodic review intervals set under IR-02.

The HRC reviews summaries of rights complaints (IR-04), restraint use and reportable incidents involving rights, with identifying information limited to what is necessary, and recommends corrective action.
The Executive Director keeps minutes of each meeting, with attendance, quorum, matters reviewed, recommendations and votes, and keeps them confidentially (IR-05).
The Executive Director reports HRC activity and recommendations to the governing authority and includes them in the CQI plan (GOV-04) at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Establish and support the HRC under N.J.A.C. 10:41A, appoint members, respond to recommendations in writing.
Review submissions, declare conflicts, keep matters confidential and make recommendations.
Prepare and present submissions and help individuals and guardians take part.
Provide data, assessments and alternatives to the HRC.
Receive HRC reports and ensure the committee has resources and independence.

documentation: HRC charter and current roster
Signed confidentiality and conflict-of-interest statements
Meeting notices, agendas and attendance/quorum records
Minutes and written recommendations
Executive Director's written responses
Status lists of active restrictions
Quarterly reports to governing authority

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All individuals served, their guardians and families, advocates, employees and the Executive Director and Residence Supervisors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give individuals and others an easy, safe and fair way to raise a complaint and get a timely answer, and to use complaints to improve services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a complaint and grievance procedure with at least two levels of hearing, the last involving the licensee or the Executive Director (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)13). Individuals, guardians, family members and advocates may complain about any aspect of services, staff, house rules or rights. No one may be retaliated against for filing a complaint or exercising a right (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1). Complaints are documented, answered in writing, and used in the continuous quality improvement system. Allegations of abuse, neglect or exploitation are not handled only as grievances. They are reported immediately under BSP-03 and BSP-04. The Executive Director verifies the current rule wording on grievances at each annual manual review (GOV-03).

definitions.definition: An expression of dissatisfaction, made verbally or in writing, about services, staff, rules or the environment.
A complaint that has not been resolved informally and is moved to formal review under this policy.
Review and written response by the Residence Supervisor, or by another manager if the complaint concerns the Residence Supervisor.
Final internal review, involving the licensee or the Executive Director, who has not been part of the decision under review.
Any adverse treatment of a person because he or she made a complaint or used a right.

procedures: On admission, and each year after, the Residence Supervisor explains the complaint procedure to the individual and guardian in an accessible way, gives a written copy and posts it in a common area. The explanation names the Residence Supervisor and the Executive Director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) as the people to contact.

Anyone may complain verbally, in writing, by telephone, through an advocate or by a method that suits the individual's communication needs. Staff must write down a verbal complaint if the person cannot or does not want to write it, and offer help from a person of the individual's choice.

Any staff member who receives a complaint records it on the same shift on the Complaint/Grievance Form, noting the date, time, complainant, what was said and what the person wants, and gives it to the Residence Supervisor by the end of the shift.

Staff immediately forward to the Residence Supervisor and Executive Director any complaint that suggests abuse, neglect, exploitation, a health or safety emergency or an immediate rights violation. Staff also report it under BSP-03 without delay. The complaint process does not delay or replace that report.
The Residence Supervisor acknowledges the complaint to the complainant within two business days and tries to resolve it informally. The Residence Supervisor records the steps taken and the outcome.

If the complainant is not satisfied or asks for a formal review, the Residence Supervisor opens a Level 1 grievance. The Residence Supervisor reviews the facts, talks with the complainant and relevant staff, and gives a written decision within five business days of receipt, with the reasons and instructions for requesting Level 2 review.
If the complaint concerns the Residence Supervisor, the Executive Director assigns another qualified manager to conduct Level 1 review.

The complainant may ask for Level 2 review in writing or verbally within ten business days of receiving the Level 1 decision. The Executive Director or the licensee, who was not involved in the Level 1 decision, meets with the complainant, who may bring an advocate, guardian, family member or other support person.

The Executive Director or licensee gives a written Level 2 decision within ten business days of the request, stating the findings, corrective action and the date by which it will be done. The decision is the agency's final internal answer.

The written decision tells the complainant that he or she may also contact the Division of Developmental Disabilities at 800-832-9173 or the NJ DHS Office of Licensing about concerns at any time, whether or not the internal procedure has been used. Staff will help the individual make the contact if asked.
The Residence Supervisor ensures that corrective actions are carried out, notes completion on the form and informs the complainant. The Executive Director spot-checks completion within 30 days.

Staff do not discourage, hinder or punish a complaint. Any staff member who retaliates against a complainant is subject to disciplinary action up to termination. A complainant who believes he or she has been retaliated against tells the Executive Director, who investigates within three business days.
The Executive Director keeps a grievance log of every complaint and its level, dates, outcome and corrective action, and reviews it monthly.

The Executive Director analyzes complaint trends quarterly, reports them to the governing authority and the Human Rights Committee (IR-03) with identifying information limited to what is necessary, and includes corrective actions in the CQI plan (GOV-04).
Complaint records are kept confidentially (IR-05) and filed in the administrative grievance file, with a copy of the outcome in the individual's record when the grievance concerns that individual.

responsibilities.duty: Conduct final Level 2 review, ensure responses and corrective action, review the grievance log and protect against retaliation.
Explain the process, receive and resolve complaints, conduct Level 1 reviews and document outcomes.
Accept and record complaints, report urgent concerns immediately and never discourage a complaint.
May raise concerns at any time through any method and may use external contacts.

documentation: Complaint/Grievance Forms
Level 1 and Level 2 written decisions
Grievance log
Corrective action and completion records
Posted procedure and acknowledgments of explanation
Quarterly trend analysis and CQI entries

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, volunteers, students and the Executive Director and Residence Supervisors of [AGENCY NAME], for all records and information about individuals served
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of individuals and their information, to specify who may see and share it, and to meet State and federal confidentiality requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps all information about individuals confidential in accordance with N.J.A.C. 10:41-2 (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)16) and, where the agency is a covered entity (for example, by billing Medicaid electronically), HIPAA. Information is used and disclosed only as allowed by law, by written authorization or as needed for care, payment and operations. Each individual's file for a group home or supervised apartment is kept at the residence (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)), secured, and made available only to authorized people and to licensing and funding agency representatives. Staff-held shift communication or critical-information logs are kept separate from individual records (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)14). Video and audio monitoring in common areas, if used, is governed by IR-11.

definitions.definition: Any information that identifies an individual or relates to an individual's health, behavior, finances, services, family or history, in any form.
Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by the agency in any form, as defined in 45 CFR 160.
A health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, such as Medicaid claims, and is therefore subject to HIPAA.
The least amount of information needed for the purpose of the use or disclosure.
A signed, dated release specifying what information may be shared, with whom, for what purpose and for how long.

procedures: The Executive Director designates a Privacy Officer, named in writing as [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] unless otherwise assigned, who receives privacy questions and complaints, and ensures compliance with this policy.

Every employee, contractor and volunteer signs a confidentiality agreement before having access to any individual's information, and receives privacy training in orientation and annually. Training records are kept in the personnel file (STF-05).

Each individual's file is kept at the residence in a locked cabinet or other secured location. Access is limited to staff who need the information for their role. The Residence Supervisor lists who has keys or passwords and changes them whenever staff leave.

Records are not left in open areas, vehicles or unattended. Files are not removed from the residence except under a documented plan, for example, for a medical appointment, and are returned the same day.

Staff keep the shift communication and critical-information logs separate from individual files. Logs use only the information needed for continuity and are stored securely (PCS-07). Individual details from logs that are needed in a record are moved into the record and the log is retained per policy.

Staff discuss individuals' information only with those who need it, in private places, never within hearing of visitors or others. Staff do not discuss individuals on social media, in public places, or with friends and family.

Staff do not take photographs or videos of individuals except with the written consent of the individual or guardian, and only with agency-approved equipment. Staff do not post any information or images of individuals online.

Information is released to family, guardians, physicians, DDD, the Office of Licensing and other parties only as allowed by law or with a signed authorization. Guardians receive information as the law allows. Release with the individual's own consent is respected when the individual has capacity. The Residence Supervisor logs each non-routine disclosure (date, recipient, content, purpose).

Records are shown to licensing inspectors, DDD and other authorized State or federal reviewers on request (GOV-07). Staff verify identification, note what was reviewed or copied, and notify the Executive Director.
Exchanges of contact information with involved family members and guardians follow IR-10 and the individual's own wishes.

Electronic records and devices are protected by unique logins, passwords, automatic locking and encryption where available, and are accessed only by authorized staff. Staff do not share credentials. Email and text messages containing individual information must use agency-approved secure methods and the minimum necessary information.

Staff report any suspected unauthorized access, loss, theft or disclosure of information to the Privacy Officer within the same shift. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits any harm, notifies the individual or guardian and any required authority as the law requires, and documents the response.

If the agency is a covered entity, it gives each individual or guardian a notice of privacy practices at admission, obtains an acknowledgment, honors individuals' rights to access and amend their information and to an accounting of disclosures, and applies the minimum necessary standard.

Individuals and guardians may ask for a copy of the individual's record or an explanation of how information is used. The Residence Supervisor responds within the time required by law and records the request and response.

Records are retained as set in REC-01, and HIPAA-related documentation (policies, authorizations, training and breach records) is kept for at least six years. Records are destroyed only by shredding or secure deletion, with the destruction documented.

Anyone who breaches confidentiality is subject to discipline up to termination. The Privacy Officer reviews incidents, complaints and audit findings at least quarterly, and results are entered in the CQI plan (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Oversee privacy compliance, training, breach response and disclosure approvals.
Secure records at the residence, control access, log disclosures and handle record requests.
Protect information, discuss it only as needed, keep logs secure and report breaches immediately.
May authorize or refuse releases, request records and raise privacy concerns.
Receive privacy reports and ensure resources for safeguards.

documentation: Signed confidentiality agreements and training records
List of authorized record users and key/password log
Signed authorizations for release of information
Disclosure log
Notice of privacy practices acknowledgments (if covered entity)
Breach reports and investigation records
Record request and response records
Record destruction log
Quarterly privacy review

policies.title: Personal Funds and Property Management
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, all direct support professionals and any staff who handle, record or have access to an individual's money or personal property
policies.purpose: To make sure that the money and valuable possessions of the individuals we support are managed soundly, kept separate from the agency's funds, protected from loss and exploitation, and always open to review by the individual and the guardian.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] acts in a fiduciary capacity whenever it holds, handles or helps manage an individual's funds or property (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3). Funds and possessions belong to the individual. They are used only for the individual's benefit and only as the individual, the guardian (where there is one) and the approved plan direct. This policy is the procedure for fiscal management of personal funds and for safekeeping of valuable personal possessions required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b). The agency keeps a written record of all financial arrangements and transactions involving entrusted funds, and the individual and guardian may see that record and receive copies on request (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10). Funds are managed so as not to jeopardize the individual's benefit entitlements. Individuals manage their own money to the greatest extent they are able, with the least restrictive support. Use of an individual's resources for the advantage of someone else is exploitation, and it is reportable under BSP-03 and BSP-04.

definitions.definition: Any money of an individual that the agency holds, deposits, safeguards, spends or records on the individual's behalf, including cash, personal needs funds, benefit deposits and money from family.
The legal and ethical duty to act solely in the individual's interest when the agency is entrusted with the individual's funds or property (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).

Using an individual's resources for another person's advantage, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. It includes any use of an individual's money or property for the benefit of staff, other individuals or the agency.
A court-appointed person or agency with authority over the individual, within the scope of the court order (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).

A person or organization appointed by the Social Security Administration to receive and manage an individual's benefits. If the agency serves in this role, it follows 20 CFR 416.665 on accounting and record-keeping.
Personal possessions of significant monetary or sentimental value, such as jewelry, electronics, identification documents, bank cards, cash and important papers.

procedures: At admission, the Residence Supervisor and the individual (with the guardian, if any) complete a Personal Funds and Property Agreement. It records who manages the individual's money (the individual, guardian, representative payee, family or the agency), what, if anything, the agency will hold or handle, and what supports the individual wants. The agreement is signed and placed in the individual's record.

Where the agency holds or handles funds, the Executive Director opens a separate ledger for each individual. The agency keeps entrusted funds apart from agency operating funds. Funds are held in an account in the individual's name or in a segregated account tracked by individual ledger at [BANK NAME]. They are never commingled with agency money.

Cash kept in the residence is held in a locked, secured location with access limited to the in-charge staff person and the Residence Supervisor. Each individual's cash is kept in a separate labeled envelope or compartment.

Staff record every deposit and withdrawal in the individual's ledger at the time it occurs. The entry shows the date, amount, purpose, balance, the staff member's signature and the individual's signature or initials where able. A receipt is attached for every purchase.

Cash is counted by the in-charge staff person at each shift change and documented on the shift cash count sheet. A second staff person verifies any withdrawal above [DOLLAR AMOUNT]. Any discrepancy is reported to the Residence Supervisor the same shift.

Spending follows the individual's choices and the approved plan. Approved individual expenses are authorized through the individual's IHP/service plan (PCS-02). Staff support the individual to make purchases. Staff may not decide for the individual how personal funds are spent unless the guardian or plan authorizes it in writing.

Staff may not borrow from, lend to, sell to or buy from an individual, use an individual's funds or property for personal use or for the agency, pool individuals' money, or accept gifts of value from an individual. Violations are handled under STF-06 and, where there is a loss or advantage to another, reported as exploitation under BSP-03 and BSP-04.

The Residence Supervisor reconciles each ledger to receipts, cash on hand and bank records within ten business days of month-end. The Executive Director (or a person independent of the handling of funds) reviews and signs the reconciliation within [FIVE] business days of receiving it.

The Residence Supervisor monitors each individual's balance against the resource limits of any means-tested benefit, as confirmed with the Social Security Administration or DDD. When a balance approaches a limit, the Supervisor notifies the individual, guardian and Support Coordinator in writing so a plan can be made before benefits are affected. Funds are never spent down in a way that conflicts with the individual's choices or the plan.

If the agency is appointed representative payee for an individual, the Executive Director keeps the records and prepares the accountings required by 20 CFR 416.665, and keeps those funds separate and identified as the individual's.

Individuals and guardians may review the financial record on request. Staff arrange review within [TWO] business days and provide copies on request. The request and the date provided are noted in the record.

At admission, two staff members, together with the individual, make a written inventory of valuables and significant personal property. The inventory is signed and dated by the individual (or guardian) and staff. It is updated at least every [SIX] months, at each IHP review and whenever items are added or removed.

Valuables that the individual asks the agency to safeguard are logged on a safekeeping receipt, stored in a locked location, and returned on request, with the individual signing at return. Individuals keep and use their own possessions in their own space unless a documented, agreed plan says otherwise.

Lost, missing, damaged or stolen funds or property are reported by staff to the Residence Supervisor before the end of the shift. The Supervisor notifies the individual and guardian within one business day, and an incident report is completed. Any suspected theft, misuse or exploitation is reported immediately under BSP-03 and BSP-04. The agency does not close a missing-funds matter until the loss is resolved and the individual made whole as determined by the Executive Director.

At discharge or transition (PCS-06), the Residence Supervisor completes a final accounting and returns all funds and property within [SEVEN] days. A receipt is signed by the individual, guardian or receiving provider, and a copy goes in the record. If an individual dies (HW-05), funds and property are secured, inventoried and released only to the legally authorized person.

The Executive Director reviews the results of ledger reconciliations, discrepancies and property losses at least quarterly in the CQI process (GOV-04). Any needed corrective actions are documented. Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains separate accounts or ledgers, sets internal controls, reviews reconciliations independently, reviews losses and discrepancies, and serves as representative payee only when authorized and documented.
Opens and maintains ledgers, completes monthly reconciliation, monitors benefit limits, keeps inventories current, and answers record requests.
Record each transaction at the time, count cash at shift change, support individuals to make their own purchases, and report any discrepancy or concern the same shift.
Direct the use of the individual's funds, and may review the record and receive copies at any time.

documentation: Personal Funds and Property Agreement, signed
Individual ledger with receipts and signatures
Shift cash count sheets
Monthly reconciliation signed by Residence Supervisor and reviewer
Property inventory and safekeeping receipts
Benefit-limit notices to the guardian and Support Coordinator
Record-access and copy requests
Incident reports for losses or suspected exploitation
Final accounting and release receipts
Representative payee accountings, if applicable

policies.title: Schedule of Charges and Fees
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors and any staff who discuss admission, costs or payment with individuals, guardians and families
policies.purpose: To make sure every individual and guardian knows in writing, before admission and whenever it changes, every charge and fee the individual is responsible for, and that no charge is made that is not on the schedule.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written list and schedule of all charges and fees for which an individual is responsible, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b). Individuals are charged only for items on the current schedule. The schedule is given to each individual and guardian at admission and again whenever it changes. Services that the agency bills to DDD as fee-for-service Individual Supports are not charged to the individual. Any contribution toward room, board or other costs is set only after the agency confirms the rules with DDD. Charges are never used as a reason to restrict rights, services or access to personal funds.

definitions.definition: The written list of every amount an individual may be asked to pay, with the amount, what it covers, when it is due and how it is paid.
The payment method through which DDD reimburses the agency for approved Individual Supports under the Community Care Program/Supports Program.
A court-appointed person or agency authorized to make decisions for the individual within the scope of the court order.

procedures: The Executive Director prepares the schedule. For each charge it lists the name, the amount, what it covers, when it is due, how it is paid and who is responsible. The schedule also lists items that are optional or that the individual chooses, so that a person can say no.

Before any room, board or other contribution amount is set, the Executive Director confirms the applicable rules with DDD and documents who was asked, the date and the answer. No charge is set while a question remains open. The SSI federal benefit rate ($994 per month in 2026) is used only as a benchmark for reasonableness and is not itself a charge.
The schedule states that no charge is made for any service the agency bills to DDD, unless DDD confirms in writing that a charge is allowed.
The schedule is reviewed by the Governing Authority before use and at least annually as part of the manual review (GOV-03).

During the admission process (PCS-01), the Residence Supervisor gives the schedule to the individual and guardian before the admission decision is finalized. The Supervisor reviews it in plain language or in the format the individual understands (IR-09) and answers questions.
The individual and guardian sign an acknowledgment of receipt. The signed acknowledgment is placed in the individual's record. A copy of the schedule goes to the individual, and one to the guardian.

When any charge changes or a new one is added, the Executive Director gives the individual and guardian written notice at least [THIRTY] days before it takes effect and obtains a new signed acknowledgment. Where DDD confirmation is required, the change does not take effect until it is confirmed.
Payment of any charge from an individual's funds is made only with the individual's or guardian's authorization and is recorded in the individual's ledger with a receipt (IR-06).
Staff do not charge or collect any amount not on the schedule, accept payment in cash without a receipt, or ask for donations or gifts from individuals or families.

Questions about a charge are referred to the Residence Supervisor, who responds within [THREE] business days. If a disagreement is not resolved, the individual or guardian may use the grievance procedure (IR-04). The agency continues to provide supports during any dispute.
Nonpayment of a charge does not by itself result in a change in services, denial of access to the individual's own funds, or discharge. Any proposed discharge follows PCS-06.
The Executive Director reviews charges collected against the schedule at least annually, and reports exceptions to the CQI process (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the schedule and any changes to it.
Prepares the schedule, confirms charge rules with DDD, issues change notices and reviews charges collected.
Reviews the schedule with the individual and guardian at admission and on change, obtains signed acknowledgments and answers questions.
Make no charge outside the schedule and refer all questions about cost to the Residence Supervisor.

documentation: Current schedule of charges and fees, with effective date
Signed acknowledgment of receipt at admission and on each change
Written change notices
Record of DDD confirmation (who, when, what answer)
Ledger entries and receipts for any payment (IR-06)
Grievance records, if any

policies.title: Informed Consent and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, nursing staff, planning team members and all direct support professionals
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals make their own choices to the greatest extent possible, that guardianship and family involvement are verified and respected without being used to take away more rights than the court order or law allows, and that consent is informed, voluntary and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports every individual to understand options, make choices and exercise rights (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1). An individual's rights are not limited because the individual has a guardian or family. Decision-making is supported with the least restrictive means. A guardian is a court-appointed person or agency (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3), and the guardian's authority is only what the court order grants. Guardianship status is verified at admission and reviewed as part of the IHP (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3). Consent for services and actions is obtained from the individual or, where the court order requires, from the guardian, and the individual's own views are always sought and respected. An individual may note disagreement with any part of the plan in the meeting summary/addendum.

definitions.definition: Agreement given voluntarily after the person has been given, in a way they can understand, the nature, purpose, benefits, risks and alternatives, including the option of saying no.
A court-appointed person or agency (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3). Authority is limited to the scope of the court order.
Help from trusted people, communication tools, time and plain-language explanations so that the individual can understand and make their own decision.
The individual, guardian, family or others the individual chooses, and agency and DDD staff who develop and review the service plan (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).

procedures: At referral and admission, the Residence Supervisor asks whether a guardian has been appointed. If one has, the Supervisor obtains a copy of the court order (and any later order) and places it in the individual's record. The Supervisor confirms who holds authority and over what areas (for example, health, finances, residence, all).

If no guardian is on file, the agency presumes the individual makes their own decisions. Staff do not ask a family member to sign consent in place of the individual unless a court order, valid power of attorney or other legal authority exists. If staff doubt the individual's ability to make a particular decision, they refer the question to the planning team. They do not assume it.

Before asking for consent, staff explain the matter in plain language, in the individual's preferred communication method and with the individual's chosen supporter present if wanted (IR-09). Staff allow time, check understanding by asking the individual to say it in their own words, and explain what happens if they say no.

Consent is obtained and documented on the agency form for each of these matters: admission and services, the IHP/service plan, any behavior support plan or restrictive measure (BSP-01, BSP-02, IR-02), release of information (IR-05), photographs and media, any monitoring (IR-11), and any other item where consent is required. Where a guardian's consent is required, the individual's own view is still recorded.

Where both the individual and the guardian hold a role, staff seek the individual's agreement and the guardian's consent. They do not treat the guardian's consent as replacing the individual's voice. If they disagree, staff do not proceed with the disputed action where it is not urgent, and refer the matter to the planning team.

The Residence Supervisor reviews guardianship status at every IHP meeting, as the IHP requires, and notes any change in the court order, any request to the court by the individual or others, and whether the least restrictive option is in use. If the individual wishes to seek restoration of rights or a change to guardianship, the Supervisor gives information on how to reach legal assistance and the Support Coordinator, and documents the request.

An individual who disagrees with any part of the plan may have the disagreement written in the meeting summary/addendum. Staff record it in the individual's own words where possible, and the plan continues to be reviewed with the individual's concern in mind.

If an individual refuses a service, treatment or support, staff do not coerce, threaten or withhold anything. Staff document the refusal and the reason given, offer alternatives, notify the Residence Supervisor, and notify the guardian and nurse as appropriate. Refusal of a health service is also handled under HW-02 and HW-04.
In a life-threatening emergency, staff call 9-1-1 immediately and do not wait for consent (HW-04). The guardian and Residence Supervisor are notified as soon as the situation is safe.

Where a guardian refuses consent or cannot be reached for a non-emergency item, the Residence Supervisor documents the attempts, notifies the Support Coordinator and, if the refusal appears contrary to the individual's welfare or wishes, takes the matter to the planning team and the Human Rights Committee (IR-03).
No staff person may limit, delay or deny any right on the basis that a guardian or family member objects, unless the guardian's authority covers it and the process in IR-02 is followed.

Consents are reviewed at least annually with the IHP and whenever circumstances change. The Executive Director reviews consent and guardianship documentation in the record audit under GOV-04, and staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures consent and guardianship procedures are followed, reviews record audits, and resolves referrals.
Obtains and files guardianship documents, obtains consents, reviews guardianship status at IHP meetings and documents disagreements and refusals.
Explain choices in the individual's own communication method, honor the individual's decisions, and report refusals and concerns.
Explains health information and risks in plain language for consent to health matters and documents refusals.
Exercises only the authority granted by the court order and takes part in planning with the individual.

documentation: Guardianship order(s) and verification of authority
Signed consent forms with the individual's own view noted
IHP guardianship review and meeting summary/addendum, with any disagreement noted
Refusal documentation
Attempts to contact a guardian
Referrals to the Human Rights Committee or Support Coordinator

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: Governing Authority, Executive Director, all staff, and all contractors and volunteers who interact with individuals, guardians, families and applicants
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals, applicants, guardians and families are treated without discrimination, and can communicate with, understand and take part fully in the services, with the language access, interpreters, alternate formats and accommodations they need.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate in admission, services, treatment, employment or contracting on the basis of race, color, creed, gender, national origin, ancestry or disability, or on any other basis protected by law. No license may be issued to or held by anyone found by a court of record or the Division on Civil Rights to have discriminated on these bases (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(n)). Individuals have the same rights as other citizens, and exercising a right is never cause for retribution (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1). Direct support professionals must be able to communicate with the individuals they work with (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5(d)). The agency provides language access, interpreters, alternate-format materials and accommodations for hearing, vision, speech and other communication needs, at no cost to the individual, guardian or family.

definitions.definition: Unfavorable treatment, exclusion or denial of services or a benefit because of a protected characteristic such as race, color, creed, gender, national origin, ancestry or disability.
Services that let a person with limited English proficiency understand and take part, including oral interpretation and translated written materials.

Aids and materials that make information accessible, such as sign language interpreters, captioning, large print, Braille, audio, plain-language or picture formats, and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) devices.
A change to a practice or environment that lets a person with a disability use a service or take part equally.

procedures: The Governing Authority designates [NONDISCRIMINATION COORDINATOR NAME AND TITLE], reachable at [PHONE] and [ADDRESS], to receive questions and complaints about discrimination and accommodation requests. The name and contact information are posted in each residence and given to individuals and guardians at admission.

Admission decisions (PCS-01) are based on the individual's needs and the agency's ability to meet them safely, not on a protected characteristic. The Executive Director documents the reasons for any denial and reviews it for possible discrimination before it is sent.

At referral and admission, the Residence Supervisor asks the individual and guardian about the individual's preferred language, how the individual communicates (speech, signs, gestures, devices, pictures), hearing, vision and literacy needs, and who helps the individual understand. The results are recorded in the individual's record and carried into the IHP.

The IHP includes a communication profile and a method for supporting each individual to communicate, including AAC tools. Staff are trained on each person's profile before working with that individual (STF-03).

When an individual, guardian or family member has limited English proficiency, the Residence Supervisor arranges a qualified interpreter or translation service at the agency's expense for admission, planning meetings, consent discussions, health and safety matters and grievances. Family members and other individuals are not used as interpreters unless the person asks, and the request is documented.

The Residence Supervisor provides written material (rights, consents, house rules, grievance procedure, schedule of charges) in the individual's preferred language and format, such as plain language, picture-supported, large print, Braille or audio. If a format is not immediately available, staff read and explain the material aloud and record that they did so.

For a person who is deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low vision, or who uses AAC, the Residence Supervisor arranges the necessary aids (for example, an interpreter, captioning, tactile or visual materials, or device charging and maintenance), and keeps them working and available. No charge is made for aids or interpretation.

The Executive Director confirms before hire or assignment that each DSP can communicate with the individuals they will work with (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5(d)). Interviewers record the language and communication skills verified, and the Residence Supervisor documents any language match in the staffing assignment (STF-01). Where no staff member shares an individual's language, the Executive Director arranges interpretation and a plan for communication on every shift.

Requests for accommodations are made to any staff member, who gives them to the Nondiscrimination Coordinator the same day. The Coordinator responds in writing within [FIVE] business days, grants the accommodation unless it would cause an undue burden or fundamentally change the service, and, if it is denied, explains why and offers an alternative.

Staff may not use demeaning language, make discriminatory remarks, or treat any individual, guardian, family member or colleague differently because of a protected characteristic. Violations are handled under STF-06 and, where they involve an individual's mistreatment, reported under BSP-03.

Any person may file a complaint of discrimination or denial of access through IR-04, or directly with the Nondiscrimination Coordinator, Executive Director or Governing Authority, or with the outside agencies listed on the posted notice. Retaliation against anyone who complains or requests an accommodation is prohibited.

The Executive Director confirms that no court of record or Division on Civil Rights finding of discrimination exists against the licensee. If any such finding or complaint is made, the Executive Director notifies the Governing Authority at once and reports to the Office of Licensing as required (GOV-02).

The Executive Director reviews accommodation requests, interpreter use, complaints and admission denials at least annually in the CQI process (GOV-04). Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually.

responsibilities.duty: Prohibits discrimination, designates the Nondiscrimination Coordinator, and takes action on any finding.
Ensures communication access resources, verifies staff communication ability, and reviews admission denials and complaint trends.
Receives complaints and accommodation requests, responds in writing and tracks outcomes.
Assesses communication needs, arranges interpreters and alternate formats, and matches staff to individuals.
Communicate in the individual's preferred way, use their tools, and report access barriers and discrimination.

documentation: Communication and language assessment in the record and IHP
Interpreter and translation requests and use logs
Records of alternate-format materials provided
Staff communication-ability verification in personnel records
Accommodation requests and written responses
Complaints and outcomes
Posted Nondiscrimination Coordinator notice
Annual CQI review

policies.title: Exchange of Family and Guardian Contact Information
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors and staff who handle admissions, records and family communication
policies.purpose: To give parents, actively involved family members and guardians who choose to participate a way to exchange contact information with the agency and one another, while protecting each person's choice and the individual's privacy.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains written procedures for exchanging contact information with parents, actively involved family members or guardians who choose to participate, as N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b) requires, under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and 9.6. Participation is voluntary. The agency records each person's choice to opt in or opt out, keeps contact information current, and uses it only for the purposes the person agreed to. The individual's own preferences about who is involved in their life are respected and recorded.

definitions.definition: A parent, relative or other person who has regular contact with, and takes an active part in the life and care of, the individual.
A person's written choice to have their contact information shared and to receive the contact information of others who have also chosen to participate.
A person's choice not to participate. The agency still keeps the contact information needed to notify the individual's guardian and emergency contacts.
A court-appointed person or agency authorized to make decisions for the individual within the scope of the court order.

procedures: At admission, the Residence Supervisor asks the individual who they want involved in their life and who they do and do not want the agency to contact. The answers are recorded. If a guardian has been appointed, the guardian is also asked.

The Residence Supervisor gives each parent, actively involved family member and guardian a written Contact Information Exchange form that explains what is shared, with whom, for what purpose and how to change one's choice.
The form lets each person choose to opt in or opt out, and to list the preferred phone, email, mailing address and best times to be reached. The person signs and dates the form.

The Residence Supervisor files each form in the individual's record. The Residence Supervisor keeps the contact list for participating persons at the residence in a confidential, access-limited place and does not post it publicly.

Contact information is shared only among persons who have opted in, and only after each has signed. Staff do not share contact information of anyone who has opted out or not responded. The agency never shares an individual's health, behavior or other information through this exchange (IR-05).
Contact information from this process is not used for marketing, fundraising, political purposes or any other purpose than communication among involved families, guardians and the agency.
The Residence Supervisor gives the participating persons the current contact list within [TEN] business days of each new opt-in and updated list whenever there is a change. The date given is logged.

Anyone may change their choice at any time by notifying any staff member. The staff member gives the request to the Residence Supervisor the same day, and the person's information is removed from distribution within [FIVE] business days. The agency notifies other participants of the removal and gives them an updated list.
The Residence Supervisor asks each participating person to confirm or update their contact information at each IHP meeting and at least annually, and records the date and any change.

Guardian and emergency contact information needed for notification of incidents, health changes and death is maintained separately in the record and is always available to staff, regardless of any person's choice in this exchange (HW-04, HW-05, BSP-04).

The Executive Director reviews current opt-in, opt-out and update records at least annually, and any complaint about misuse of contact information goes through IR-04 and may be an unauthorized disclosure to be reviewed under IR-05.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains this procedure, reviews its implementation annually and addresses misuse of contact information.
Offers the exchange, collects forms, distributes lists, updates changes and keeps the lists secure.
Route requests to change contact choices to the Residence Supervisor the same day and do not share contact information on their own.
Decide whether to participate and notify the agency of changes.

documentation: Signed Contact Information Exchange forms (opt-in or opt-out)
Individual's stated preferences about family involvement
Current contact lists with distribution dates
Change and removal requests with dates completed
Annual verification of contact information

policies.title: Video/Audio Monitoring in Common Areas (if used)
policies.applies_to: Governing Authority, Executive Director, Residence Supervisors and all staff, in any residence where video or audio monitoring of common areas is used or proposed
policies.purpose: To set out the rules that apply if [AGENCY NAME] uses video or audio monitoring in the common areas of a residence, so that safety is supported without violating individuals' privacy, dignity and rights.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] [DOES NOT USE / USES, IN THE LOCATIONS LISTED BELOW,] video or audio monitoring in common areas. If monitoring is used, this policy governs it, as N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b) requires. Monitoring is never used in bedrooms, bathrooms or any other place where privacy is expected. Monitoring is not used in place of required staffing or supervision and is not used to punish. Individuals have the same rights as other citizens (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1), and monitoring is reviewed by the Human Rights Committee required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1(e) before it begins. Recordings that identify individuals are confidential and protected with reasonable safeguards (45 CFR 164.530(c)).

definitions.definition: A shared space in the residence used by all individuals, such as the living room, dining room, kitchen, hallways and entrances. It does not include bedrooms, bathrooms or other private spaces.
The use of cameras, audio devices or both to observe or record activity in a common area, whether live or recorded.
The committee the licensee uses under N.J.A.C. 10:41A to review matters affecting individuals' rights (IR-03).

procedures: The Governing Authority decides whether monitoring will be used, in which residence and in which common areas, and records the reason (for example, safety, prevention of abuse or theft). Monitoring is not started unless less intrusive alternatives have been considered and documented.

Before installation, the Executive Director submits the written proposal (locations, camera and audio type, who will view, how long recordings are kept) to the Human Rights Committee (IR-03). Installation does not begin until the Committee has reviewed the proposal and any conditions have been addressed.

The Executive Director seeks legal advice before any audio recording is used, because recording of conversations is regulated by law. Without that advice and written approval of the Governing Authority, audio is not recorded.

The Residence Supervisor gives written notice, in the individual's preferred format (IR-09), to each individual and guardian before monitoring starts or any change. The notice states what is monitored, where, why, who can view, and how long recordings are kept. The individual, or guardian where required, may state concerns or objections, which are recorded and addressed by the planning team (IR-08).

Monitoring begins only after notice has been given and each individual and guardian has had the chance to object. If an individual objects and monitoring would intrude on their privacy in a way that restricts a right, it is handled as a rights restriction under IR-02 with documentation. The individual's objection is respected and recorded in the IHP.

New staff are told in orientation, and all staff are told in writing, which areas are monitored. Visible signs are posted in the residence at each monitored area and at each entrance, stating that video (or audio) monitoring is in use.

Cameras may not be installed or aimed in bedrooms, bathrooms, changing areas or any place where an individual receives personal care, and may not be positioned so as to see into those spaces. The Residence Supervisor checks camera angles at installation and quarterly.

Only the Executive Director and [OTHER NAMED ROLES] may view live or recorded footage, for a stated purpose such as an incident review, an investigation, or a quality check. Each viewing is entered in an access log with date, person and reason. Footage is not shared with anyone else, posted or copied for personal use.

Recordings are stored on a secured, access-limited, password-protected system and kept for [NUMBER OF DAYS] days, then securely deleted. Recordings related to an incident, allegation or investigation are preserved until the matter is closed (BSP-03, BSP-04).

A guardian or individual who asks to see footage in which the individual appears is given access to it consistent with the privacy of others on the recording. The Executive Director decides and documents the response within [FIVE] business days. Requests from outside parties, including law enforcement, are handled only on the advice of the Executive Director and in line with IR-05.

Staff who misuse monitoring or recordings are disciplined under STF-06. An improper disclosure is treated as a privacy event under IR-05. Any individual, guardian or staff member may raise a concern about monitoring through IR-04.

The Executive Director and Human Rights Committee review use of monitoring at least annually, including the continued need, the access log, complaints and objections, and whether alternatives exist. The result is recorded and reported to the Governing Authority. If monitoring is discontinued, recordings are deleted and notices are removed.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether monitoring is used, approves locations and retention, and reviews annual results.
Submits proposals to the Human Rights Committee, controls access and storage, keeps the access log and responds to requests.
Reviews proposals before installation and monitoring use at least annually.
Gives notices, posts signage, checks camera angles and takes individuals' concerns to the planning team.
Know which areas are monitored, never disclose or copy footage, and report concerns.

documentation: Governing Authority decision with the reason and locations
Human Rights Committee review and minutes
Notices to individuals and guardians, with objections noted
Signage photographs or checklist
Camera location and angle check log
Footage access log
Retention and deletion records
Annual review report

policies.title: Referral, Pre-Admission and Admission
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, nursing staff, and all staff involved in referral, screening and admission to any community residence or supervised apartment operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every person is admitted through the proper referral channels, only to a residence the Office of Licensing has approved, within licensed capacity, and with a complete individual file, so that the person's needs, choices and rights are known and can be met from the first day.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits only adults age 21 or older who are eligible for DDD services and Medicaid/NJ FamilyCare and who are referred through DDD and the person's support coordinator. No one is placed in a residence before the NJ DHS Office of Licensing has approved that residence under the license. Occupancy never exceeds the capacity stated on the license for that residence. Admission follows the admission requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4, as required by the procedure manual rule (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2). An individual file is opened at the residence on the day of admission with the identifying information required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9. Admission decisions are based on whether the agency can safely and appropriately meet the person's needs, on the person's own choices, and on compatibility with current residents. They are never based on disability type alone or on a person's exercise of rights. Procedures follow normalization, age appropriateness, least restriction and person-centered planning.

definitions.definition: A residence providing food, shelter, personal guidance and/or training and integration with the community for up to 16 individuals, not located on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution serving a similar population (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
An apartment setting serving up to 4 individuals per apartment, with staff support as described in the program description (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
A person legally appointed by a court to make decisions for an individual, to the extent of the court order (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
The DDD-approved service under which [AGENCY NAME] provides residential supports; it requires that the agency be approved as a DDD provider (DDD Combined Application).
The person or agency assigned through DDD to help the individual plan for, arrange and monitor services.

procedures: The Executive Director (or designee) accepts referrals only from DDD or the person's support coordinator. A person or family who contacts the agency directly is referred to the DDD Community Services Office (800-832-9173) to start eligibility and service authorization. The agency does not place anyone without DDD authorization of Individual Supports.

On receipt of a referral, the Executive Director logs the date, referral source, person's name, and the residence considered on the Referral Log, and acknowledges receipt to the support coordinator in writing.

Before any placement discussion goes further, the Executive Director confirms in writing that (a) the Office of Licensing has approved the specific residence and (b) a vacancy exists within the licensed capacity shown on that residence's license. A copy of the license is attached to the referral file. If either is not met, the referral is declined or deferred and the support coordinator is told the same day.

The Executive Director verifies the person is age 21 or older, has DDD eligibility, has active Medicaid/NJ FamilyCare, and has DDD approval or authorization for Individual Supports. Verification is dated and initialed in the referral file.

The agency requests a referral packet from the support coordinator and guardian: current evaluations, the current service/habilitation plan, medical history, medication list and orders, any behavior support plan, guardianship papers, dietary needs, communication needs, and emergency contacts. Missing items are requested in writing and tracked.

A pre-admission screening team (Executive Director, Residence Supervisor, nurse, and, if a behavior support plan exists, the behavior clinician) reviews the packet. The team documents whether the agency can meet the person's health, behavioral, accessibility, supervision and staff-training needs on every shift, including any specialized training that must be completed before arrival.

The team considers compatibility with current residents and asks current residents for input on a new housemate in a way each resident can understand. Residents' preferences are documented but do not override the new person's right to be considered on a nondiscriminatory basis.

The person (and guardian and family, as the person chooses) is invited to visit the residence, tour it, meet staff and housemates, see available rooms, and ask questions. The visit is documented on the Pre-Admission Visit Form, including the person's own stated preferences and choices.

The Executive Director issues a written decision to the support coordinator, the person and the guardian within 10 business days of receiving a complete packet. If the person is not accepted, the written reason is limited to a documented inability to safely meet needs, no licensed vacancy, or no DDD authorization. A copy is kept in the referral log file.

Before the admission date, the Residence Supervisor ensures: staff are trained on the person's needs and any plans they will implement; prescriber orders and medications are available; adaptive equipment, accessibility features and a bedroom are ready; and a medication reconciliation is arranged with the nurse.

On the day of admission the Residence Supervisor, in language and format the person understands, provides and explains the Division's rights document, the house rules, the grievance procedure, the schedule of charges and fees, and the confidentiality notice, and obtains signed acknowledgments from the person and the guardian where applicable. A person's rights are never limited because the person has a guardian or family.

The Residence Supervisor opens the individual file at the residence and records at minimum: full name, date of birth, sex, Social Security number, Medicaid/insurance numbers, and the date of admission (readmission or transfer, as applicable), plus the signed acknowledgments, guardianship papers, consents and referral packet.

The Residence Supervisor and the person together inventory the person's belongings and any funds brought to the residence; both sign the inventory. Funds are handled under the personal funds policy (IR-06).

The nurse completes an admission health review within 72 hours or as the prescriber and plan require, and medications are administered only by staff who have completed required medication training (HW-01, HW-02).

The Executive Director notifies DDD and the support coordinator of the actual admission date, and the billing staff set up the person's authorization, service record and EVV so services are billed only after admission (GOV-05, GOV-06).

The Residence Supervisor puts an interim support plan in place on day one using the referral packet and the person's preferences, and schedules the Individual Plan meeting within 30 days of admission, or sooner if DDD or the support coordinator requires (PCS-02).

Within 7 days of admission the Executive Director audits the file against the Admission Checklist, signs it, and corrects any gaps. Readmissions and transfers between agency residences follow the same steps and are recorded with their dates in the file.

responsibilities.duty: Verifies licensure approval, licensed capacity and DDD authorization before any placement; issues written decisions; audits each admission file.
Coordinates visits, prepares the residence and staff, conducts the admission day process and maintains the individual file.
Reviews health information, reconciles medications and completes the admission health review.
Welcome the person, follow the interim support plan, and report any concern to the Residence Supervisor.
Set up the authorization and EVV record and bill only from the confirmed admission date.

documentation: Referral Log and referral packet
Copy of the license showing the residence and its capacity
Eligibility and DDD authorization verification
Pre-admission screening team notes and Pre-Admission Visit Form
Written admission or non-admission decision
Signed rights acknowledgments, house rules, grievance and fee notices
Individual file face sheet (name, DOB, sex, SSN, Medicaid/insurance numbers, admission date)
Property and funds inventory
Admission Checklist with Executive Director sign-off

policies.title: Person-Centered Planning and the Individual Plan (IHP/Service Plan)
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, planning team members, nurse, behavior clinician, and Direct Support Professionals
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual has a written plan developed with the person at the center, that it is implemented, reviewed and evaluated, and that it contains all required elements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows this written procedure for developing, implementing, reviewing and evaluating each individual's habilitation or service plan (Individual Habilitation Plan, IHP) as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3 and N.J.S.A. 30:6D-10 et seq. The plan is developed by the planning team led by the individual, built on the person's preferences, strengths and needs, and designed on normalization, age appropriateness, least restriction and person-centered planning. The plan contains all fourteen required elements. The plan and monthly documentation of progress are kept in the individual's record. Planning is conducted at times and places convenient for the person, in the person's preferred language and communication method, with the people the person chooses to invite. This follows the federal person-centered planning requirements for Medicaid home and community-based services.

definitions.definition: The plan of services for an individual and the group of people, including the individual, who develop it (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
The comprehensive written plan with the contents required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(c).
A step toward a goal written so progress can be observed and counted, in the order the steps will be taught or supported.
A court-appointed decision maker, to the extent of the court order (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).

procedures: Within 30 days of admission, or sooner if DDD or the support coordinator requires, the Residence Supervisor schedules the IHP meeting. Thereafter the plan is reviewed at least annually and whenever the person's needs, goals or circumstances change significantly or the person or guardian asks.

The Residence Supervisor asks the person when, where and with whom they want to meet, and sets the meeting accordingly. Invitations go to the person, guardian, family or friends the person chooses, the support coordinator, the nurse, the behavior clinician if applicable, and the Direct Support Professionals who know the person best, at least 10 days in advance.

Before the meeting, the Residence Supervisor gathers evaluations and summaries, the prior plan, monthly progress documentation, incident and health information, and the person's own statements about what is important to them. Material is prepared in plain language or the person's communication format.
At the meeting, the facilitator makes sure the person speaks first and is supported to express choices. Staff do not speak for the person when the person can speak.

The team documents each required element: (1) cover page; (2) evaluation summaries; (3) progress on prior goals; (4) preferences, capabilities and needs; (5) goals; (6) measurable sequential objectives; (7) the method for each objective; (8) team members and responsible persons; (9) services with start dates, duration and frequency; (10) barriers; (11) guardianship review; (12) meeting summary or addendum; (13) attendance sign-off; and (14) authorization for approved individual expenses.

Goals reflect what the person wants, including community integration, relationships, employment interests and control of personal resources, and are written using the least restrictive approach that is safe.
Each objective states who does what, how often, and how progress is measured. The team names the responsible staff person or role for each.
The team identifies barriers (health, transportation, communication, finances, staffing) and who is responsible for addressing each.
The team reviews the person's guardianship status and records whether a guardian's consent is needed for the plan or specific expenses. The person keeps all rights not limited by a court order.
Any disagreement among team members, including the person's, is written in the meeting summary or an addendum with the person's own words wherever possible.

Attendees sign the attendance sheet. Individuals and guardians receive a copy of the plan within 10 days of the meeting. The original is filed in the individual's record at the residence, and a copy is sent to the support coordinator.

Expenses the plan authorizes (for example, adaptive equipment or recreation costs) are listed with the person's or guardian's approval; staff may use the individual's funds only for authorized or person-chosen expenses (IR-06).

Within 5 days of the meeting, the Residence Supervisor trains every Direct Support Professional who will implement the plan, documents the training, and places the objectives and methods in the plan binder or electronic system used on each shift (PCS-03).

Behavior support plans, rights restrictions and health protocols referenced in the plan are reviewed against the plan to confirm they are consistent, least restrictive, and approved through the proper processes (BSP-01, IR-02).

The Residence Supervisor writes a monthly progress summary on each objective, comparing it to the target, and files it in the record. If the person is not progressing or no longer wants the objective, the Residence Supervisor calls a team review rather than waiting for the annual meeting.

The Executive Director reviews a sample of plans each quarter for completeness against the fourteen elements and the quality of person-centered content, and reports findings to the Quality Improvement process (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the planning process is implemented, plans are complete and timely, and audits are done.
Schedules and facilitates the meeting, writes the plan, trains staff, writes monthly summaries and calls reviews as needed.
Leads the planning and decides who participates, to the extent the person chooses.
Provide health and behavioral input and ensure related protocols match the plan.
Contribute what they know about the person, implement the plan and document progress.

documentation: Signed Individual Habilitation Plan with all fourteen elements
Meeting invitations, attendance sign-off and summary or addendum
Evaluation summaries and progress on prior goals
Staff training record on each plan
Monthly progress documentation
Quarterly plan audit tool

policies.title: Implementation of Supports and Daily/Monthly Documentation
policies.applies_to: All Direct Support Professionals, Residence Supervisors, nursing staff and billing staff
policies.purpose: To ensure the supports in each person's plan are actually delivered every day, staff are trained in what they are carrying out, and what happens is documented accurately for the record, for the plan review and for billing.
policies.policy: Staff implement each individual's plan as written. The plan and monthly documentation of progress are kept in the individual's record at the residence (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3 and 2.9). Staff are trained on every plan they implement, including behavior support plans, before they work independently with the person. Staff are on site whenever any individual is present, as supervision needs require (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8). Each shift documents supports, and the in-charge person is named on the schedule. Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) is used for covered service hours through HHAeXchange, and EVV records are reconciled with the staff schedule and daily documentation before billing. Documentation is truthful and timely; falsification is prohibited and results in discipline.

definitions.definition: Entering false information in a record or intentionally altering or omitting information to mislead (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
Information that staff on the next shift must know to support the individuals safely and appropriately (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
An electronic system that records the date, time, location, service, individual and worker for services covered by the federal EVV requirement; DDD uses HHAeXchange for Individual Supports.
Staff who provide direct care, support and training to individuals (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).

procedures: The Residence Supervisor keeps each person's current plan, objectives, methods, health protocols and behavior support plan (if any) in the place staff can reach on every shift, and removes superseded versions.

Before a Direct Support Professional implements a plan, the Residence Supervisor trains the DSP on it, including any behavior support plan, health protocol or specialized support, and documents the training with date, trainer, and DSP signature. A DSP who has not been trained does not implement that part of the plan alone.

The Staff Coverage schedule shows at least two weeks of staff names and the in-charge person for each shift. At least one person on each shift has completed each required specialized training (STF-01, STF-09).

Staff are on site whenever any individual is present at a group home or supervised apartment. When no individual is present, trained, paid agency staff who know the individuals remain reachable by phone for emergencies (STF-08).
At the start of each shift, staff read the Critical Information Log and the notes from the prior shift, and sign that they have done so (PCS-07).
During the shift, staff carry out the daily routine and the objectives scheduled for that day using the method written in the plan, offering choices and never forcing participation in activities.

Staff record the supports and activities provided, the person's response, choices the person made, refusals, community outings, health observations, and any incident on the daily record before the end of the shift. Entries are factual, dated, timed and signed or electronically attributed to the staff person who observed the event. Staff never document for someone else or in advance.
Corrections are made by a single line through the error, with the date and initials; no obliterating, white-out or deletion of original entries.

Staff who clock in for any EVV-covered service use the approved EVV method at the start and end of each visit. If EVV cannot be used (outage, technical issue), staff notify the Residence Supervisor, record the actual times manually, and the correction is entered in HHAeXchange as allowed by DDD within the required window. Live-in workers are handled under the DDD Live-In Worker Attestation only where the worker actually lives with the person served.
The Residence Supervisor reviews each week's daily documentation for completeness, objectives not addressed, refusals, and concerns, and addresses gaps with staff within 3 days.
