By the 10th day of each month, the Residence Supervisor writes the monthly progress summary for each person on each objective, signed and dated, and files it in the individual's record. Any lack of progress, regression or expressed dislike of an objective triggers a team review (PCS-02, PCS-04).

Billing staff compare EVV records, staff schedules and daily documentation before each claim is submitted. A service is billed only if supported by the record. Discrepancies are resolved or the claim is held (GOV-05, GOV-06).
The Executive Director reviews a sample of records monthly for compliance and reports patterns to the Quality Improvement process (GOV-04).

Staff who falsify documentation or EVV entries are subject to discipline up to termination, and the Executive Director evaluates the matter as a possible compliance and abuse/neglect/exploitation concern under the agency's policies (BSP-03, GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Implement plans as trained, document accurately and on time, use EVV correctly and read the Critical Information Log.
Trains staff on plans, reviews weekly documentation, writes monthly summaries and keeps plans accessible.
Reconcile EVV, schedules and documentation before billing and correct or hold discrepancies.
Audits records, ensures coverage and training requirements are met and addresses falsification.

documentation: Daily records / shift notes
Monthly progress summaries in the individual record
Staff training records on each plan
Two-week staff schedule with in-charge named
Critical Information Log sign-offs
EVV records and reconciliation reports
Monthly record audit tool

policies.title: Changes in Supports and Services
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, nurse, planning team members and Direct Support Professionals
policies.purpose: To make sure any change in an individual's supports or services is based on the person's needs and choices, is made through the planning team, is reflected in the written plan, and is communicated to everyone who needs to know before it takes effect.
policies.policy: Changes in the amount, type, frequency, provider or setting of an individual's supports are made only through the person-centered planning process, using the least restrictive approach and respecting the person's choices. Changes that involve admission, transfer or discharge follow the admission requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4 (see PCS-01 and PCS-06). The plan is updated in writing before or at the time a change takes effect, and the individual, guardian, support coordinator, and DDD (where required) are told. An emergency change needed to protect health or safety is allowed immediately and reviewed by the team as soon as possible. A change is never used as discipline, and a person's exercise of rights is never a reason for reducing services. The procedure is reviewed annually as part of the procedure manual.

definitions.definition: Any increase, decrease, addition, removal or substitution in a service, staffing level, supervision level, schedule, equipment, or setting described in the person's plan.
The individual and the people who develop and review the person's plan, including guardian, support coordinator, and staff.
A temporary change made without prior team meeting because it is necessary to protect the health or safety of the person or others.
The DDD-assigned person or agency who helps the individual plan and monitor services.

procedures: Any staff member, the person, guardian, family, nurse or support coordinator may ask for a change. The staff member who receives the request records it on the Change Request Form the same day and gives it to the Residence Supervisor.

The Residence Supervisor reviews the request within 3 business days, asks the person what they want and why, and gathers relevant information (health, incidents, progress summaries, clinical recommendations).

The Residence Supervisor informs the guardian and support coordinator that a change is being considered and schedules a team meeting at a time and place convenient for the person. The meeting occurs within 14 days, or sooner if the need is urgent.

At the meeting the team considers whether the change is needed, what the person prefers, the least restrictive alternatives tried, risks and benefits, who is responsible, and the date it will start. Disagreement, including the person's, is recorded in the meeting summary.

If the change would restrict a right or limit a choice, it is not implemented until it has gone through the rights restriction and Human Rights Committee processes (IR-02, IR-03). If it involves a new or revised behavior support plan, it follows BSP-01.
The nurse reviews any change affecting health, diet, medication, equipment or supervision and writes any needed protocol or order request (HW-02).
The Residence Supervisor updates the plan in writing, including services, start dates, duration and frequency, and responsible persons; the guardian and person sign or the refusal is noted.

The Executive Director confirms whether the change requires a DDD authorization or approval (for example, a change in service amounts or staffing that affects the authorized services or rates) and submits the request through the support coordinator or DDD before implementing, where required. Billing staff are told so claims match the authorization (GOV-05).

Before the effective date, the Residence Supervisor notifies the person, guardian, support coordinator and all staff in writing, and trains staff on the changed plan, documenting the training (PCS-03).
The Residence Supervisor adds anything staff must know immediately to the Critical Information Log (PCS-07).

For an emergency change, the in-charge staff or Residence Supervisor makes the minimum necessary change, notifies the Executive Director immediately, and notifies the guardian and support coordinator within 24 hours. The team meets within 5 business days to decide whether the change continues, ends or is modified.

If the person or guardian objects to a change, the Residence Supervisor explains the right to file a grievance and to ask the support coordinator or DDD for help, and the objection is documented (IR-04).

Thirty days after implementation, the Residence Supervisor reviews how the change is working with the person and records the result in the monthly progress summary; the team revises or reverses the change if it is not helping.
Change Request Forms and decisions are filed in the individual record and are reviewed quarterly by the Executive Director for patterns and quality improvement (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves changes affecting authorizations, staffing or budget; ensures DDD notifications; reviews trends.
Receives requests, convenes the team, updates the plan, notifies everyone and trains staff.
Reviews health-related changes and prepares orders or protocols.
Bring needs and concerns forward, follow the updated plan once trained.

documentation: Change Request Form
Team meeting summary with any disagreements
Updated plan pages with signatures
Notifications to guardian, support coordinator and DDD
Staff training record
30-day review note
Emergency change report, if applicable

policies.title: Community Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, planning team members and Direct Support Professionals
policies.purpose: To ensure that each person lives as a full member of the community: choosing activities, relationships, work and daily schedule, and having the training and support to do so.
policies.policy: A community residence provides food, shelter, personal guidance and/or training, and integration with the community (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3). [AGENCY NAME] supports each person to participate in the community to the same degree as people who do not receive services, including having the opportunity to seek competitive integrated employment, engage in community life, and control personal resources, consistent with the HCBS settings requirements under the NJ FamilyCare Comprehensive Demonstration and the Statewide Transition Plan that apply to N.J.A.C. 10:44A homes. Individuals receive training and support to understand options, make choices and exercise rights, and rights are never limited because a person has a guardian or family (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1). Exercising choices is never a cause for retribution. Each person's preferences and activities are documented in the person's plan.

definitions.definition: Active participation in the broader community (work, shopping, worship, recreation, volunteering, relationships) alongside people without disabilities.
Work in the community for at least minimum wage alongside coworkers without disabilities.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, a residence not on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution serving a similar population.
A decision the person makes about their own life with accurate information and support, as the person understands it.

procedures: During plan development and at each annual review, the Residence Supervisor asks each person, in the way the person communicates best, about interests, work, school, volunteer, spiritual, social and recreational goals, and who they want to spend time with. Answers are written in the plan in the person's words (PCS-02).

The planning team discusses employment with each person of working age at least annually: whether the person wants a job, what kind, the benefits of employment, and how supports can help. The discussion and the person's decision are documented, including a decision not to seek work. The Residence Supervisor offers referral to DDD employment supports through the support coordinator and, if the person wishes, helps to make contact.

The Residence Supervisor makes sure the residence staffing and weekly schedule allow each person to go to work, day programs, activities and appointments of the person's choice, and that transportation is arranged (HES-05).
Each person has a personalized weekly schedule written with the person, not a uniform house schedule. Staff do not require attendance at group activities and offer alternatives.

Staff support each person to use community resources of their choice: shops, restaurants, libraries, parks, houses of worship, community groups, public transportation, and to meet people outside the residence. The outings, who chose them, and how the person responded are recorded in the daily record (PCS-03).

Individuals decide their own visitors, phone and internet use, mealtimes and snacks, bedtime and wake time, and personal space decoration, subject only to a documented, individually based restriction approved under the rights restriction process (IR-01, IR-02).

Staff teach and support the skills a person wants to build (money management, travel, communication, self-advocacy) with the method written in the plan, and give each person information about options in a form they understand (IR-09).
The person controls their own money to the extent of their ability and any court order; staff support budgeting and spending choices and do not use a person's funds without authorization (IR-06).

The Executive Director makes sure the residence and any supervised apartment sites stay integrated in ordinary neighborhoods and that signage, vehicles, and practices do not mark the home as an institution.

The Residence Supervisor reviews, at least quarterly, each person's community participation and employment progress against the plan, speaks with the person about whether they are satisfied, and calls a team meeting if participation is limited by staffing, transportation or other barriers (PCS-04).
Staff who restrict, discourage or punish a person for making a choice are subject to discipline; the concern is addressed as a rights matter (IR-01, STF-06).
The Executive Director reports community integration and employment participation measures to the Quality Improvement process quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures staffing, transportation and policies support community integration and employment choice; monitors results.
Develops individual schedules and goals with each person, documents employment discussions and reviews participation.
Support outings, work and activities of the person's choice and document them.
Considers employment and community participation at each plan meeting and reduces barriers.

documentation: Preferences and goals pages in the plan
Annual employment discussion note
Individual weekly schedule
Daily records of community activities
Quarterly participation review
Rights restriction documentation, if any

policies.title: Transition, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, nurse, planning team members and billing/records staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a person moves, is transferred or leaves, the transition is planned with the person, the person's rights and protections are honored, supports continue without gaps, and records and personal property are handled correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not terminate services or require a person to leave the residence except through a planned process described here. Dates of discharge or transfer are recorded in the individual file (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9). Eviction means the actual expulsion of a person from the premises (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3). Any involuntary discharge follows the discharge requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4, DDD requirements, and the federal protection that individuals in provider-owned or controlled residential settings have the same responsibilities and protections from eviction that tenants have under landlord-tenant law. Before issuing any involuntary discharge notice, the Executive Director confirms the notice period and appeal rights currently in effect with the Office of Licensing and DDD. Discharge is a last resort after the agency has tried reasonable alternatives. The person is never discharged because of exercising rights or filing a complaint, and the person's health and safety are protected throughout. The agency coordinates every transition with the guardian, the support coordinator and DDD.

definitions.definition: The actual expulsion of an individual from the premises (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
A move chosen by the person (or guardian) to another residence, home, or service.
A discharge initiated by the agency, not requested by the person or guardian.
A written plan for the move that covers supports, health, medications, belongings, funds, records and the new provider.

procedures: Voluntary transition: when a person or guardian says they want to move, the staff member records the request the same day and tells the Residence Supervisor. The Residence Supervisor notifies the Executive Director and the support coordinator within 1 business day and convenes the team within 10 days.

Involuntary discharge may be considered only if (a) the agency can no longer safely meet the person's documented needs despite documented efforts, including added supports and clinical consultation, (b) the person's presence poses a documented danger to others that cannot be reduced, (c) services are no longer authorized or paid and no alternative is available, or (d) the residence is closing or losing its license. The Executive Director documents which reason applies and the alternatives tried.

Before issuing a notice, the Executive Director consults the Governing Authority, the support coordinator, DDD, and, as needed, the Office of Licensing, and confirms the notice period and appeal rights currently required. The agency does not move a person without these steps and without a safe, agreed destination.

The Executive Director issues a written notice to the person (in an understandable format), the guardian, the support coordinator and DDD within the required period, stating the reason, the planned date, where and how to appeal or file a grievance, and who can help (IR-04). The notice is explained to the person in person.

The team convenes to develop a written transition plan. The plan includes the person's preferences for the new setting, the visits the person will make, the new provider's readiness, transportation, supports during and after the move, and how the person will keep friends and community connections.

The nurse prepares a health transfer summary: diagnoses, allergies, medication list and last administration times, prescriber orders, diet and swallowing needs, seizure or other protocols, equipment, upcoming appointments, and immunization and TB records. Medications and supplies leave with the person according to the medication policy (HW-01).

The Residence Supervisor ensures the new provider receives, with proper consent or authority, the current plan, behavior support plan, rights documents and relevant records, and arranges a direct staff-to-staff handoff. Information is released only as allowed by the confidentiality policy (IR-05).

The person's personal funds, valuables and belongings are inventoried with the person and guardian, compared to the admission and ongoing inventories, and returned or transferred to the person or authorized representative with signed receipt within the time allowed by the personal funds policy. Any accounts or benefits are closed or transferred according to IR-06.

The Executive Director notifies DDD and the support coordinator of the planned and actual dates of discharge or transfer. Billing staff end the service authorization and EVV as of the actual date and bill only for services delivered (GOV-05, GOV-06).

The Residence Supervisor records the discharge or transfer date, destination and reason in the individual file, completes a discharge summary within 7 days, and gets the person's and guardian's acknowledgment of the transition plan, or notes their refusal.

Emergency transfers to a hospital are not discharges; the person's bed is held in accordance with DDD requirements and the agency's admission agreement unless a planned discharge process is completed (HW-04).
In the event of the person's death, the death policy applies, not this policy (HW-05).

The Executive Director reviews all involuntary discharges and discharges due to behavioral or health needs in the Quality Improvement process to identify system improvements (GOV-04). Records are retained under the record retention policy (REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Decides on and signs any involuntary discharge notice after consultation; notifies DDD; ensures safe transition.
Coordinates the transition plan, inventories belongings, completes the discharge summary and hand-off.
Prepares the health transfer summary and medication hand-off.
End authorizations and EVV, and secure and retain the record.
Is informed of every involuntary discharge and reviews it.

documentation: Request to move or discharge decision documentation
Alternatives tried and basis for any involuntary discharge
Written notice and proof of delivery
Transition plan and attendance sign-in
Health transfer summary and medication hand-off record
Inventory and receipt of funds and belongings
Notification to DDD and support coordinator
Discharge summary and file entry of discharge/transfer date
Quality Improvement review notes

policies.title: Shift Communication and Critical Information Log
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, in-charge staff, Residence Supervisors, nursing personnel and administrative staff at every community residence and supervised apartment operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure information that affects an individual's health, safety or supports is passed from shift to shift and is reviewed and followed up by management. The policy also meets the requirement that the procedure manual include a separate internal communication log of critical information (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)14).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a separate internal communication/critical-information log at each residence. It is kept apart from individuals' records. Staff enter all critical information in it as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, and enter the licensee's or designee's follow-up. Every entry is dated and signed with the staff member's full name. Staff review the log at the start of each shift and before leaving a shift. The log is not a substitute for daily documentation in the individual's record, an incident report, or a call to 9-1-1 or a supervisor when one is required. Staff who see critical information must make the entry on the same shift. The log is written in factual, respectful, person-first language and contains only the information needed to carry out supports.

definitions.definition: As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, information that affects an individual's health, safety or supports and must be communicated to staff on later shifts and to management. It includes unexpected behavioral outbursts, unexplained mood swings, PRN medication given, transportation problems, unexpected doctor or hospital visits, routine visits needing follow-up, reportable communicable diseases and missed medical appointments.
The bound or controlled electronic log, kept separate from individual records, in which critical information and the licensee's follow-up are entered.
The action taken by the Residence Supervisor, Executive Director, nurse or designee in response to a log entry, with the date and the name of the person who took it.
The staff member designated for the shift under STF-01 who is responsible for the residence during that shift.

procedures: The Residence Supervisor sets up one communication log for each residence or supervised apartment site. Pages are numbered and the log is labeled 'Communication/Critical Information Log - Not Part of Individual Record.'
The log is kept in a designated, secure staff-only location at the residence and is not stored in or filed with any individual's record.
At the start of each shift, every staff member reads all entries made since their last shift and initials or signs a review line in the log.

The outgoing in-charge staff member gives the oncoming in-charge staff member a verbal report on each individual's status, with attention to entries from the past 24 hours, before leaving. The oncoming staff member does not assume responsibility until this report is complete.

Staff enter critical information the same shift in which it occurs or is learned. Entry categories include: unexpected behavioral outbursts; unexplained mood swings; PRN medication given (name, dose, time, reason, result); transportation problems; unexpected doctor or hospital visits; routine visits needing follow-up; reportable communicable diseases; and missed medical appointments.

Each entry shows the date, the time, the individual's name or initials as the residence has defined them, and a factual description of what was seen, heard or done. Staff write what they observed, not opinions or labels.
Each entry is signed with the staff member's full name, not initials alone. Staff do not enter on behalf of another person unless they say so in the entry and sign their own name.

Staff correct mistakes by drawing a single line through the error, writing 'error,' and dating and signing. White-out, erasure and removal of pages are prohibited. Staff may not alter or backdate entries (see GOV-05 on falsification).

When an entry involves a possible reportable incident, abuse, neglect, exploitation, a missing person, or a medical emergency, staff first follow BSP-03, BSP-04, BSP-05 or HW-04. They then record the critical information in the log and note that the incident procedure was started.

The in-charge staff member notifies the Residence Supervisor, or the on-call administrator under STF-08 after hours, of any entry that needs same-day management action. The notice is made by phone to [PHONE], and the call is noted in the log.

The Residence Supervisor reviews the log at least once each workday that the Supervisor is on site, and at least weekly if the Supervisor is not on site daily. The Supervisor records follow-up beside each entry, with the date and full signature.

Follow-up includes making or confirming a medical appointment, notifying the nurse, guardian or planning team, requesting review of a behavior support plan, or referring the matter to the incident process. Follow-up that is open stays on a 'pending' line until it is closed.

The nurse reviews entries involving PRN medication, communicable disease, unexpected medical visits and missed appointments under HW-02. The nurse documents recommendations in the log or the health record.

The Executive Director or designee reviews a sample of log pages at least monthly. Patterns such as repeated PRN use, repeated behavioral outbursts, missed appointments or transport problems go to the CQI process under GOV-04.

When a log is full, it is retained in the administrative office for the period required under REC-01 and kept available for the Office of Licensing inspection. New staff are trained on this policy during orientation under STF-03.

responsibilities.duty: Reads the log at each shift start, enters critical information the same shift, signs entries with full name, and gives and receives a verbal shift report.
Makes sure the shift report is completed, notifies the Residence Supervisor or on-call administrator of urgent entries, and confirms that all critical information from the shift is logged.
Maintains the log, reviews it at the set frequency, records dated and signed follow-up, and trains staff on proper entries.
Reviews health-related entries, advises on follow-up and documents recommendations.
Reviews log samples monthly, addresses gaps in entries or follow-up, and sends trends to the CQI team.

documentation: Communication/critical-information log with dated, fully signed entries and signed follow-up
Staff shift-start review signatures or initials
Monthly Executive Director or designee log review note
Record of staff training on this policy
Cross-references to incident reports or individual record notes when they were also required

policies.title: Medication Administration, Self-Medication and Staff Competency
policies.applies_to: All staff who assist with, supervise or administer medication; Residence Supervisors; nursing personnel; the Executive Director; and all individuals served who take medication
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals receive medication safely and exactly as prescribed, that they self-administer as far as they are able, and that only trained and competent staff give or assist with medication. The policy also meets the requirement that the procedure manual include medication administration and self-medication procedures (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)17).
policies.policy: Individuals self-administer their medication to the extent possible, as determined by the planning team and documented in the individual's record (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(a)). When an individual cannot self-administer, [AGENCY NAME] or its designee assists and supervises administration as prescribed (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(b)). Staff complete medication training and demonstrate competency before administering any medication, and show competency again at least annually (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(b)). A record is kept of all medication administered, including the individual's name, the date and the name of the medication (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(c)). [AGENCY NAME] follows the current Subchapter 5 health and safety requirements (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.1 to 5.8) for medications and gives PRN doses only according to a complete label and a prescriber's order. Medication is prescribed by a licensed prescriber, which may include an Advanced Practice Nurse. Medication is never used as punishment, for staff convenience, or as a substitute for needed supports.

definitions.definition: The individual takes medication independently or with the level of cueing or supervision set by the planning team and recorded in the record.
Staff trained and shown competent in medication administration help the individual take medication as prescribed and document it.

Medication given as needed under a prescriber's order. The label must show the individual's name, date, medication, dosage, interval, maximum amount per 24 hours, stop date where appropriate, and the conditions for giving it (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(c)).
The record of every medication given or refused, with the individual's name, the date, the medication name and the staff member's signature, kept as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2(c).
Observed and documented ability of a staff member to perform medication tasks correctly, shown before first administration and annually.

procedures: Before any individual self-administers, the planning team assesses the individual's ability, considering knowledge of what each medication is for, ability to take the right dose at the right time, and safe storage. The team decides the level of support: independent, cueing/supervision, or staff administration. The decision is documented in the individual's plan and file.

The nurse or Residence Supervisor reviews each individual's self-medication status at least annually and when the individual's condition, medication or skills change. Changes go to the planning team and are recorded.

No staff member may give or assist with any medication until medication training is complete, competency has been demonstrated and recorded, and the Residence Supervisor has confirmed this in writing. Competency is re-shown at least annually before the previous one expires.
Medication training records, including dated trainer and trainee signatures, the curriculum and competency results, are kept in the administrative office per N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(e).
A staff member who fails a competency check does not give medication until retrained and found competent. The Residence Supervisor documents retraining.

On receipt of a new or changed medication order, the staff member confirms it against the prescriber's order, the pharmacy label and the MAR. Any discrepancy is reported to the nurse or Residence Supervisor before the dose is given.

Before each dose, staff check the individual, medication, dose, route, time and date against the label and MAR. Staff confirm allergies, and wash hands. Staff stay with the individual until the dose is taken.

Staff record each dose on the MAR immediately after it is given or taken, with their signature. Staff never pre-charting or sign for a dose they did not observe. Refused doses are recorded as refused with the reason, and the nurse or prescriber is notified when the refusal is clinically significant.

Medication for each person is kept in its original labeled container, in a locked storage area, with controlled substances double-locked and counted each shift by two staff with both signing the count. Refrigerated medication is stored in a locked container in the refrigerator. Oral drops are stored separately from eye, ear and other non-oral drops.

PRN medication is given only when the conditions on the label are met, within the interval and the 24-hour maximum, and before any stop date. The staff member records time, reason, dose and result on the MAR. If the individual's response is not as expected, staff call the prescriber or nurse.
Each PRN dose is entered in the communication/critical-information log and reported to the oncoming shift as critical information (see PCS-07).

Over-the-counter products are given only as ordered or approved by a prescriber and as described in HW-06. Where a manufacturer's label is acceptable under current DHS requirements, the label is read against the written order before the first dose.

Medication errors, including wrong dose, wrong time, wrong individual, omitted dose or wrong route, are reported immediately to the nurse and Residence Supervisor. Staff follow the prescriber's or poison control's direction, document the error and the response, and start an incident report under BSP-04. Staff call 9-1-1 for any life-threatening reaction (see HW-04).

Medications that are discontinued, expired, or refused by the individual and no longer needed are removed from use and disposed of in a way that is documented and witnessed by two staff. The record shows the name, amount, date and disposal method.

When an individual goes on an outing, home visit or day program, medication is sent in a labeled container with written instructions, and a log signed by the staff member and the receiving person shows what was sent and returned.

The nurse or Residence Supervisor reviews MARs at least monthly for gaps, refusals and PRN patterns and reports findings to the Executive Director and the CQI process (GOV-04). Individuals' medications are reviewed with their prescribers at least annually and as required by the plan.
Medication labels, storage and MARs are checked monthly by a designated staff member. Findings are documented and corrected within five business days.

responsibilities.duty: Takes part in decisions about medication, self-administers to the extent possible, and reports side effects or concerns.
Gives or assists with medication only after training and competency, follows the five checks, records every dose, reports errors and PRN use.
Confirms staff competency before first administration, reviews MARs and storage, and reports errors.
Provides medication training and competency checks, reviews orders and self-medication assessments, and advises on errors.
Determines the extent to which the individual can self-administer and documents it.
Makes sure this policy is carried out, resources are available, and findings are sent to CQI.

documentation: Self-medication assessment and planning team decision in the individual file
Medication Administration Record with the name, date and medication name for every dose, and staff signatures
PRN label information and documentation of reason and result for each dose
Staff medication training records and annual competency checklists with dated trainer and trainee signatures
Controlled substance count sheets
Medication error and incident reports
Disposal records
Critical-information log entries for PRN doses
Monthly MAR and storage review notes

policies.title: Nursing Oversight and Health Care Coordination
policies.applies_to: Nursing personnel, the Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, direct support professionals and planning team members at all [AGENCY NAME] residences
policies.purpose: To make sure each individual's health care needs are identified, scheduled, followed up and carried out, and that health tasks requiring nursing skill are done only by nursing personnel or under nursing delegation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides health care coordination for every individual, including routine and follow-up care consistent with the health and safety standards in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.1 to 5.8. Although N.J.A.C. 10:44A does not require a nurse consultant, [AGENCY NAME] retains a licensed registered nurse ('Nurse') to oversee medication practice, delegation, and the review of health care plans. Feeding tube responsibilities are delegated to nursing personnel (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)). Direct support professionals are not to perform feeding tube care or any other nursing task unless nursing personnel have trained, delegated and supervised them under the NJ Nurse Practice Act. Missed or unexpected medical visits are critical information. Individuals choose their own health care providers to the extent possible and take part in all decisions about their health.

definitions.definition: A registered nurse licensed in New Jersey who is employed or contracted by [AGENCY NAME] to provide nursing oversight.
Scheduling, transport, accompaniment, information sharing and follow-up that make sure the individual receives routine, preventive, specialty and follow-up care.
The Nurse's documented assignment of a nursing task to a trained staff member where permitted by the NJ Nurse Practice Act.

As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. For this policy it includes unexpected doctor or hospital visits, routine visits needing follow-up, reportable communicable diseases and missed medical appointments.

procedures: The Executive Director appoints or contracts with a Nurse and records the Nurse's name, license number, role and contact information in the table of organization. The Nurse's role covers medication oversight, delegation, review of health care plans, staff health training and advice on changes of condition.

At admission, the Nurse or a designee gathers the individual's health history, diagnoses, allergies, medications, treatments, equipment, diet, immunizations, providers and last examinations. This information is entered in the individual file under PCS-01 and REC-01.
The planning team records each individual's health needs and care schedule in the person-centered plan under PCS-02, including the individual's own preferences about providers and care.

Each individual has a primary care provider and, where needed, a dentist and specialists, chosen by the individual or guardian. The Residence Supervisor keeps a health care calendar of routine, preventive and follow-up visits for each person.

Staff accompany or arrange transport for the individual to each appointment, bring the current medication list, recent incident or change-of-condition notes, and questions from the individual. The individual's own concerns are voiced first.

After each visit, the staff member records the date, provider, findings, orders and next appointment in the health record, and gives the visit summary to the Residence Supervisor and the Nurse the same day. Orders go to the MAR or care plan per HW-01.

Any routine visit that needs a follow-up is entered in the communication/critical-information log. The Residence Supervisor schedules the follow-up and records the date. Any unexpected doctor or hospital visit is entered in the log and reviewed under BSP-04 to decide whether it is also a reportable incident.

When an appointment is missed or cancelled for any reason, staff enter it in the log the same day, tell the Residence Supervisor, and reschedule within [NUMBER] business days or sooner when the provider or Nurse says so. The reason is documented and any risk to the individual is assessed by the Nurse.

Feeding tube care, including tube feedings, site care and flushes, is done only by nursing personnel or by staff to whom the Nurse has delegated the task, taught and checked in writing. The delegation, the competency check and the date are filed in the training record.

The Nurse reviews each individual's health care plan, medication list and diet orders at least [FREQUENCY] and when there is a change in condition, new diagnosis, hospitalization or medication change. The Nurse documents the review and gives recommendations to the planning team.

The Nurse provides or approves training on health topics under HW-01 and HW-03 and checks staff competency on assigned health tasks. Training is arranged as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 and STF-09.

Staff report suspected or confirmed reportable communicable diseases to the Residence Supervisor and the Nurse immediately. The Nurse directs precautions under HES-03 and the Executive Director makes reports under REC-02 as required.

The Nurse is reachable through [PHONE] for questions during and after hours, or the Residence Supervisor uses the on-call procedure in STF-08 if the Nurse cannot be reached. A life-threatening emergency is always a call to 9-1-1 first (HW-04).
Guardians and family members, where the individual agrees, are told about significant health changes, hospital visits and new orders in line with IR-05 and IR-10.
The Nurse reports health trends such as repeated missed appointments, falls, infections, PRN use and weight changes to the CQI process each quarter under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees medication practice, delegates and checks nursing tasks, reviews health plans, advises on changes of condition and reports health trends.
Keeps the health care calendar, makes sure appointments happen, records follow-up and logs missed appointments.
Supports the individual at appointments, records visit results, follows orders and reports changes and missed visits.
Builds health needs and preferences into the plan and acts on Nurse recommendations.
Maintains nursing coverage, defines the Nurse's role in writing and makes sure delegation limits are followed.

documentation: Nurse role description and delegation records
Health history and health care plan in the individual file
Health care calendar and appointment records
Visit summaries and orders
Critical-information log entries for unexpected visits, follow-up visits and missed appointments
Nurse review notes and recommendations
Training and competency records for delegated tasks

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, Residence Supervisors and nursing personnel who support individuals with seizure disorders, choking or swallowing risks, physical disabilities or other identified medical needs
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals' health is observed daily, that written individual protocols exist for seizures and choking, and that staff are trained to carry them out on every shift.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] monitors each individual's health according to the needs recorded in the individual's plan. Staff who work with individuals who have seizure disorders, physical disabilities or other identified medical needs complete specific training within 90 days of employment (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)). Required training includes specialized feeding techniques, mobility devices and safe transport, seizure, physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans. [AGENCY NAME] makes sure at least one trained person is on every shift for each specialized need of the individuals in the residence. Each individual with a seizure disorder or choking or swallowing risk has a written individual protocol in the plan and file. Staff follow Subchapter 5 health and safety standards (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.1 to 5.8). A life-threatening emergency is always a 9-1-1 call (HW-04).

definitions.definition: A written, individual-specific set of instructions, written with the Nurse and approved by the planning team and prescriber where needed, that tells staff what to watch for and what to do.

Training in feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure, physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans, completed within 90 days of employment (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d)).
A sudden episode of abnormal brain activity that may cause changes in awareness, movement or behavior.
A documented risk of airway blockage because of swallowing difficulty, diet texture, eating pace or other factors.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, including unexpected medical visits and PRN medication given.

procedures: At admission and at each plan review, the Nurse and planning team identify each person's health monitoring needs, including seizure history, swallowing and choking risk, mobility, skin, weight, hydration, bowel function, sleep and pain.

Staff observe and record the health indicators set in the plan, such as seizure activity, meals eaten, fluids, bowel movements, skin checks, weight and vital signs. Entries go in the daily record under PCS-03.

For each person with a seizure disorder, the Nurse writes a seizure protocol with the prescriber's input. It lists seizure types, triggers, what to do during and after a seizure, when to give any ordered rescue medication, how long to observe, and the point at which staff call 9-1-1 and the Nurse.

For each person with a choking or swallowing risk, the Nurse, with the planning team and, where needed, a speech-language pathologist or physician, writes a choking protocol. It covers diet texture, liquid consistency, positioning, pacing, supervision during meals, equipment, and first aid for choking. Modified diet orders are carried out under HES-04.
Protocols are filed in the individual's record and posted or kept where staff can reach them at once on every shift. Posting is done in a way that respects the individual's privacy under IR-05.

Each new direct support professional receives specialized training in feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure, physical and medical needs, mental health needs and behavior support plans within 90 days of employment. Training is documented per N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(e) and STF-09.
Before working alone with an individual who has a protocol, a staff member must be shown the protocol, have the questions answered, and sign that they have read it.

The Residence Supervisor checks each two-week schedule under STF-01 to make sure at least one person trained in each required specialized area is on every shift. When there is no trained person, the Supervisor changes the schedule or arranges coverage under STF-08 before the shift begins.

During a seizure, staff keep the individual safe, note the time it started and ended, stay with the person, and follow the protocol. Staff call 9-1-1 right away if the protocol says to, if the seizure is longer than the protocol allows, if the person is injured or has trouble breathing, or if staff are not sure.
During choking, staff give first aid as trained, call 9-1-1 right away when the person cannot breathe, cough or speak, and stay with the person until emergency responders arrive (HW-04).

After every seizure, choking event, fall or other health event, staff record what happened, the time, duration, response and recovery in the daily record, tell the Residence Supervisor and the Nurse, and enter it in the communication/critical-information log as needed. Events that meet incident criteria go through BSP-04.
Staff who help individuals use wheelchairs, walkers or other mobility devices check that equipment works, brakes and belts are used, and that transport is done safely under HES-05.
The Nurse reviews seizure and choking events at least [FREQUENCY], and after every event. If a pattern appears, the Nurse notifies the prescriber and the planning team, and protocols are updated.
Staff refresh their knowledge of protocols at least annually and whenever a protocol changes. Records of the review are kept in the personnel file.
Monitoring data and events are summarized for the CQI process each quarter under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Completes specialized training, reads and follows protocols, observes and records health indicators, calls 9-1-1 when needed and reports events.
Makes sure a trained person is on every shift, keeps protocols current and available, and follows up on events.
Writes and updates seizure and choking protocols, trains staff, reviews events and advises prescribers and the planning team.
Approves protocols, supports the individual's preferences and updates the plan when needs change.
Makes sure training and staffing resources are in place.

documentation: Individual seizure and choking protocols in the plan and file
Staff acknowledgment of protocol review
Specialized training records with dated trainer and trainee signatures
Two-week schedules showing trained coverage per shift
Daily health monitoring records and event notes
Critical-information log entries and incident reports where applicable
Nurse event reviews

policies.title: Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care (Danielle's Law)
policies.applies_to: All staff, including temporary agency staff, who work at or supervise a [AGENCY NAME] residence
policies.purpose: To make sure staff recognize a change in an individual's condition, call 9-1-1 at once for any life-threatening emergency as required by Danielle's Law (N.J.S.A. 30:6D-5.1 et seq.; N.J.A.C. 10:42A), and give correct first aid and follow-up.
policies.policy: Staff must call 9-1-1 immediately for any life-threatening emergency, before making any other call, as required by Danielle's Law, N.J.S.A. 30:6D-5.1 et seq., and N.J.A.C. 10:42A (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)6). No staff member needs permission to call 9-1-1, and no one may tell staff to wait. Staff do not delay a 9-1-1 call to reach a supervisor, nurse, guardian or on-call person. When staff are unsure whether an emergency is life-threatening, they call 9-1-1. Every direct support professional holds current first aid and CPR certification from an ECC-compliant entity (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(a)). Emergency coverage and on-call procedures are in STF-08. Unexpected doctor or hospital visits are critical information (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3) and may also be reportable incidents.

definitions.definition: A situation in which an individual shows signs of a condition that could cause death or serious permanent harm without immediate medical care, such as not breathing, no pulse, unconsciousness, choking, severe bleeding, signs of stroke or heart attack, prolonged or repeated seizures, or a severe allergic reaction. If in doubt, treat it as life-threatening.
Any new or worsening physical, mental, behavioral or functional sign or symptom, such as fever, new pain, confusion, loss of appetite, new weakness or sudden mood change.
A first aid and CPR training provider whose courses meet the Emergency Cardiovascular Care guidelines, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(a).
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. It includes unexpected doctor or hospital visits.

procedures: When staff see signs of a possible life-threatening emergency, they call 9-1-1 immediately. The call comes before any other notification, and before calling a supervisor, nurse, or guardian.
Staff give the 9-1-1 dispatcher the address, the individual's name, what happened, the person's condition and any known allergies or diagnoses, and stay on the line until told to hang up.

While waiting for responders, staff give first aid and CPR as trained and follow any individual protocol, such as the seizure or choking protocol in HW-03. If more than one staff member is present, one calls and one gives care. The other individuals in the home are supervised and kept calm.

A staff member unlocks and opens the door, turns on lights and sends someone to meet responders. Staff collect the individual's current medication list or MAR, face sheet, guardian and physician contacts, and insurance card, and give them to the responders.

A staff member goes with the individual to the hospital, or follows as quickly as coverage permits, and stays until relieved or a guardian or representative arrives. Staffing at the residence is maintained under STF-01 and STF-08.

As soon as the 9-1-1 call is made and the individual is safe, staff notify the Residence Supervisor or the on-call administrator at [PHONE], then the Nurse, and then the guardian or designated contact as required by IR-10. Each notice is documented with the time and the person told.

For a change of condition that is not life-threatening, staff check and record the person's signs, call the Nurse or the individual's physician for direction, and follow it. If the condition worsens or the Nurse cannot be reached and staff are concerned, staff call 9-1-1 or take the person to emergency care.

Staff record the change of condition in the daily record, including what was seen, the time, who was called, and what instructions were given. Staff add the entry to the communication/critical-information log under PCS-07 so later shifts are told.

Every unexpected doctor, urgent care or hospital visit is entered in the log as critical information. The Residence Supervisor decides, with the Executive Director, whether the event is a reportable incident under BSP-04 and makes reports as required under REC-02.

After a hospital visit or admission, staff obtain discharge instructions, new orders and medication changes, give them to the Nurse, update the MAR and plan under HW-01 and PCS-04, and arrange any follow-up visit.
If the individual dies, staff follow HW-05 immediately.

First aid and CPR certificates are checked at hire and tracked for expiration. Staff may not work unsupervised after certification expires, and the Residence Supervisor keeps a current tracking list. New direct support professionals complete first aid and CPR within the 90 days permitted by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(a), and [AGENCY NAME] schedules shifts so that at least one staff member on each shift holds current certification, to the extent possible during that period.

The Executive Director reviews each emergency call within [NUMBER] business days. The review looks at response time, whether 9-1-1 was called first, first aid given, notifications and documentation. Findings go to the CQI team under GOV-04.

Danielle's Law and this policy are covered in orientation and at least annually. Staff sign that they understand that they must call 9-1-1 for any life-threatening emergency. Staff who do not call 9-1-1 as required face discipline and referral to the proper authorities.

responsibilities.duty: Calls 9-1-1 immediately for a life-threatening emergency, gives first aid and CPR, accompanies the individual, documents and notifies.
Directs the response, assigns roles, keeps other individuals safe and makes the required notifications.
Confirms follow-up care, reviews documentation, tracks first aid and CPR and decides on incident reports.
Gives guidance on changes of condition, reviews discharge orders and updates health plans.
Makes sure Danielle's Law is followed, reviews each emergency and makes required reports.

documentation: Daily record entries on change of condition and emergency care
Communication/critical-information log entries
Incident report where applicable
Notification record with times and persons contacted
Hospital or physician discharge instructions
First aid and CPR certificates and tracking list
Staff acknowledgment of Danielle's Law training
Emergency review notes and CQI summary

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Residence Supervisor, nursing personnel, the Executive Director and the licensee of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure that when an individual dies, emergency care is given, the death is reported and investigated, the family or guardian is treated with respect, other individuals are supported, and the lessons learned improve care.
policies.policy: The death of an individual is a reportable unusual incident (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8) and is investigated under the investigation procedure (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)9). The date of discharge from services is recorded in the individual's file (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)). [AGENCY NAME] notifies the guardian, DDD and other authorities as current DHS and DDD incident reporting rules require, and does not delay notice. Findings from the review of each death are sent to the continuous quality improvement system (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)22). The individual is treated with dignity, and the wishes of the individual and family are honored.

definitions.definition: An event that [AGENCY NAME] must report to the Office of Licensing, DDD or other authorities under BSP-04 and REC-02, which includes the death of an individual.
A prompt, documented review of the facts and circumstances of the death, carried out by a person who was not directly involved, under BSP-04.
A review of the circumstances of a death, carried out through the CQI process to identify any actions that could prevent future deaths.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, the person legally authorized to make decisions for the individual.

procedures: When staff find an individual who is not breathing or has no pulse, they call 9-1-1 immediately and begin CPR unless a valid do-not-resuscitate order or other medical order is in the file and shows otherwise (see HW-04). Staff do not decide that a person has died. Emergency responders or a physician do.

Staff preserve the scene, and do not move or clean the room, except as needed to give care, until responders and any authorities give permission. Staff keep medications, MARs, protocols and records safe and make them available as requested.
The in-charge staff member notifies the Residence Supervisor or the on-call administrator at [PHONE] immediately. That person tells the Executive Director and the Nurse without delay.

The Executive Director or designee notifies the guardian or next of kin directly and in person or by phone, not by text or message. If the guardian cannot be reached, [AGENCY NAME] keeps trying and records each attempt. Notification follows the person's wishes and IR-10.

The Executive Director makes notifications to DDD, the Office of Licensing, law enforcement and others as current DHS and DDD incident reporting requirements direct, and confirms the required timelines with the DDD incident reporting rules. Each notification is recorded with the date, time, method and person told.
Staff stay with the individual's body until the proper authorities arrive, unless safety requires otherwise. Staff cooperate fully with the medical examiner, police, emergency staff and funeral home.

A written incident report is started the same day under BSP-04 by the staff members involved. Each staff member writes a factual statement and signs and dates it. Staff do not discuss the death outside the agency and refer all inquiries to the Executive Director to protect privacy under IR-05.

The Executive Director assigns an investigator who was not directly involved in the individual's care. The investigator reviews the incident, records, medication, protocols, health history, staffing and documentation, interviews staff and others, and issues a written report with findings and recommendations. The report is completed within the time required by current DHS and DDD rules.
[AGENCY NAME] reports any evidence or suspicion of abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately under BSP-03. Any suspected abuse is reported as required and is never held for the investigation.

The Executive Director or designee records the date of death as the date of discharge from services in the individual file under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b), and records the admission, discharge and any other file entries in line with REC-01. The file is sealed and kept for the retention period under REC-01.

Personal property and funds are secured and inventoried by two staff members, who sign and date the inventory. They are released only to the legal representative or as the law directs, as set out in IR-06. Billing for services ends as of the date of death under GOV-05.

The Residence Supervisor and Executive Director support the other individuals in the home. They tell them about the death in a way suited to each person, offer chances to grieve, to attend services if they wish and to speak with a counselor, and update their plans if needed.
[AGENCY NAME] offers support to staff, such as time to talk and access to the employee assistance resources [EAP RESOURCE]. Staff may be given time away from the shift when it is safe to do so.
The Nurse reviews the individual's health record, medication, recent changes of condition and follow-up of care, and writes a clinical summary for the review team.

The CQI team holds a mortality review of each death within [NUMBER] days of the investigation report, under GOV-04. The review looks at causes, contributing factors, whether policies were followed and whether the response was timely. It records corrective actions, with owners and due dates.

The Executive Director tracks corrective actions until complete, shares findings with staff in training, and sends the review to the CQI minutes. [AGENCY NAME] provides the investigation and review records to the Office of Licensing and DDD as requested.

responsibilities.duty: Calls 9-1-1, gives emergency care, preserves the scene, notifies the supervisor immediately and writes a factual statement.
Notifies the Executive Director, supports other individuals and staff, secures property and records and starts the incident report.
Provides a clinical summary and takes part in the review.
Notifies the guardian, DDD and other authorities, assigns the investigator, records discharge and leads the CQI mortality review.
Receives the report and review, makes sure corrective actions are completed and supports the family and staff.

documentation: Incident report and staff statements
Notification log with dates, times and persons contacted, including the guardian and authorities
Investigation report with findings and recommendations
Nurse clinical summary
Individual file with date of discharge recorded
Property and funds inventory and release record
CQI mortality review minutes and corrective action tracking
Support provided to other individuals and staff

policies.title: Over-the-Counter Medications and First Aid Supplies
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, the Residence Supervisor, the Registered Nurse, and any employee who assists with health care or maintains the residence or vehicles.
policies.purpose: To make sure over-the-counter (OTC) medications and first aid supplies are available, properly authorized, safely stored, accurately recorded, and used only as directed, in line with N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 5 (Health and Safety) and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows an OTC medication to be given only when a physician or Advanced Practice Nurse (APN) has stated in writing that the individual may use it, with the dose, frequency, maximum amount in 24 hours, and the conditions for use. Individuals self-administer OTC medications to the extent possible, as decided by the planning team and documented in the individual's record. When an individual cannot self-administer, only staff who have completed medication training and shown current competency may assist with or supervise administration, as prescribed. Every OTC medication given is recorded with the individual's name, date, and medication name, and also with time, dose, reason, and the staff member's signature. The manufacturer's original label is accepted as the label for an OTC product. Each residence keeps a stocked, accessible first aid kit that includes a CPR mask and protective gloves. A first aid kit is also kept in each agency vehicle used to transport individuals. OTC medications are never shared between individuals and are never used to manage behavior.

definitions.definition: A medication, vitamin, supplement, or topical product that can be bought without a prescription, such as acetaminophen, antacids, or topical ointments.
A medication ordered by a physician or Advanced Practice Nurse for a specific individual, which requires a pharmacy label.

A medication given 'as needed' under written conditions. Under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-5.2 the label must show the individual's name, date, medication, dosage, interval, maximum amount per 24 hours, stop date where appropriate, and the conditions for giving it.
The individual takes their own medication, with only the supports the planning team has decided are needed, as documented in the record.
The individual, guardian or family as appropriate, and agency and DDD representatives who develop and review the individual's service plan.
A nurse licensed in New Jersey with prescriptive authority who may write medication and OTC-use orders.

procedures: At admission and at least annually, the Registered Nurse asks each individual's physician or APN for a written statement of which OTC medications, vitamins, and topical products the individual may use, with dose, frequency, 24-hour maximum, and conditions for use. The nurse files the statement in the individual's health record.
The Residence Supervisor keeps a current OTC list for each individual at the medication station. It includes the allowed products, any known allergies or interactions, and the prescriber's name.

No staff member gives, offers, or suggests any OTC product that is not on the individual's authorized list. If an individual or staff member believes an unlisted product is needed, the staff member calls the nurse or the prescriber for an order before giving it.

The planning team decides how much of OTC use the individual can manage alone. The decision is recorded in the individual's plan and the medication record. Individuals who can safely keep and use their own OTC products are supported to do so.

When staff assist with or supervise an OTC medication, they first confirm the person is the right individual, the product is the authorized one, and the dose, time, frequency, and 24-hour maximum are allowed. They check the manufacturer's label for expiration date and condition.

Before giving a PRN OTC, the staff member checks that the conditions for use in the order are met, reviews how many doses were given in the past 24 hours, and, where the order requires it, calls the nurse for consultation first.

Immediately after giving or supervising a dose, staff record the individual's name, date, time, medication, dose, reason, and the individual's response on the medication record, and sign it. If an individual refuses, staff record the refusal and notify the nurse.

Staff report any medication error, adverse reaction, or unexpected change in the individual's condition to the nurse and the Residence Supervisor right away. They follow HW-01, HW-04, and BSP-04. If the condition is life-threatening, staff call 9-1-1 first.

OTC medications are stored in the original manufacturer's container in a clean, dry, locked storage area appropriate for each product. Individuals who self-administer may keep their own products in a place of their choosing that the plan has approved. Staff never store OTC products with cleaning supplies or poisons.

Each month the Residence Supervisor or designee checks all OTC medications and first aid supplies. They remove and properly dispose of expired, discolored, damaged, or unlabeled products and record the check with the date and signature.

Each residence has a first aid kit in a known, accessible place. Each agency vehicle used for transporting individuals has one as well. Every kit contains at least a CPR mask, protective gloves, adhesive bandages, sterile gauze and tape, an antiseptic, a thermometer, scissors, tweezers, and a first aid reference card. The Administrator may add more items.
Staff replace any used first aid item the same day or tell the Residence Supervisor that day that it needs replacing. The monthly check includes an inventory of kit contents on a checklist.

Staff who give first aid use protective gloves, follow HES-03, and dispose of used items safely. They document any first aid given, including date, time, injury, treatment, and the individual's condition, in the daily record. They report any injury that requires more than routine first aid to the Residence Supervisor and the nurse the same shift.
Staff never use OTC medications to control behavior, to make an individual sleepy, or as a substitute for a call to the nurse, prescriber, or 9-1-1 when symptoms warrant medical evaluation.

The Registered Nurse reviews OTC use as part of the regular health review. The nurse looks for patterns such as frequent pain relievers or laxatives that could signal an undiagnosed condition, and refers the individual to the prescriber when needed.
The Administrator reviews OTC and first aid findings as part of the continuous quality improvement system (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Provides funds and supplies for first aid and OTC needs, makes sure staff are trained and found competent, and reviews OTC and first aid findings in the quality system.
Obtains prescriber statements on OTC use, trains and checks staff competency, answers staff questions, and reviews OTC use patterns.
Keeps authorized OTC lists current, completes the monthly checks, restocks first aid kits, and follows up on any error or reaction.
Give or supervise OTC medications only as authorized, record each dose, report concerns, and give first aid with protective gloves.
Share health information and preferences, and take part in decisions about self-administration.

documentation: Physician or APN written statements on OTC use, kept in the individual's health record
Authorized OTC list for each individual
Medication administration record entries for OTC and PRN doses, including refusals
Planning team decision on self-administration
Monthly OTC and first aid kit inspection checklist
First aid kit inventory for each residence and vehicle
Incident or medication error reports, if any

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support and Behavior Support Plans
policies.applies_to: All employees who support individuals, the Behavior Support Clinician, the Registered Nurse, the Residence Supervisor, and members of planning teams.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] supports individuals through positive, person-centered approaches that address the reasons for behavior. Where a behavior support plan is needed, it must be written, individualized, the least restrictive option that works, and implemented by trained staff, in line with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, 2.7, and subchapter 5.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats behavior as communication. We start by understanding the individual's needs, preferences, health, history, and environment. We teach skills and make environmental changes before using any planned response to a behavior. A behavior support plan is any individualized written planned action(s) taken before or after a target behavior to modify its frequency or intensity. A behavior support plan is used only when the planning team decides one is needed. It is developed by a qualified clinician, reviewed by the Human Rights Committee when it includes any restriction, and included in the individual's plan. All behavioral supports used with an individual are identified in writing, and staff do not use any behavioral support that is not identified. Each employee who works with an individual who has a behavior support plan is trained in that plan within 90 days of employment, and before working alone with the individual wherever possible. Employees who work with individuals with identified mental health needs receive specific training in those needs. We always use the least restrictive approach, and we never use any behavioral support as punishment, for staff convenience, or in place of a program of activities and supports.

definitions.definition: Any individualized written planned action(s) taken before or after a target behavior to modify its frequency or intensity (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
A specific, observable behavior the planning team has identified for support, described so that all staff recognize it the same way.
An approach that identifies the purpose of a behavior, changes the environment and routines, teaches new skills, and rewards desired behavior.
The approach that works while interfering the least with the individual's rights, choices, and freedom of movement.
The group, including the individual and their guardian or family as appropriate, that develops and reviews the individual's service plan.
Any strategy, device, environmental change, or response used to prevent, reduce, or respond to a target behavior, whether or not it is part of a formal plan.

procedures: During pre-admission and admission (PCS-01) and at every plan review, the Residence Supervisor and planning team ask about the individual's communication, triggers, health, trauma history, preferences, and any behavior of concern. They record what is learned.

If a behavior of concern appears or changes, the Residence Supervisor first asks the Registered Nurse to rule out pain, illness, medication effects, or other medical causes, and arranges a medical or mental health evaluation when indicated.

The Behavior Support Clinician, [BEHAVIOR SUPPORT CLINICIAN NAME AND CREDENTIAL], carries out a functional assessment. It includes direct observation, staff and family interviews, review of incident records, and the person's own view of what is happening and what would help.

The planning team decides whether a behavior support plan is needed. The team starts with proactive supports such as environmental changes, communication tools, preferred activities, relationships, and skill teaching, and records the decision in the individual's plan.

If a plan is needed, the Clinician writes it in plain language. It states the target behavior, likely function, preventive strategies, skills to be taught, how staff should respond, how data will be collected, and who is responsible. It lists every behavioral support used. It is the least restrictive plan that is likely to work.

A plan containing any restriction of rights or movement, or a response involving physical contact, is sent to the Human Rights Committee before it is put into effect (IR-02, IR-03, BSP-02). It also needs the informed consent of the individual or guardian (IR-08). The plan is never used until these steps are done, except in an emergency as set out in BSP-02.

The Residence Supervisor makes sure each employee who works with an individual with a behavior support plan is trained on that plan by a qualified trainer within 90 days of employment. Training covers the plan's strategies, signs of escalation, data collection, and reporting. Trainer and trainee sign and date the record (STF-03, STF-09).
Staff with identified mental health training needs complete training on mental health needs within 90 days of employment, and ongoing training thereafter as the plan requires.

Staff follow the plan exactly. They do not add, change, or improvise supports. They record each use of the plan, the behavior, what happened before and after, and the individual's response on the data sheet the same shift.

Staff report to the Residence Supervisor the same shift when a plan is not working, the behavior worsens, an injury occurs, or any intervention goes beyond what the plan permits. Such events are also reported as incidents under BSP-04.

The Clinician reviews data at least monthly, meets with the planning team at least every six months and whenever data show a problem, and records whether the plan is working, should be changed, or can be reduced or ended.

Any change to the plan follows the same approval steps as a new plan. The Residence Supervisor updates staff training and the plan copy at the residence the day the change takes effect and removes prior versions.

The Registered Nurse reviews any psychotropic medication used for behavior or mental health, makes sure it is part of the documented plan, and does not allow medication to be used as a behavioral support unless it has been prescribed and approved as treatment (HW-01).

The Administrator reviews behavior data and use of behavioral supports at least quarterly in the continuous quality improvement system (GOV-04), and acts on any pattern of overuse, injury, or rights concerns.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the clinical resources and training are available, reviews behavior support data, and makes sure plans are least restrictive and approved.
Completes assessments, writes and reviews plans, trains staff, and analyzes data.
Rules out medical causes, reviews psychotropic medication use, and supports staff on health needs.
Ensures staff are trained, follow plans, and collect data, and tells the Clinician when a plan is not working.
Know each person's plan, implement it exactly, record data, and report problems.
Reviews plans that include restrictions and advises on rights protections.
Decides whether a plan is needed and approves it with the individual's informed consent.

documentation: Functional assessment
Behavior support plan, with the list of all behavioral supports used, signed and dated
Planning team decision
Human Rights Committee review and consent records
Staff training records with trainer and trainee signatures and dates
Daily behavior data sheets and monthly data summaries
Review and change records
Incident reports for events beyond the plan

policies.title: Restrictive Interventions, Restraint and Seclusion
policies.applies_to: All employees, the Behavior Support Clinician, the Registered Nurse, the Residence Supervisor, the Human Rights Committee, and any contracted or agency staff.
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from unnecessary or unsafe restrictions by limiting restrictive interventions to what the rules in N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 5 and Division requirements permit. These are used only as a last resort, with Human Rights Committee review under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-3.1, and are always the least restrictive option.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use restraint, seclusion, or any restriction as punishment, for staff convenience, to make up for too few staff, or as a substitute for active support. Seclusion, mechanical restraint, and chemical restraint are prohibited at this agency. Physical contact to stop an individual from moving is not used unless it is permitted by the current requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A subchapter 5 and the Division. It may be used only in an emergency where there is imminent danger of serious harm to the individual or others, when less restrictive measures have not worked or cannot work in time. It must be done by staff trained in a technique approved by the Division, under the direction of a qualified trainer, and it must end the moment the danger passes. Any restriction of an individual's rights, freedoms, or belongings goes through the individual's plan, informed consent, and the Human Rights Committee before it starts. Any restraint or seclusion that is not permitted or not approved is treated as abuse under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3 and reported as such under BSP-03 and BSP-04. The Administrator confirms the current text of subchapter 5 and Division guidance when this policy is reviewed each year and whenever the rules change.

definitions.definition: Any physical, mechanical, or chemical means that restricts an individual's freedom of movement or normal access to their body.
Holding an individual's body or limbs so that they cannot move freely.
Use of any device, material, or equipment attached or adjacent to the body to restrict movement. This is prohibited at [AGENCY NAME].
Use of a medication to control behavior or restrict movement when it is not part of a prescribed treatment for a diagnosed condition. This is prohibited at [AGENCY NAME].
Involuntarily confining an individual alone in a room or area from which they are prevented from leaving. This is prohibited at [AGENCY NAME].
Any limit on an individual's freedom, choice, access, or belongings that is not generally applied to others in the home, other than rules everyone follows.
Includes wrongful physical, verbal, or psychological abuse by a caregiver, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
A situation in which serious physical harm to the individual or others is about to happen.

procedures: Staff use preventive and de-escalation supports first. They stay calm, give space, offer choices and preferred items, reduce noise and demands, and follow the individual's behavior support plan (BSP-01).

Staff never use seclusion, mechanical restraint, or chemical restraint, and never use any hold that restricts breathing, applies pressure to the neck, chest, or joints, or places the person face down. Staff never block a person in a room or take away food, sleep, communication, visitors, medication, or access to the bathroom as a consequence.

Staff may use physical contact to prevent imminent harm only if the technique is Division-approved, is included in the individual's plan if the person is known to be at risk, and the staff member has current training from a qualified trainer.
