Physical contact is used only for as long as the danger lasts and is never used as a response to refusal, noise, property damage without danger, or verbal behavior.

During any physical intervention, one staff member watches the individual's breathing, color, and signs of distress. Staff talk calmly and tell the person what is needed to end the hold. If the person shows any difficulty breathing, injury, or medical distress, staff release immediately and call 9-1-1 (HW-04).

Staff call the in-charge staff person and the on-call administrator right away (STF-08) when a physical intervention is used or when injury or danger remains. The in-charge staff person makes sure that other individuals in the home remain supported and supervised.

After any physical intervention, a nurse or qualified staff member checks the individual for injury and records findings. The staff member offers emotional support and the individual is given a chance to say what happened in their own words.

Staff report the event as an unusual incident under BSP-04 immediately, by the deadline in current DHS/DDD policy. The report states what happened before, what was tried, which technique was used, who was involved, how long it lasted, and any injury. If it was not an approved technique used within these rules, staff also report it as an allegation of abuse under BSP-03.

Within one business day, the Behavior Support Clinician and Administrator review the incident with the staff involved. They decide whether the intervention was justified and followed the rules, what led to the crisis, and what should change. Staff who did not follow this policy are removed from direct support pending review and disciplined under STF-06.
The Administrator notifies the guardian and the individual's DDD representative of any physical intervention as soon as safety allows, and no later than the same day.

Any proposed restriction (such as limits on access to items, rooms, money, phone, visitors, or food) must be justified in writing in the individual's plan. The justification states the specific need, less intrusive measures tried, a plan to end it, data collection, and a review date. The planning team and the individual (or guardian) must agree, and the Human Rights Committee must review it before it starts (IR-02, IR-03, IR-08).

The Human Rights Committee reviews each restriction at least annually, and sooner if data show a problem. A restriction that is no longer needed is removed immediately. The Residence Supervisor makes sure staff are told when any restriction ends.

Only a qualified trainer teaches approved intervention techniques. Employees are trained before using them and retrained as the trainer requires. Training records are kept in the administrative office with the trainer's and employee's signatures and dates (STF-09, STF-03).

The Administrator reports use of physical intervention and restrictions in the continuous quality improvement system at least quarterly. The review looks for trends, repeated use for the same person, time of day, staff involved, and possible gaps in support. The Administrator acts on what is found (GOV-04).
Every individual may report concerns about restraint or restriction without retaliation and is told how, using the grievance process (IR-04) and the abuse and neglect reporting lines (BSP-03).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy is followed, confirms current subchapter 5 requirements each year, reviews every intervention, makes required notifications, and reports trends in the quality system.
Develops plans, helps prevent crises, debriefs every incident, and recommends changes.
Checks individuals for injury after an intervention and reviews health effects.
Directs the response, protects others in the home, makes first notifications, and ensures reports are written.
Use only permitted techniques they are trained in, release at once when the danger ends, and report every event.
Reviews and approves proposed restrictions and reviews them at least annually.

documentation: Incident reports for every physical intervention or suspected unapproved restraint or seclusion
Post-intervention injury check
Debriefing record and corrective actions
Plan justifications and consent for restrictions
Human Rights Committee review minutes and decisions
Technique training records with qualified trainer and employee signatures and dates
Quarterly quality system review of interventions and restrictions
Notifications to guardian and DDD

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, interns, volunteers, contracted and temporary agency staff, the Administrator, and the governing authority.
policies.purpose: To protect individuals from abuse, neglect, and exploitation, and to make sure every allegation is reported and addressed promptly. This policy contains the written statement required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] expressly prohibits abuse, neglect, and exploitation of any individual, by anyone. Every employee, intern, volunteer, and contractor is obligated to report each allegation or suspicion of abuse, neglect, or exploitation, as required by the statutes cited in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8 and Department policy. This is true even if the employee is not sure, if the person involved is a coworker or supervisor, or if the individual did not ask for a report to be made. No one may delay, discourage, or alter a report. Anyone who reports in good faith is protected from retaliation. Failure to report is itself a violation that results in discipline up to termination and may be referred to authorities. The individual's safety is first: we protect them from further harm before any other step. We check the Central Registry of Offenders Against Individuals with Developmental Disabilities (N.J.S.A. 30:6D-73 et seq.; N.J.A.C. 10:44D) and the DCF Child Abuse Registry for every employee under STF-02, and we train each direct support professional on preventing abuse and neglect within 90 days of employment.

definitions.definition: As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. It includes wrongful physical, verbal, or psychological abuse by a caregiver and any act that causes or is likely to cause harm to an individual.
Failure by a caregiver to provide the care, supervision, food, health care, or protection the individual needs, whether on purpose or through carelessness.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. It includes taking advantage of an individual's money, property, labor, or person for another's benefit.
The Central Registry of Offenders Against Individuals with Developmental Disabilities (N.J.S.A. 30:6D-73 et seq.; N.J.A.C. 10:44D).
The registry kept by the NJ Department of Children and Families, which [AGENCY NAME] checks for each employee.
Any report, observation, disclosure, rumor, or suspicion that abuse, neglect, or exploitation occurred, regardless of source or proof.
Any person who provides care or supports to the individual, paid or unpaid.

procedures: At hire, each employee signs a statement acknowledging this policy, including the prohibition and the duty to report every allegation. Staff receive the policy again at orientation and when it changes (STF-03, STF-05).

Within 90 days of employment, each direct support professional completes the Division-required training on preventing abuse and neglect, and the certificate is kept on file (STF-03). The Administrator provides refresher training at least annually.

Before an employee has any contact with individuals, the Administrator checks the Central Registry and the Child Abuse Registry and meets the screening requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4 (STF-02). No one who is on a registry or otherwise disqualified may work with individuals.

Anyone who sees, suspects, or is told of abuse, neglect, or exploitation first makes sure the individual is safe. They stop the harm, separate the person from the alleged abuser, and get medical care. If anyone is in immediate danger or needs urgent care, they call 9-1-1.

The employee then tells the in-charge staff person and the Administrator (or on-call administrator under STF-08) immediately. The report may not be delayed or made only through a supervisor. If the allegation involves the Administrator or in-charge person, the employee reports to the governing authority [GOVERNING AUTHORITY CONTACT].

The employee or Administrator reports the allegation to the State at once through the reporting channel set by DHS and DDD. DDD's published number for these issues is 800-832-9173. The Administrator confirms the current abuse and neglect reporting line and reporting method with DHS every year and posts it at each residence and in the staff handbook. Reporting to the Administrator does not take the place of the employee's own duty to report.

Where law enforcement involvement is appropriate, such as a suspected crime, injury, or sexual assault, staff call 9-1-1 or the police. If the individual is a minor, or a minor is involved, a report is also made to the DCF Child Abuse Hotline as the law requires.

The Administrator immediately removes the alleged employee, volunteer, or contractor from all contact with individuals until the investigation is complete, and keeps any individual involved from contact with the alleged abuser. This is not a finding of guilt and is done without prejudice.

Staff preserve evidence. They do not clean or alter the scene, wash the individual or their clothes if a physical or sexual assault is suspected, or discard objects. They write down what they saw, heard, and were told, with exact words where possible, using the incident report form, and sign and date it before the end of the shift.

The Administrator notifies the guardian and the individual's DDD representative as soon as safety allows, and no later than the same day, unless the guardian is the alleged abuser, in which case the Administrator follows the direction of DDD and investigators.

Staff who report abuse in good faith are protected from retaliation. Any threat, schedule change, or discipline following a report is reviewed by the Administrator, or by the governing authority if the Administrator is involved.

The Administrator opens an internal investigation under BSP-04 unless an outside agency directs otherwise. [AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with DHS, DDD, the Office of Licensing, and law enforcement, and does not interfere with any outside investigation.

The nurse or other health professional examines the individual as needed. Counseling, advocacy, or other supports are offered to the individual, who is told what will happen next in a way they can understand.

When disclosure of protected health information is needed to report abuse, neglect, or exploitation to a government authority authorized to receive these reports, staff follow 45 CFR 164.512(c) and IR-05. Staff may share only what is needed for the report. Privacy rules do not stop or delay a report.

If an allegation is substantiated, the Administrator takes corrective action, which includes termination and a report to the Central Registry as required. The Administrator also reviews what systems failed and makes changes, which are reviewed in the quality system (GOV-04).

Every individual and guardian receives information, in an accessible format, on how to report abuse, neglect, or exploitation to the agency or directly to the State, without fear of retaliation (IR-01, IR-04, IR-09).

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure the prohibition and reporting duty are in place and takes over any allegation involving the Administrator.
Ensures prompt reporting, removes alleged abusers from contact, notifies guardian and DDD, runs the investigation, and acts on findings.
Ensures safety, reports immediately, preserves evidence, and gets care.

responsibilities.role: All employees, interns, volunteers, and contractors
responsibilities.duty: Never abuse, neglect, or exploit, and report every allegation immediately.
Evaluates the individual's health and records injuries.
Completes registry and screening checks before contact and keeps training and acknowledgment records.

documentation: Employee acknowledgment of the written prohibition and duty to report
Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry check results
Training certificate on preventing abuse and neglect for each direct support professional
Incident reports and written statements
Report records (date, time, person who reported, agency, reference number)
Notifications to guardian and DDD
Investigation file, findings, and corrective actions
Records of removal from contact and return to duty

policies.title: Reportable Incidents and Investigations
policies.applies_to: All employees, the Residence Supervisor, the Administrator, the Registered Nurse, and the governing authority.
policies.purpose: To make sure all unusual incidents are responded to, reported, investigated, and learned from, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8 and (b)9, and that records are ready when the Office of Licensing inspects.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has one process for reporting all unusual incidents and a separate process for investigating them. Staff respond to the person's safety first, report in writing before the end of the shift, and notify the Administrator immediately. The Administrator reports to DHS, DDD, the guardian, and others by the deadlines and in the manner set by the current DHS and DDD incident reporting policy, which the Administrator confirms each year, posts at each residence, and uses over any shorter or different timeline in this policy. Every allegation of abuse, neglect, or exploitation is reported and investigated under BSP-03 and this policy. Investigations are objective, prompt, and written, and are led by someone who was not involved in the incident. Incident patterns are reviewed in the continuous quality improvement system. Critical information about an incident is shared shift to shift through the critical information log (PCS-07).

definitions.definition: Any event that is out of the ordinary and affects, or could affect, the health, safety, rights, or well-being of an individual, including those listed in this policy and any category in current DHS/DDD policy.
An unusual incident that must be reported to the State, guardian, or other outside party under current DHS/DDD requirements.
A fact-finding review of an incident to find out what happened, why, and what should change.
As defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. Information staff need to know on the next shift to keep individuals safe and supported.
A step taken to fix a problem and keep it from happening again.
A written response to deficiencies found at a licensing inspection (GOV-07).

procedures: Staff treat unusual incidents as events that need a report. At a minimum these are: allegations of abuse, neglect, or exploitation; death; serious injury or illness; hospitalization or emergency room or 9-1-1 call; missing person or elopement; medication error or refusal with risk; use of physical intervention or any restriction; police contact or suspected crime; fire, evacuation, or utility emergency; property damage that affects safety; unplanned transfer or discharge; and any other event in current DHS/DDD incident categories.
The first staff member on scene makes sure the individual is safe, gets first aid or calls 9-1-1 as needed (HW-04), and secures the area.
The staff member informs the in-charge staff person at once, and the in-charge person calls the Administrator or on-call administrator right away (STF-08), by phone and not just by message.

Before the end of the shift, the staff member completes the written incident report. It records the date, time, place, individuals and staff involved, a factual description, what happened before and after, injuries or damage, actions taken, and who was notified. It records what staff saw and heard, not opinions.

The Administrator decides which category applies and makes all required outside reports to DHS, DDD, the Office of Licensing, law enforcement, and other agencies by the deadline and method in current DHS/DDD policy. The Administrator records the date, time, method, person contacted, and any reference number.
The Administrator notifies the guardian and, when appropriate, family members promptly and in line with the individual's consent and privacy (IR-05). Notifications are documented, including attempts.
Staff record critical information from the incident in the separate critical information log, and give it to the next shift face to face (PCS-07).

The Administrator assigns an investigator the next business day for any incident needing review. The investigator must have no involvement in the incident and no conflict. If the Administrator is involved, the governing authority assigns an independent investigator.

For abuse, neglect, or exploitation allegations, the alleged abuser is removed from contact with individuals right away (BSP-03). Where the State or law enforcement opens its own investigation, [AGENCY NAME] cooperates and does not interview witnesses in a way that interferes unless told it may.

The investigator collects statements from the individual, witnesses, and staff, reviews records, schedules, logs, and the scene, and keeps evidence. Statements are signed and dated. The individual is interviewed in a way that fits their communication needs and with support if wanted.

The investigator writes a report that states the allegation, steps taken, evidence, findings of fact, conclusion (substantiated, unsubstantiated, or inconclusive), and recommendations. The report is complete within the time set by DHS/DDD. If none is set, it is complete within 30 days. The Administrator reviews and signs it.

The Administrator takes corrective action based on the findings, including retraining, discipline, changes to the plan, environment, or staffing, and records the date each action was done. The Administrator tells the guardian and the individual the outcome as the law permits.
The Administrator sends any follow-up report or investigation findings to the State as required and makes sure no required report is missing from the file.

At least quarterly, the quality team reviews all incidents for trends by type, individual, time, location, staff, and cause, and checks that reports were timely and corrective actions were completed (GOV-04). The Administrator also reviews incident trends before each annual review of procedures (GOV-03).
Incident and investigation files are kept confidential, and are available for the Office of Licensing and DDD to review during inspections (GOV-07). They are kept under REC-01 and REC-02.

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, in-charge staff, the Residence Supervisor, the Administrator, and on-call staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure that when an individual is missing or at risk of leaving without support, staff search at once, call for help quickly, and tell the right people, while respecting the rights and choices of individuals who go out on their own as their plans allow.
policies.policy: A missing-person event is an unusual incident under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8 and is handled and reported under BSP-04. An individual is missing when staff do not know where the person is, the person was expected to be with staff or back by a set time and is not, and the absence is not covered by the person's plan. Supervision follows each individual's needs as set out in the plan, and staff are on site whenever any individual is present, as N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(d) requires. Elopement risk, with the individual's triggers, warning signs, and prevention supports, goes in the individual's plan. The policy does not limit a person's right to come and go as their plan allows. When the whereabouts of a person at risk are unknown, staff start searching immediately and call 9-1-1 right away if the person is at high risk or is not found within 15 minutes. The Administrator confirms current DDD definitions and time thresholds for missing persons each year and uses any shorter threshold the State sets.

definitions.definition: An individual whose whereabouts are unknown, who is not where the plan says they should be, and who is not at a place or with a person known to staff.
When an individual leaves the residence or a supervised setting without staff knowing, in a way that puts the person at risk or is outside the person's plan.

A person who cannot be safe alone, such as someone who cannot keep safe in traffic, cannot communicate their name or address, has a medical condition or medication need, has a history of elopement, or is in crisis.
A one-page sheet with a recent photograph, description, communication needs, medical needs, likely places, and contacts, kept current for each individual.
The employee designated for the shift on the posted schedule (STF-01).
The level of staff presence and observation an individual needs, as written in the plan.

procedures: At admission and at each plan review, the planning team assesses the individual's risk of elopement or getting lost, including triggers, past events, road and water hazards, health needs, and ability to find help. The team records supervision needs and prevention supports in the plan (PCS-01, PCS-02).

The Residence Supervisor keeps a missing person profile for each individual in the office, with a recent photograph, description, clothing worn if known, communication, health needs, medications, favorite places, and people they may contact. It is updated at least every six months and after any change.

Individuals who are able to go out on their own have a written plan for how they tell staff where they are going and when they expect to return, and what staff do if the person does not return. Staff do not treat this independence as elopement.

When staff notice a person may be missing, they tell the in-charge staff person at once. The in-charge person starts a search immediately, with no wait period, and notes the time the person was last seen.

The in-charge person assigns searchers and makes sure that the other individuals in the home remain supervised as their plans require. Staff do not leave an individual who needs supervision alone to search. If staff cannot do both, the in-charge person calls the on-call administrator for added staff (STF-08).

Searchers check inside the residence first, including closets, bathrooms, yards, vehicles, and nearby hazards. They then check nearby areas, usual and favorite places, bus stops, stores, and places listed on the missing person profile. Staff call the individual's phone if they have one.

Staff call 9-1-1 at once and give the police the profile, photo, description, last-seen time and place, and any health or safety risk if the person is high-risk, may be in danger, or is not found within 15 minutes of starting the search. Staff call sooner if there are signs of crisis, bad weather, traffic or water hazards, or the person cannot ask for help.
The in-charge person calls the Administrator or on-call administrator right away, by phone. The Administrator takes charge of the response and decides on additional staff or search help.

The Administrator notifies the guardian and any family members promptly and informs the DDD representative, and makes the required incident reports to DHS and DDD by the deadline in current policy (BSP-04). Notifications are recorded with date and time.

Staff keep a written timeline of the search, who searched where, who was called and when, and what was learned. They do not post on social media or give information to the public, and they give information only to the police and the individuals' representatives to protect privacy (IR-05).

When the person is found, staff make sure they are safe, treat them with respect, check for injury or illness, and call the nurse or 9-1-1 if needed (HW-04). Staff do not punish or scold the person. They tell the police, guardian, Administrator, and DDD that the person is found.

The in-charge person records critical information about the event in the critical information log and passes it on to the next shift in person (PCS-07). Staff give extra attention to the individual for the next 24 hours.

Within three business days, the Administrator, Residence Supervisor, and Behavior Support Clinician review what happened with the individual and the staff involved. They look at what led to the event and what could prevent it, including supervision, environment, health, routine, relationships, and unmet needs. The planning team then updates the plan, supervision needs, and profile.
If the review finds that staff did not follow supervision requirements or the plan, the Administrator takes corrective action and considers a report of neglect under BSP-03.
At least once a year, the Administrator reviews missing-person events in the quality system (GOV-04), and the staff practice the search steps at staff meetings or as part of drills.

Keeps profiles current, makes sure plans cover elopement risk, and leads follow-up.

policies.title: Residential Environment, Capacity and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: All community residences and supervised apartments operated by [AGENCY NAME]; Licensee/Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, maintenance staff and all direct support staff
policies.purpose: To make sure each residence operated by [AGENCY NAME] is lawfully obtained, stays within its licensed capacity, meets the fire safety and physical environment requirements, and is physically accessible to the individuals who live there.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates each residence only at the location and within the maximum capacity stated on its license. A community residence serves no more than 16 individuals, and a supervised apartment serves no more than 4 individuals per apartment. A community residence is not located on the grounds of, or immediately adjacent to, a public institution serving a similar population. Housing is cleared with the DDD Office of Housing and Resource Development before it is acquired, leased or renovated. Before opening and on an ongoing basis, the agency keeps documentation of any required Fire Official inspection, Department of Community Affairs (DCA) registration, and the certificate from the local enforcing authority (or documentation that none is issued). Each home is maintained clean, safe, in good repair and homelike, and its accessibility features are matched to the assessed needs of the people living there. Accessibility is not limited to what the building already has. Where an individual's needs require it, the agency makes reasonable modifications, using the process in IR-02 for any restriction on an individual's rights. Inspectors review physical plant and insurance documents, so these records are kept current and available at all times.

definitions.definition: A residence serving up to 16 individuals with developmental disabilities, not located on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution serving a similar population (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
An apartment setting serving up to 4 individuals per apartment (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3).
The maximum number of individuals the license permits at a specific residence location.
Physical features such as ramps, grab bars, wide doorways, roll-in showers, lifts, visual alarms and other adaptations that let an individual use the home safely and independently.
The local government official or agency that inspects and, where applicable, certifies the residence for fire and building safety.

procedures: Before the agency signs a lease, purchase agreement or other site control document for any new or additional residence, the Executive Director contacts the DDD Office of Housing and Resource Development, obtains clearance, and files the written clearance in the Licensing File.
The Executive Director confirms the site is not on the grounds of or immediately adjacent to a public institution serving a similar population and records this on the Site Approval Checklist.

Before the home is occupied, the Residence Supervisor and the Executive Director complete a Physical Environment Checklist built from the current text of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-6 and applicable local codes. It covers bedrooms, bathrooms, living and dining space, kitchen, exits, alarms and utilities. The Executive Director signs and dates it.

The Executive Director obtains and files the Fire Official inspection documentation, the DCA registration where required, and the certificate from the local enforcing authority (or written documentation that none is issued). The Executive Director tracks renewal dates on the Compliance Calendar and renews each before it expires.

The Executive Director confirms that the licensed capacity and address on the license match the actual home. The posted and admission-file capacity for each residence is the licensed capacity. No admission or temporary stay may cause the home to exceed it.

Before each admission (PCS-01), the Residence Supervisor reviews the person's physical, mobility, sensory and communication needs and compares them with the home's accessibility features. The Residence Supervisor records the result on the Accessibility Review Form.

If the home does not meet the person's needs, the Executive Director either arranges a modification before move-in or tells the person, guardian and DDD support coordinator that the home cannot meet the person's needs. The Executive Director documents the decision and the reason. Needed modifications are made promptly, with any required permits and landlord approval.

Whenever an individual's condition or equipment changes (HW-04, PCS-04), the planning team and Residence Supervisor repeat the accessibility review. Any change is recorded in the Individual Plan and the maintenance log.

The Residence Supervisor inspects the home at least monthly using the Home Safety Inspection Checklist. It covers building condition, floors and stairs, handrails, lighting, water temperature, pest control, furniture, locks and individual bedrooms. Findings are recorded with the date and the name of the person who completed the inspection.

Direct support staff report any hazard, broken equipment or accessibility barrier to the in-charge staff person immediately. Hazards that threaten safety are corrected or controlled the same shift (for example by blocking off an area or moving individuals). The maintenance request is logged with date, repair and completion date.

The Executive Director does not change the use of rooms, add or remove beds, change the number of occupants, or perform structural renovation without first checking that it fits the license, the local code and the Fire Official's certificate. Any change that needs notice to or approval from the Office of Licensing or DDD is requested in writing before it begins.

Individuals may decorate and furnish their own bedrooms and personalize shared space to their preferences. Any limit is handled only through the rights restriction process in IR-02 and recorded in the Individual Plan.

The Executive Director keeps current insurance documents, the license, inspection and certification records, and the maintenance and inspection logs in the administrative office. They are produced to the Office of Licensing inspector on request, including at unannounced visits.
The Executive Director reviews this policy and the Compliance Calendar at least annually under GOV-03 and includes physical plant findings in the quality review under GOV-04.

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness, Evacuation and Fire Drills
policies.applies_to: All residences operated by [AGENCY NAME]; all staff, including temporary and on-call staff, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure staff and individuals know exactly what to do in a fire, gas leak or other major emergency that requires evacuation, and that fire safety systems and drills meet the requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written major emergency and evacuation plan for each residence, as required in the procedure manual. It covers fire, gas leaks and other emergencies in which individuals may need to leave the home or be moved to safety. Fire safety systems, drills and records follow subchapter 6 of N.J.A.C. 10:44A and the requirements of the local Fire Official. Staff are on site whenever an individual is present in the home. Every staff person, including temporary staff, is oriented to the plan before working alone. Evacuation drills are held on every shift, including sleeping hours, and every individual takes part according to the support in his or her plan. Temperature and utility emergencies are handled under HES-06, and emergency coverage and on-call procedures are handled under STF-08.

definitions.definition: An event such as a fire or gas leak that threatens health or safety and may require evacuation of the home.
A practice exit of the building by all individuals and staff on duty using the posted routes, timed and recorded.
A one-page description for each person that states the help, equipment and communication method needed to exit safely, including at night.
The safe outdoor location where everyone gathers after evacuating and is counted.
A pre-arranged alternate location where individuals are sheltered if the home cannot be re-entered.

procedures: The Executive Director and Residence Supervisor write the Emergency and Evacuation Plan for each residence. It covers fire, gas leak, flood, severe weather, loss of utilities, bomb threat and other hazards relevant to the area. It names the exits, primary and secondary routes, assembly point, relocation site and transport arrangements.

The Residence Supervisor completes an Individual Evacuation Profile for each person at admission and updates it with every change in mobility, sensory ability, behavior or equipment. The profile states who helps, how, and what is needed (wheelchair, communication aid, medications).

Floor plans with exit routes and the assembly point are posted in each home. Emergency numbers, including [ADDRESS] of the home for dispatch, [PHONE] for the Residence Supervisor and the on-call administrator, are posted by the staff telephone.

In any fire or smoke event, staff follow the order: get individuals out and away, call 9-1-1 from outside the building, account for every person by roster at the assembly point, then notify the Residence Supervisor or on-call administrator. Staff do not re-enter the building. For a suspected gas leak, staff evacuate without using switches or phones inside, then call from outside.

The in-charge staff person takes the individual roster and the emergency medication and information folder when it is safe to do so, accounts for all individuals and stays with them until emergency responders release the scene.

The Residence Supervisor obtains and keeps current the Fire Official inspection documentation, DCA registration where required, and the local certificate. Smoke and fire detection, alarms, extinguishers and emergency lighting are inspected and tested at the frequencies required by subchapter 6 and local code. The Executive Director records the confirmed frequencies on the Compliance Calendar. Staff record each test, inspection and repair and the date.

The Residence Supervisor schedules evacuation drills at or above the frequency required by subchapter 6, and at least monthly as agency standard. Drills rotate across all shifts and include sleeping hours, so that every individual and every regular staff person practice. Alternate routes are used on a rotating basis.

During each drill, the person conducting it records the date, time of day, shift, staff and individuals present, exit route, total evacuation time, individuals who needed help, problems found and the signature of the person conducting it. Individuals who refuse to participate are encouraged, not forced, and the refusal and support offered are recorded.

If a drill reveals a problem (a blocked exit, slow evacuation, an individual who could not leave without more support), the Residence Supervisor corrects it within 7 days, updates the Individual Evacuation Profile or plan, and repeats the drill if needed. The correction and date are recorded on the drill form.

All new employees are oriented to the Emergency and Evacuation Plan, exit routes, extinguisher use and the Individual Evacuation Profiles before working alone. The Residence Supervisor signs the New Employee Orientation Checklist.

Staff are present in the home whenever an individual is present. Staffing patterns are set so that the evacuation needs of everyone in the home can be met on every shift (STF-01). The in-charge person for each shift is named on the posted schedule.

Emergency coverage and on-call procedures are posted in each home. When an emergency occurs, the in-charge person calls the on-call administrator under STF-08 and the administrator responds, arranges additional staff and relocation if needed.

After any real evacuation or fire event, the Residence Supervisor prepares an incident report under BSP-04, makes any required notification to the Office of Licensing and DDD, and lists lessons learned. The Executive Director reports findings to the quality improvement system in GOV-04.
The Executive Director reviews each plan and its drill records at least annually and whenever the residents, building or staffing changes, and updates it under GOV-03.

Writes and updates plans and Individual Evacuation Profiles, schedules and documents drills, tests equipment and corrects problems.

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All residences operated by [AGENCY NAME]; all staff, including nursing, temporary agency and on-call staff, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among individuals and staff, to protect employees from bloodborne pathogen exposure, and to make sure communicable diseases are identified, treated and reported.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows standard precautions in every residence, keeps protective gloves and a CPR mask in each first aid kit, trains staff in infection control, and screens employees for tuberculosis as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4. The agency maintains a written Exposure Control Plan for employees with potential exposure to blood or other infectious materials under the federal bloodborne pathogens standard. Reportable communicable diseases are critical information and are shared with staff on each shift through the critical information log. Individuals' dignity and right to community participation are protected, and restrictions on movement are limited to what a health authority or licensed health professional directs.

definitions.definition: Practices applied to all individuals and all blood and body fluids, including hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, safe handling of sharps and soiled items, and cleaning.
Information that staff on the next shift must know, including reportable communicable diseases, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
Contact of eyes, mouth, mucous membranes or broken skin with blood or other potentially infectious material during work duties, including a needlestick.
Interferon-gamma release assay, a blood test for tuberculosis infection.
Gloves, masks, gowns, eye protection and CPR masks provided by the agency at no cost to employees.

procedures: The Executive Director, with the agency's nurse or health consultant, writes the Infection Control Procedures and the Exposure Control Plan. They are reviewed annually and updated when practices, products or the residents' needs change.

Before any employee who may contact individuals begins work, the agency obtains a written TB screening result (Mantoux 5 TU PPD or IGRA blood test) taken within one year before or upon starting work, and files it in the personnel file (STF-04). Repeat screening is done at the interval required by the current rule and by the nurse or local health department. The Administrator confirms the current interval and records it on the Compliance Calendar. Staff with a positive screening or symptoms are referred to a health care provider and do not work until cleared in writing.

Each home keeps a stocked first aid kit that includes protective gloves and a CPR mask, along with the other contents required by subchapter 5. The Residence Supervisor checks the kit monthly and after each use, replaces used or expired items and initials the check log.

All direct support staff are trained in hand hygiene, standard precautions, correct use of PPE, cleaning of blood and body fluid spills, and handling of laundry and waste during orientation and annually. Training is documented under STF-03 and STF-09.

The agency provides gloves, masks, soap, hand sanitizer, disinfectants, sharps containers and other supplies at no cost to staff and keeps them available in each home. Staff wash hands before and after personal care, medication administration, food preparation and glove use.

Staff clean and disinfect bathrooms, kitchens and high-touch surfaces on the cleaning schedule posted in each home. Spills of blood or body fluids are cleaned immediately by staff wearing gloves, using an EPA-registered disinfectant per label directions, and the waste is bagged and discarded appropriately. Contaminated laundry is handled with gloves, washed separately in hot water and detergent.

Sharps, such as lancets and needles used for diabetes or other prescribed care, are discarded immediately into a puncture-resistant container kept in a safe place. Containers are never overfilled and are disposed of as regulated medical waste under the nurse's direction.

Food safety: staff wash hands before preparing food, keep raw and ready-to-eat food apart, keep refrigerated food cold, cook food to safe temperatures, store leftovers in covered and dated containers, and thaw frozen food in the refrigerator rather than on the counter.

Individuals' personal items such as razors, toothbrushes, towels and nail clippers are labeled and not shared. Staff teach and support individuals in hand washing and hygiene according to their plans.

The agency offers the hepatitis B vaccine series to employees with potential exposure, at no cost and within 10 working days of assignment, unless the employee has already been vaccinated or declines in writing. The Administrator keeps the vaccination records or declination in a confidential medical file.

After an exposure incident, the employee washes the area immediately, reports to the in-charge person and Residence Supervisor, and is sent for confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee. The agency records the event on an exposure incident report. Required post-exposure steps are carried out under the Exposure Control Plan.

When an individual shows signs of a communicable illness (fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or other symptoms), staff notify the nurse or health care provider the same day, follow their directions for treatment and isolation of the individual, and record the matter in the critical information log (PCS-07).

The nurse or Residence Supervisor reports any reportable communicable disease to the local health department as required by New Jersey law, and tells the Executive Director immediately. If an outbreak is suspected, the Executive Director follows the health department's directions and informs the individuals' guardians, DDD and the Office of Licensing as required (BSP-04, REC-02).

Staff who are ill with fever, vomiting, diarrhea or a contagious condition notify the Residence Supervisor before the shift and do not work until they meet the return-to-work criteria in the Infection Control Procedures. Coverage is arranged under STF-08.
Individuals' immunizations and screenings are tracked and coordinated with the primary care provider through nursing oversight (HW-02).
The Executive Director reviews infection incidents, exposure incidents and cleaning logs quarterly and reports trends to the quality improvement system (GOV-04).

policies.title: Food, Nutrition and Modified Diets
policies.applies_to: All residences operated by [AGENCY NAME]; direct support staff, nursing staff, Residence Supervisors and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals eat nutritious meals of their own choosing, can reach food in a homelike way, receive any modified diet or specialized feeding support safely, and are supported by trained staff.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports each individual to choose, shop for and take part in preparing meals and snacks, and to have access to food consistent with the individual's rights under IR-01. Menus and meals meet the food and nutrition requirements of subchapter 5 of N.J.A.C. 10:44A, which the Administrator confirms and records in the Compliance Calendar. Modified diets are provided only as ordered by a licensed prescriber or registered dietitian and are written into the individual's plan. Staff who support specialized feeding are trained before they do so under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7. Feeding tube duties are delegated to nursing, and direct support staff do not perform them unless the nurse delegates and trains them as the rules allow. Any limit on food access is treated as a rights restriction under IR-02.

definitions.definition: A diet ordered by a licensed prescriber or dietitian that changes the content, texture, consistency or amount of food or liquids, for medical, swallowing or other reasons.
Feeding techniques needed by individuals with eating, swallowing or other needs, including positioning and assistance, and tube feeding.
A tube placed to deliver nutrition, fluids or medication directly into the stomach or intestine; related duties are delegated to nursing.
The written instructions in the individual's plan describing diet order, texture, positioning, supervision level, adaptive equipment and mealtime support.

procedures: At admission and at least annually, the nurse or Residence Supervisor collects each individual's food preferences, cultural and religious practices, allergies, intolerances, medical dietary needs and swallowing or chewing concerns, and records them in the individual's plan (PCS-02).

Each individual helps plan menus and shopping. The Residence Supervisor holds a house meeting or individual conversations at least monthly to gather choices. Menus are kept in the home, show what was actually served and are kept as required by REC-01.

The agency offers three meals a day plus snacks at times that fit each individual's schedule, work and activities, and does not set a single mealtime for everyone unless people choose it. Individuals have access to food and drink at any time except where a rights restriction has been approved under IR-02.

Before any modified diet starts, staff obtain the written order from the licensed prescriber or dietitian and the nurse records it in the plan and in the dining plan. The order names the diet, texture, thickened liquids, calorie, or other requirement, the reason, and a review date.

The nurse posts a dining plan in a discreet but accessible place, such as inside a kitchen cabinet, and reviews it with all staff before they support that individual. Staff follow the dining plan exactly and report any change in swallowing, weight, appetite or choking incidents to the nurse the same day (HW-03).

Before staff support specialized feeding, they complete the specialized feeding training under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d) within 90 days of employment and are shown how to do it for each individual by the nurse. The trainer, date and signatures are recorded under STF-09. Staff who have not completed the training do not do specialized feeding.

Feeding tube duties, including formula, flushes and medications through a tube, are delegated and supervised by nursing. Direct support staff perform only the tasks the nurse delegates in writing for a named individual, after the nurse has trained them and checked their competency. Without a trained and delegated staff person on duty, the nurse is called for guidance and the Residence Supervisor makes sure nursing coverage is arranged.

Staff stay with individuals at risk of choking for the whole meal as stated in the plan, ensure correct posture, prepare food at the required texture, and keep adaptive utensils available. Staff know the choking emergency response and call 9-1-1 for choking emergencies (HW-03, HW-04).

Food is stored, prepared and served safely. Refrigerators are kept cold, food is stored covered and labeled with dates, and kitchens and equipment are kept clean. Food is thawed in the refrigerator (HES-03). Residents' own food is labeled and honored. Staff who prepare food wash hands first.

Staff record any notable meal refusal, weight change, allergic reaction or intake concern in the daily notes. The nurse reviews weights and diet concerns as required by the plan and refers to the prescriber or dietitian when needed.

Staff do not use food as a reward or punishment and do not withhold food or drink. Any proposal to limit food access for health reasons goes through the planning team and IR-02, with a written plan, consent, time limit and review.
The Administrator confirms the current menu, meal and food storage requirements in subchapter 5 at least annually and updates this policy and the Home Safety Inspection Checklist accordingly.
