policies.title: Transportation and Vehicle Safety
policies.applies_to: All residences operated by [AGENCY NAME]; all staff who drive or accompany individuals, and all individuals served
policies.purpose: To make sure individuals travel safely, in well-maintained vehicles, with trained and qualified staff, and that transportation problems are reported and corrected.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges transportation so individuals can reach medical appointments, work, community activities and places of their choice. Vehicles owned, leased or used by the agency are legally registered, insured, inspected and maintained. Staff who drive agency vehicles, or personal vehicles for agency business, hold a valid license and a satisfactory driving record check. Staff who support individuals with mobility devices are trained in mobility procedures and the safe use of the devices, including those needed for transport, under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d). Problems with transportation are critical information and are recorded in the critical information log. Support for public transit, rideshare and other community travel is encouraged consistent with each person's plan and with IR-01.

definitions.definition: Any vehicle owned, leased or regularly used by [AGENCY NAME] to transport individuals.
A wheelchair tie-down and occupant restraint system that meets manufacturer and safety standards.
A breakdown, accident, missed or late ride, unsafe condition, injury or behavior event during transport, or any lack of transport that affects an individual's care or activities.
A review of a driver's license status and driving history obtained from the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission or equivalent source.

procedures: Before a staff member drives any individual, the Administrator verifies a valid driver's license and obtains a current driving record check. The check is filed in the personnel file under STF-05, and staff are rechecked at least annually. Staff with a license suspension or disqualifying record do not drive.

The Executive Director keeps current registration, inspection and insurance for each agency vehicle, with minimum coverage appropriate for passenger transport. Copies are kept in the vehicle and in the administrative office. Staff who use personal vehicles for agency business must show proof of insurance.

Each agency vehicle is serviced on the manufacturer's schedule. The assigned driver completes a pre-trip check of tires, lights, brakes, fluids, seat belts, doors and any wheelchair lift or ramp before use, and records problems on the Vehicle Check Log. A vehicle with a safety defect is taken out of service until repaired.

Staff who support individuals with wheelchairs, walkers or other mobility devices complete the mobility and transport training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d) within 90 days of employment, taught by a qualified trainer (STF-09). The training includes safe use of lifts and ramps, securement of wheelchairs and occupant restraint. Staff who have not completed it do not transport mobility device users alone.

Before each trip, the driver confirms who is traveling, the destination, any needed medications, emergency information, equipment and support in the individual's plan. Where behavior or health supports apply, staff follow the transport instructions in the plan (BSP-01, HW-03).

All passengers use seat belts or an approved securement system at all times. Staff secure wheelchairs with a four-point tie-down and a lap and shoulder belt that comply with the manufacturer's instructions. Drivers do not use handheld phones and do not leave individuals unattended in a vehicle.

Staff ratios during transport are set by each individual's plan and the supervision needs of those riding. The driver is not the only person responsible for an individual who needs continuous supervision, and the Residence Supervisor assigns an additional staff person when required.

Each vehicle carries a first aid kit, a copy of emergency contacts, a charged phone, a flashlight and a fire extinguisher where the agency has determined these are needed. Staff carry the individual's face sheet and medication information on medical trips.

If a vehicle breaks down or an accident occurs, the driver moves everyone to safety, calls 9-1-1 for any injury or danger, then calls the Residence Supervisor or on-call administrator (STF-08). Individuals are evaluated by medical staff after any accident even if no injury is apparent. Where injury or other incident criteria apply, an incident report is made under BSP-04.

The driver records any other transportation problem, such as a missed ride, an unsafe condition or a behavior event, in the daily notes and the critical information log (PCS-07) before leaving the shift. The Residence Supervisor reviews the matter within 1 working day and corrects it.

Staff support individuals who choose to use public transit, rideshare, or other community travel through travel training and support set out in the individual plan (PCS-05). Staff do not limit travel except through the rights restriction process in IR-02.
The Executive Director reviews vehicle maintenance, driving record checks, accidents and transportation problems at least quarterly and reports trends to the quality improvement system (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains vehicle registration, insurance and inspections, and ensures staff drivers are qualified.
Assigns qualified drivers, reviews vehicle logs and transportation problems, and arranges repairs and added staff.
Drive safely, complete pre-trip checks, secure passengers and report transportation problems.
Obtains driver license verification and driving record checks and files them.
Trains staff in mobility device use and transport safety and documents it.

documentation: Driver license verification and driving record checks
Vehicle registration, inspection and insurance records
Vehicle Check Log and maintenance records
Mobility and transport training records
Daily notes and critical information log entries for transportation problems
Incident reports and accident reports

policies.title: Temperature and Utility Emergencies
policies.applies_to: All residences operated by [AGENCY NAME]; all staff, the Residence Supervisor, on-call administrators and individuals served
policies.purpose: To protect individuals when indoor temperatures become unsafe or utilities fail in situations where evacuation may not be required, and to make clear who decides what to do and who must be notified.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] addresses emergencies in which evacuation may not be required, including indoor air temperature below 68 degrees F or above 82 degrees F for four consecutive hours, as well as loss of heat, cooling, electricity, water or gas. Protective action starts as soon as conditions become unsafe, and staff do not wait for the four-hour mark when an individual is at risk. The in-charge person has authority to take immediate protective action, and the Residence Supervisor or on-call administrator decides whether to relocate individuals. Individuals who rely on powered medical equipment or are especially sensitive to heat or cold are identified in advance and have a plan.

definitions.definition: Indoor air temperature below 68 degrees F or above 82 degrees F for four consecutive hours, or any lower threshold at which an individual is at risk.
Loss of electricity, heat, air conditioning, water, gas or sewage service that affects health or safety.
A person who is more vulnerable to heat, cold or utility loss, for example because of age, medication, medical condition or reliance on powered equipment.
A pre-arranged alternate location where individuals can stay safely until the home is fit to return to.

procedures: Each home has at least one working thermometer in the main living area, and in other areas as the Residence Supervisor determines. Staff check the indoor temperature at least once each shift and record it on the Temperature Log. During heat waves and cold snaps, staff check every 2 hours.

When the indoor temperature goes below 68 or above 82 degrees F, the in-charge person records the time, tells the Residence Supervisor or on-call administrator (STF-08), and begins protective action immediately. The four-hour clock starts when the reading first falls outside the range, and the person logging it notes the start time.

Protective action for cold includes warm clothing and blankets, closing off unused rooms, safe supplemental heating that the Residence Supervisor approves (no gas ovens or unvented fuel heaters), warm fluids and watching for signs of hypothermia. Protective action for heat includes fans, cooling the home with approved equipment, closing blinds, extra fluids, light clothing, moving individuals to the coolest area and watching for signs of heat illness.

Staff watch each individual for signs of cold or heat illness. Individuals whose medications, health conditions or limited ability to communicate raise their risk are monitored more closely. Staff call the nurse for advice on any concern and call 9-1-1 for any life-threatening condition (HW-04).

If the home cannot be brought back within 68 to 82 degrees F within four consecutive hours, or earlier if anyone is at risk, the Residence Supervisor or on-call administrator decides whether to relocate individuals. The decision, the time and the name of the decision-maker are recorded.

For relocation, the administrator arranges transportation, staffing, medications, medical equipment, records and personal items, and goes to a pre-arranged relocation site named in the Emergency and Evacuation Plan, such as another [AGENCY NAME] home, a family member's home with consent, or a hotel with accessible rooms. Staff keep the staffing ratio required in each person's plan at the relocation site.

For loss of electricity, staff use flashlights and battery lanterns rather than candles. They keep refrigerated food closed, throw away food that has been above safe temperatures for more than 2 hours, and keep powered medical equipment running on battery or backup power or relocate the individual who needs it. The nurse is consulted about medications that need refrigeration.

For loss of water or sewage service, staff provide bottled water for drinking and hygiene, use hand sanitizer and safe toilet options, and relocate if conditions cannot be kept sanitary. For a gas or heating system failure with any suspected leak or carbon monoxide alarm, staff evacuate under HES-02.

The Residence Supervisor keeps contact numbers for the utility companies, heating and cooling repair services and the landlord posted in each home. A repair is requested immediately. The date, time and name of each call and each response are logged.

Each home keeps emergency supplies appropriate for its needs, such as flashlights, extra batteries, blankets, bottled water and a battery-powered radio. The Residence Supervisor checks them quarterly and replaces anything that is used or expired.

The Residence Supervisor identifies at-risk individuals at admission and annually and records in the Individual Evacuation Profile and plan the extra support each person needs for temperature and utility emergencies. Individuals who use oxygen concentrators, lifts, powered beds or other powered devices have a written backup plan.

The Executive Director or on-call administrator notifies guardians and family of any relocation, and notifies DDD and the Office of Licensing as required for an incident under BSP-04 and REC-02. The Executive Director records the incident and notifications in an incident report.

The in-charge person documents the event, including readings, actions taken, individuals' condition and the time services were restored, in the daily notes and critical information log (PCS-07). The Residence Supervisor reviews the event within 2 working days.

The Executive Director reviews temperature and utility events at least annually and includes corrective actions, such as upgrading heating and cooling systems, in the quality improvement system (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures working heating, cooling and utilities, funds repairs and approves relocation sites and notifications.
Decides on relocation, arranges staff, transport and repairs, and makes notifications.
Monitors temperature, starts protective action at once, calls the administrator and documents the event.
Check on individuals, follow protective measures and report signs of cold or heat illness.
Advises on at-risk individuals, medication storage and medical equipment during emergencies.

documentation: Temperature Log with time and reading for each check
Emergency and Evacuation Plan with relocation sites
Individual Evacuation Profiles noting at-risk individuals
Incident reports and notification records
Utility and repair call log
Daily notes and critical information log entries
Emergency supply check log

policies.title: Staff Coverage, Two-Week Schedule and In-Charge Designation
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Executive Director, Residence Supervisors, in-charge employees, direct support professionals (DSPs) and scheduling staff at every community residence and supervised apartment program operated by [AGENCY NAME]
federal: 29 CFR Part 516 (Fair Labor Standards Act recordkeeping: records of hours worked and pay must be kept)
policies.purpose: To make sure a qualified, trained and identifiable staff person is on duty and in charge whenever individuals are present. Coverage must match the approved program description and each individual's supervision needs. The written schedule must always be available for review.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will staff each residence according to its program description and the supervision needs in each individual's plan, in line with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8. For each residence, a written schedule covering at least two weeks will be kept on site. It will use staff members' full names, show the on-site coverage the program description requires, and name the employee in charge for every shift. Staff will be on site at all times when any individual is present in a group home or supervised apartment. N.J.A.C. 10:44A does not set a numeric staff-to-individual ratio or an awake-overnight rule. [AGENCY NAME] will therefore set daytime, evening and overnight coverage, including whether overnight staff are awake, from the program description and the individual plans. It will confirm that approach with the Office of Licensing and never staff below the level it has set. At least one person on each shift will have completed each specialized training the individuals on that shift require. Paid, trained agency staff who know the individuals will always be reachable for emergencies. No temporary agency worker will be designated in charge unless the conditions in STF-10 are met.

definitions.definition: A residence licensed under N.J.A.C. 10:44A for up to 16 individuals with developmental disabilities, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
An apartment serving up to four individuals, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, supported by staff from a staff residence or office.
The employee designated in writing on the schedule as responsible for the residence and the individuals during a given shift.
An employee who provides direct assistance, training and support to individuals, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
The approved description of the services and staffing [AGENCY NAME] provides at each residence, on file with the Office of Licensing and DDD.

procedures: The Administrator will keep a written staffing pattern for each residence. It will state the number of staff for each shift (day, evening, overnight, weekend), whether overnight staff are awake, and the basis for each. The basis will be the program description and the supervision levels in each individual's plan.

Before opening, and whenever an admission or a change in an individual's needs affects supervision, the Administrator will review the staffing pattern. The Administrator will confirm in writing with the Office of Licensing how overnight and other coverage is to be set, since no numeric ratio appears in N.J.A.C. 10:44A. The answer will be kept in the administrative file.

The Residence Supervisor will prepare a written schedule covering at least two consecutive weeks. It will list each staff person by full first and last name, not initials or nicknames, with the position and hours of each shift.

The schedule will name one in-charge employee for every shift. The in-charge employee must have completed orientation and the training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 and must know the individuals present and the emergency procedures.

The Residence Supervisor will post or keep the current two-week schedule at each residence where inspectors, staff and the on-call person can find it immediately. Past schedules stay on file as described in the Documentation section.

The Residence Supervisor will schedule so that a staff person is on site whenever any individual is present at a group home or supervised apartment. A shift may not start with fewer staff than the staffing pattern requires.

The Residence Supervisor will check each shift's roster against the specialized training matrix (STF-09). At least one person on every shift must have completed each specialized training needed by the individuals present (for example seizure response, feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, behavior support plan implementation). If no one on a shift is qualified, the Supervisor will change the schedule before the shift starts.

When no individual is present at the residence, such as when all are at day programs or on overnight visits, staff need not be on site. Trained, paid agency staff who know the individuals will still be reachable for emergencies, and the on-call plan in STF-08 will apply.

For supervised apartments, the Administrator will confirm that the staff residence or office is located so response time meets each individual's supervision needs. The assessed response time for each apartment will be recorded in the individual plan or program file.

When an employee calls out or does not arrive, the in-charge employee or the person who took the call will notify the Residence Supervisor or on-call person immediately. Staff already on duty will not leave until relieved. The on-call person will arrange a replacement who meets the training requirements. The change will be recorded on the schedule, and the original entry will not be erased.

If coverage cannot be filled, the on-call person will notify the Administrator at once. The Administrator will arrange emergency coverage under STF-08 and record the event and the corrective action taken.
Temporary agency staff may fill shifts only if they have completed the required training and orientation. They may not be designated in charge unless the conditions in STF-10 are met.

The Residence Supervisor will keep Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) records consistent with the schedule (GOV-06). Any difference between scheduled and worked time, and any manual correction, will be explained in writing and reviewed by the Administrator.

The Administrator will review actual coverage against the staffing pattern at least monthly and will report any uncovered shifts, repeated call-outs or unqualified in-charge assignments to the quality improvement process (GOV-04).
The Administrator will keep time and payroll records, including schedules and records of hours worked, for the period required by federal wage-hour recordkeeping rules.

responsibilities.duty: Sets and approves the staffing pattern, confirms coverage questions with the Office of Licensing, arranges emergency coverage and reviews coverage monthly.
Writes and posts the two-week schedule with full names, designates the in-charge employee for each shift, checks specialized training coverage and documents schedule changes.
Is accountable for the residence and the individuals during the shift, confirms required staff are present and notifies the Supervisor or on-call person of any gap.
Report on time, stay until relieved, and report absences and coverage problems immediately.
Responds to coverage and emergency calls and arranges qualified replacement staff (STF-08).

documentation: Written staffing pattern and its basis for each residence, with any confirmation from the Office of Licensing
Two-week schedules (current and past) with full staff names and the in-charge employee for each shift
Specialized training coverage matrix by shift
Call-out, replacement and emergency coverage logs
Assessed response time for each supervised apartment
EVV records and explanations of any schedule or time discrepancies
Monthly coverage review notes and time/payroll records

policies.title: Background Checks, Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Executive Director, licensee and owners, human resources staff, and all employees, contractors, temporary agency staff and volunteers who may have contact with individuals
policies.purpose: To protect individuals by making sure no person with a disqualifying criminal history, or a listing on the Central Registry or the Child Abuse Registry, is employed in or assigned to any role that may bring them into contact with individuals.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will complete required background screening before any person has contact with individuals. No agency head will be paid or contracted until criminal history clearance has been obtained under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69. The owner or licensee will also be checked if different from the agency head (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4). Every employee who may contact individuals must comply with the screening requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4. [AGENCY NAME] will check the Central Registry as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3 and will make sure no employee appears on the Department of Children and Families (DCF) Child Abuse Registry, as N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2 requires.

definitions.definition: The registry defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, which [AGENCY NAME] checks as part of employee screening.
The DCF registry of individuals with substantiated findings of child abuse or neglect, which must be checked for every employee.
The result of the State Police and FBI criminal history check required under N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69.
The community agency head, licensee or executive director responsible for the agency, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
Any in-person, supervised or unsupervised interaction with individuals in the residence, in the community or in transport.

procedures: The Administrator will confirm in writing with the Office of Licensing, before the first hire, the current fingerprinting procedure, how results are returned, and the timelines for criminal history clearance. These details are not set out in this manual and will be added to the hiring checklist once confirmed.

Before the agency head is paid or contracted, [AGENCY NAME] will obtain criminal history clearance for that person. It will do the same for any owner or licensee who is a different person, and will keep the clearance on file. No compensation, contract or access to individuals will begin before clearance is received.

For every other applicant who may contact individuals, the Administrator or designee will make any job offer conditional on completion of all screening. The applicant will sign a screening consent form and a statement disclosing any criminal charges or convictions and any registry listing.

Before any contact with individuals, the designee will submit the applicant for criminal history checking as directed by the Office of Licensing and will verify the Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry status. No applicant will work alone or have unsupervised contact until all results are in the file and reviewed.

The Administrator will review each result personally. Any record or registry hit will be evaluated against N.J.S.A. 30:6D-63 through 69 and Office of Licensing guidance. A person with a disqualifying result will not be hired or assigned to a role with contact with individuals.

The designee will record the date each check was requested, the date the result was received, the outcome and the reviewer's name and signature on a screening checklist in the personnel file (STF-05).

Contract workers, temporary agency staff and volunteers who may contact individuals will meet the same screening requirements. [AGENCY NAME] will obtain written proof of clearance from the staffing agency or complete the checks itself. Proof will be on file before the first shift.

[AGENCY NAME] will repeat Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry checks at least annually as its own practice, and at any time the Administrator learns of a concern. Results will be filed in the personnel file.

Each employee must report to the Administrator within one business day any new arrest, charge, conviction, registry listing or substantiated finding. Failure to report is grounds for discipline up to termination.

If a current employee is found to have a disqualifying result, the Administrator will remove the employee from all contact with individuals immediately, document the action, and notify the Office of Licensing or DDD if required. Employment decisions will follow STF-06 and agency personnel procedures.
The Administrator will check that the New Employee Orientation Checklist (STF-03) includes the employee's acknowledgment of the screening requirements and of the duty to report in step 9.
Screening results will be kept confidential and stored in a locked or access-controlled record, separate from general personnel information (IR-05).
During quality reviews (GOV-04), the Administrator will audit a sample of personnel files each quarter to confirm every employee, contractor and volunteer has complete, dated screening documentation.

responsibilities.duty: Obtains and files own and owner clearances before payment or contract, reviews all results, makes hiring and removal decisions and confirms procedures with the Office of Licensing.
Initiates checks, tracks requests and results, prepares the screening checklist and maintains annual registry rechecks.
Does not schedule any person for contact with individuals until the Administrator confirms clearance.
Consent to screening and report any new charge, conviction or registry listing within one business day.

documentation: Criminal history clearance for the agency head and any separate owner/licensee, dated before pay or contract start
Screening checklist per person showing request dates, result dates, outcome and reviewer signature
Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry results at hire and annually
Signed consent and disclosure forms and signed duty-to-report acknowledgments
Staffing agency/contractor clearance proof
Records of any removal from duty and related notifications
Quarterly personnel file audit results

policies.title: Direct Support Professional Qualifications, Orientation and Basic Training
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Executive Director, human resources staff, Residence Supervisors, trainers and all newly hired and current direct support professionals (DSPs)
policies.purpose: To make sure every DSP meets minimum qualifications, completes orientation and completes required basic training within the required time. Required training will be documented and available for inspection.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will hire as DSPs only persons who are at least 18 years old, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, can communicate with the individuals they support, and can provide the direct assistance or training the job requires (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5). Every new employee will complete the New Employee Orientation Checklist required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2. Within 90 days of employment, each DSP will complete the DDD basic training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7: DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid and CPR from an entity that complies with ECC guidelines. A valid certificate for each will be on file. Training in all relevant agency policies not covered in orientation will be delivered by a qualified trainer. Medication administration is permitted only after medication training and demonstrated competency (HW-01).

definitions.definition: The Division-required basic training course that every DSP must complete within 90 days of employment.
A first aid and CPR training provider whose courses comply with Emergency Cardiovascular Care guidelines, and who issues a valid certificate.
The written checklist [AGENCY NAME] uses to document orientation topics reviewed with each new employee, required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2.
A person with the knowledge, credentials and experience to teach the subject, as described in STF-09.
An employee who provides direct assistance, training and support to individuals, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.

procedures: Before offering a DSP job, the hiring manager will verify age (government-issued identification) and obtain proof of a high school diploma or equivalent. Copies go in the personnel file.

During the interview and reference check, the hiring manager will assess whether the applicant can communicate with the individuals who live in the residence, including any need for sign language, other languages, picture systems or communication devices. The assessment will be documented. An applicant who cannot communicate effectively with the individuals will not be assigned to them.

The hiring manager will review the job description and assess the applicant's ability to provide the direct assistance or training the job requires, such as personal care, lifting and transfer, medication support or community support. The assessment will be documented.
No applicant will begin work until screening is complete (STF-02), the health requirements are met (STF-04) and the personnel file contains the items above.

On the first day, the Residence Supervisor or designee will begin orientation using the New Employee Orientation Checklist. The checklist will be reconciled against the topics the Office of Licensing identifies as required, and the Administrator will keep that reconciliation on file.

Orientation will cover at least the agency philosophy, individual rights, abuse/neglect/exploitation prohibition and reporting, emergency and evacuation procedures, medical emergencies and calls to 9-1-1, incident reporting, confidentiality, personal funds, the critical information log, and the grievance procedure. The new employee and the orienting staff person will both sign and date the completed checklist.

During the first shifts, the new DSP will work alongside an experienced, fully trained DSP. The new DSP will not be designated in charge and will not administer medication until training and competency are documented.

The Residence Supervisor will enroll each new DSP in DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid and CPR on or before the first day of work. All three must be completed within 90 days of the date of employment. The supervisor will track the due date on the training tracker.

Each DSP will give the training coordinator the original certificate within five days of completing each course. Certificates must be valid on the date of the check. The coordinator will file them with the training records.

The Administrator will deliver, or arrange for a qualified trainer to deliver, training on all agency policies relevant to the DSP's job that were not covered in orientation. Each session will be recorded with the date, topic and the signatures of trainer and trainee.

Specialized training required within 90 days of employment will follow STF-09. Medication training and competency will follow HW-01. The Residence Supervisor will assign shifts so that no DSP performs a task before required training for that task is completed.

Each month the training coordinator will review the tracker. Any DSP who is within 14 days of a 90-day deadline, or who is overdue, will be reported to the Administrator. Overdue DSPs will not be scheduled alone or as in-charge until training is complete.

Any DSP whose first aid/CPR certificate lapses will be rescheduled for retraining before the certificate expires. The Residence Supervisor will not count a DSP with an expired certificate toward required coverage on a shift.
[AGENCY NAME] may provide additional training beyond what N.J.A.C. 10:44A requires. Additional training will be documented in the same manner.
The Administrator will report training completion rates, late completions and corrective actions to the quality improvement committee quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures hiring standards are met, approves the orientation checklist, ensures training is provided and monitors compliance.
Verifies age, education, communication ability and ability to perform the job before hire.
Conducts orientation, schedules new DSPs with experienced staff and prevents untrained staff from performing restricted duties.
Tracks 90-day deadlines, files certificates and training records, and reports overdue training.
Complete orientation and all required training on time and submit certificates.

documentation: Proof of age and education, and documented assessments of communication ability and ability to provide assistance
Signed and dated New Employee Orientation Checklist and the reconciliation to required topics
Valid certificates for DDD Shifting Expectations, preventing abuse and neglect, and first aid/CPR
Records of training on agency policies with curriculum, dates and trainer/trainee signatures
Training tracker with 90-day due dates and Division-required results
Training records kept at the administrative office

policies.title: Employee Health and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees who may have contact with individuals, including direct support professionals, supervisors, nurses, contractors and temporary agency staff, and the Administrator/Executive Director
federal: 29 CFR 1910.1030 (OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard: exposure control plan, hepatitis B vaccine offer, training and post-exposure follow-up)
policies.purpose: To protect individuals and staff from communicable disease by documenting tuberculosis (TB) screening and basic health clearance before work. It also provides for protection from workplace blood and body fluid exposure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will require each employee who may contact individuals to complete TB screening as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.4. The screening is either a Mantoux tuberculin skin test (5 TU PPD) or an IGRA blood test, done within one year before or upon beginning work. Written results will be given to [AGENCY NAME] and kept in the confidential employee health record. The Administrator will confirm with the Office of Licensing whether the current rule requires repeat testing and the repeat interval, and the agency will follow it. Until that is confirmed, [AGENCY NAME] will repeat TB screening annually as its own practice. The Administrator will also confirm the time frame required for staff physicals under the 2023 amendments and follow it. [AGENCY NAME] will also protect staff under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard.

definitions.definition: A 5 TU PPD skin test read by a qualified health professional 48 to 72 hours after placement.
Interferon-gamma release assay, a TB blood test accepted in place of the skin test.
A documented prior positive TB skin test or IGRA, for which repeat skin testing is generally not appropriate and follow-up is directed by a licensed clinician.
The confidential record of an employee's TB results, health clearance and exposure follow-up, kept separate from the general personnel file.

procedures: The Administrator will confirm in writing with the Office of Licensing the current TB requirements. The confirmation will cover repeat testing interval, handling of previous positive results, and the time frame for staff physicals. It will be filed and used to update the hiring checklist.

The hiring manager will tell each applicant in the conditional offer that TB screening is required. The employee may use a provider of their choice, and [AGENCY NAME] will give the employee a copy of this policy.

Before or upon the first day of work, the employee will submit written results of a Mantoux skin test (5 TU PPD) or IGRA blood test completed within the preceding year. The written result must show the date, test type, result and the signature or stamp of the health care provider.

If a skin test is used, the employee will also return for the reading by a qualified health professional and submit the written reading. An employee whose test has not been read will not work alone with individuals.

If the employee reports a previous positive result, the employee will give the licensee documentation of the prior result and a written clearance from a licensed clinician. The clearance will follow the rule and the clinician's direction, such as symptom screening or chest imaging. The Administrator will file it.

If a test is positive or the employee has symptoms of active TB, the employee will be removed from contact with individuals the same day. The employee may return only with written medical clearance from a licensed clinician or the local health department.
The Administrator will report any suspected or confirmed active TB case to the local health department and will cooperate with contact tracing. Confidentiality will be maintained (IR-05).
[AGENCY NAME] will obtain the written physical or health clearance for new employees as required by the time frame confirmed in step 1 and will keep it in the employee health record.

The human resources designee will track the due date of every repeat screening and will notify employees at least 30 days in advance. Employees overdue for screening will not be scheduled until written results are received.
Under 29 CFR 1910.1030, the Administrator will maintain a written exposure control plan covering tasks that carry exposure to blood or body fluids. The plan will be reviewed annually.
[AGENCY NAME] will offer hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure risk within the time the standard requires. Declinations will be signed and filed.
Employees will receive bloodborne pathogens training at hire and annually, covering universal precautions, protective equipment, sharps handling and exposure response (HES-03).

After any exposure incident, the in-charge employee will direct immediate first aid and wound washing and notify the Administrator. The Administrator will arrange a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up at no cost to the employee and will document the incident.
Employees with a communicable illness, such as vomiting, diarrhea, fever or rash, will not work with individuals until symptom-free for the period set by HES-03 or cleared by a provider.
The Administrator will review TB and health file completeness quarterly as part of quality improvement (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Confirms current requirements with the Office of Licensing, removes employees from duty when required, handles public health reporting and maintains the exposure control plan.
Collects results, maintains the employee health record, tracks due dates and notifies employees.
Does not schedule employees without documented screening and sends symptomatic employees home.
Obtain screening on time, report symptoms and exposures and cooperate with follow-up.

documentation: Written TB results (test type, date, result, provider signature) for each employee
Clinician clearance for any previous positive result
Written physical/health clearance as required
Confirmation from the Office of Licensing of current repeat testing and physical requirements
Hepatitis B vaccination records or signed declinations
Bloodborne pathogens training records and the exposure control plan
Exposure incident reports and follow-up records
Tracking log of due dates

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: Administrator/Executive Director, human resources staff, Residence Supervisors and the training coordinator
federal: 29 CFR Part 516 (Fair Labor Standards Act recordkeeping)
8 CFR 274a.2 (Form I-9 employment eligibility verification and retention)
policies.purpose: To keep complete, accurate, secure and current records for every employee and contractor. This lets [AGENCY NAME] show inspectors, DDD and other reviewers that each person is qualified, screened, trained and authorized to work.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will maintain a personnel file for every employee, containing the items listed below, and will keep training records at the administrative office as N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 requires. The licensee will verify professional credentials required by law for any employed or contracted professional, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.5. A written job description for each position on the table of organization will be kept and made available to DDD for review under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4. Personnel files will be complete before the employee works unsupervised and will be available to the Office of Licensing during announced and unannounced inspections.

definitions.definition: The record for each employee containing hiring, qualification, screening, health, training and performance documents.
A separate confidential record of TB results and health information (STF-04).
The record of curriculum, dated trainer and trainee signatures, certificates and Division-required results kept at the administrative office.
A license, certification or registration required by law for a professional role, such as nurse, therapist or behavior analyst.

procedures: The human resources designee will open a personnel file for each new employee before the first day of work. The file will be organized by a standard table of contents so missing items are visible at a glance.

The file will contain the signed application and resume, reference checks, job description signed by the employee, and proof of age and education (high school diploma or equivalent for DSPs; the degree and experience documentation required for the Administrator).

The file will contain screening records from STF-02: criminal history clearance, Central Registry result and Child Abuse Registry result, with dates. It will also contain the employee's signed acknowledgment of the duty to report new charges or listings.
The file will contain, or cross-reference, the employee health record: TB screening results and the physical or health clearance required by STF-04.
The file will contain the employee's controlled dangerous substance testing results as required by STF-07, kept in a confidential section.

The file will contain the signed New Employee Orientation Checklist and a record of ongoing training. The training record will include certificates for first aid and CPR, DDD Shifting Expectations, and preventing abuse and neglect, specialized training, and annual medication competency (STF-03, STF-09, HW-01).

The training coordinator will keep each employee's training records at the administrative office. They will include the curriculum or training plan, dated trainer and trainee signatures and Division-required results.

The Administrator will verify, before an employed or contracted professional works with individuals, any license or credential required by law. Verification will be done directly with the licensing board and documented with the date, the credential number and the expiration date. The designee will track expirations.

The human resources designee will complete Form I-9 within the required federal time frame, examine original documents and retain the form as federal rules require. I-9 forms will be kept separate from the general personnel file.

The Administrator will keep a written job description for each position on the table of organization and will make job descriptions available to DDD. Job descriptions will be updated when duties change.

Personnel records will be kept in locked cabinets or access-controlled electronic systems. Only the Administrator, the human resources designee, the employee's supervisor (limited) and authorized reviewers may access them. Medical and test results will be kept separately and confidentially.
Employees may review their own files on request, in the presence of the human resources designee. Employees will not remove or alter file contents.

The training coordinator will run a monthly check of all files for missing, invalid or expiring items, such as certificates or credentials, and will give the Administrator a list of corrections needed with due dates.
The Administrator will complete a personnel file audit at least quarterly. Findings will be reported to the quality improvement committee (GOV-04).
When an inspector requests staff files, schedules, credentials or screening records, the Administrator will produce them promptly (GOV-07). A copy of each item provided will be logged.

Time and payroll records, including hours worked, will be retained for the period required under federal wage-hour recordkeeping rules. Personnel files of former employees will be kept for at least [RETENTION PERIOD] and then securely destroyed according to the agency's records policy.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures files are complete, verifies professional credentials, maintains job descriptions and conducts quarterly file audits.
Creates and maintains personnel files, completes I-9s, tracks expirations and secures records.
Keeps training records at the administrative office and tracks certificate and competency dates.
Does not schedule employees whose files are incomplete in any required element, and reports changes in credentials.

documentation: Personnel file with standard table of contents for each employee
Application, references, education proof and signed job description
Screening, TB/health and controlled dangerous substance testing records
Orientation checklist and training records with certificates and signatures
Professional credential verification log with expiration tracking
Form I-9 files kept separately
Table of organization and job descriptions for DDD review
Monthly deficiency lists, quarterly audit results and inspector request log

policies.title: Staff Conduct and Professional Boundaries
policies.applies_to: All employees, contractors, temporary agency staff, volunteers, the Administrator/Executive Director and members of the governing authority
policies.purpose: To set clear expectations for professional conduct so individuals are treated with respect, are free from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and are not placed at risk by boundary violations.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] prohibits abuse, neglect and exploitation of any individual in writing and requires every person covered by this policy to report each allegation (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2). Exploitation includes using an individual or an individual's resources for another person's profit or advantage, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3. No staff person will handle an individual's money or property except under the personal funds procedure (IR-06). Staff must be able to communicate with the individuals they support and must respect each individual's rights and dignity. This policy also sets rules on gifts, loans, personal relationships, social media and discipline. These rules are [AGENCY NAME] policy, because N.J.A.C. 10:44A does not specify them.

definitions.definition: Any act, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3, that harms or is likely to harm an individual, including physical, verbal, emotional and sexual abuse.
The act or process of using an individual or the individual's resources for another person's profit or advantage, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.
The limit between a staff person's professional role and any personal, financial, romantic or social relationship with an individual or the individual's family.
A relationship in which a staff person has a second role with an individual, such as friend, landlord, employer, romantic partner or business partner.
Altering or making false entries in a record, as defined in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.3.

procedures: At hire and annually, each employee will read this policy and sign an acknowledgment. The signed acknowledgment goes in the personnel file (STF-05). Contractors and volunteers will sign before any contact with individuals.

Staff will treat each individual as an adult with dignity. Staff will use the individual's preferred name, speak respectfully, offer choices, protect privacy in personal care and never use threats, ridicule, punishment or coercion.

Staff will never abuse, neglect or exploit an individual. They must report any suspected or witnessed abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately under BSP-03 and BSP-04, without waiting for proof or for permission from a supervisor.

Staff will not borrow money or property from an individual, accept a loan, sell items to an individual, use an individual's property, or use an individual's money, benefits, bank account, cards or belongings for any personal purpose.

Staff may not hold, spend or manage an individual's funds outside the personal funds procedure (IR-06). Any handling of funds must be recorded and receipted, and countersigned as that policy requires.

Staff will not accept gifts, tips, bequests or favors from an individual or family. A gift of nominal value, such as a card or a shared snack, may be accepted only with the Residence Supervisor's approval and is recorded. Staff will report any offer of a gift or a request for one.

Staff will not engage in any romantic, sexual or intimate relationship with an individual. Staff will not have any financial or dual relationship with an individual or their guardian or family. Staff will report any attempt to create one to the Administrator.

Staff will not take an individual to their own home or on personal outings, or give a personal phone number or address, unless it is an approved part of the individual's plan and the Administrator has approved it in advance in writing.

Staff will not post, photograph or record individuals, or share their names, information or images on social media or personal devices. Photos or video may be taken only for agency purposes with the written consent of the individual or guardian (IR-05).
Staff will not use alcohol or controlled dangerous substances while on duty, and will not report to work impaired. Testing requirements are in STF-07.

Staff will not use physical force or restrictive interventions except as allowed by BSP-02 and an approved plan. Staff will not use or threaten punishment, withholding of food, visits or belongings as a consequence.
Staff will document accurately and truthfully. Falsifying records, including schedules, logs, EVV entries, medication records and incident reports, is prohibited.
Staff must maintain confidentiality and must not discuss an individual's information except with authorized persons who need it to provide supports (IR-05).

Staff will report to the Residence Supervisor or Administrator any conflict of interest, any boundary concern and any conduct by a coworker that appears to violate this policy. No one will retaliate against a person who reports in good faith.

The Administrator will review each reported concern promptly. Where there is an allegation of abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator will follow BSP-03 and BSP-04 and remove the accused from contact with individuals while it is investigated.

A confirmed violation of this policy will result in discipline up to and including termination, according to the agency's progressive discipline procedure. The Administrator will record each action in the personnel file and will make any required reports to external authorities.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces this policy, reviews boundary concerns, directs investigations and decides on discipline.
Models professional conduct, approves or declines nominal gifts, reports concerns and monitors staff interactions with individuals.
Follow this policy, report violations and concerns and sign annual acknowledgments.
Ensures the Administrator applies this policy equally and without retaliation, including to the Administrator.

documentation: Signed annual acknowledgments of this policy
Gift approval and nominal-gift log
Records of boundary concerns, investigations and outcomes
Disciplinary actions in personnel files
Written approvals for any off-duty or personal contact tied to an individual's plan
Consents for photos and recordings

policies.title: Employee Controlled Dangerous Substance Testing
policies.applies_to: All applicants and employees of [AGENCY NAME] who will work or are working in any community residence, including direct support professionals, residence supervisors, nurses on the agency payroll, on-call staff, and the Executive Director/agency head.
policies.purpose: To keep individuals safe by making sure that no person who provides supports at [AGENCY NAME] is impaired by a controlled dangerous substance, and to meet the requirement in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)18 that the procedure manual contain written procedures for testing employees for controlled dangerous substances in accordance with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] tests employees for controlled dangerous substances under a written program designed to conform to N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5. The program includes pre-employment testing and random testing of employees. The Administrator confirms the current testing requirements in the statute and in any Department or DDD guidance at each annual manual review, and revises this policy and the testing program when the requirements change. No employee may provide supports while impaired. A verified positive result, or a refusal to test, is addressed under this policy and may lead to discipline up to and including termination. Testing is applied fairly and consistently, results are kept confidential, and the program is carried out with respect for the dignity of the employee.

definitions.definition: A drug or substance regulated as a controlled dangerous substance under New Jersey law, or a substance listed in the agency's testing panel, which is set in accordance with N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5.
A CDS test completed, with a verified result, before a new employee is scheduled to work alone or provide supports to any individual.
A test of employees chosen by an unpredictable, documented selection method that gives every covered employee an equal chance of selection each time.
A test required when a supervisor documents specific, observable signs that an employee may be impaired while on duty.

A licensed physician engaged by the testing vendor who reviews laboratory results and any legitimate medical explanation (such as a valid prescription) before a result is reported as verified positive.
A laboratory-confirmed positive result that the MRO has reviewed and has not attributed to a legitimate medical explanation.

procedures: The Administrator designates a Testing Coordinator ([TESTING COORDINATOR NAME]) and contracts with a certified laboratory/collection vendor ([TESTING VENDOR]) that uses a chain-of-custody process and an MRO.

Each time this manual is reviewed (annually, under GOV-03), the Administrator checks the text of N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 and any Department or DDD guidance, and records the check and any program changes in the manual review log.

Before an offer of employment becomes final, the Human Resources designee gives each applicant the written CDS testing notice and the consent form. The applicant signs and dates both, and the designee places them in the confidential testing file.

The applicant completes the pre-employment test within [NUMBER] business days of the offer. The applicant may not work shifts, be counted in staffing, or have unsupervised contact with individuals until a negative or MRO-cleared result is received.

The Testing Coordinator reviews the result when it arrives. A negative or MRO-cleared result is recorded on the testing log, and the Human Resources designee notes in the personnel file only that the requirement is met. The test report itself is not placed in the general personnel file.

Each [QUARTER/MONTH], the Testing Coordinator makes the random selection with a documented method (for example, a computer-generated list of all covered employee IDs). The coordinator records the date, the method, the number selected, and who witnessed the selection, and keeps the results sealed from supervisors until notice is given.

The Testing Coordinator notifies each selected employee on the day the employee is on duty and sends the employee to the collection site immediately or within the time stated in the notice. The employee's supervisor arranges coverage so required staffing is maintained, and the employee is paid for testing time.

If a supervisor sees specific signs of possible impairment (for example, slurred speech, unsteady gait, odor, or erratic behavior), a second manager, where available, confirms the observations. The supervisor completes the Reasonable-Suspicion Observation Form, removes the employee from duty, arranges safe transportation (the employee may not drive), and sends the employee for a test.

If an employee is removed from duty, the supervisor first makes sure the individuals are safely supervised by calling the on-call person under STF-08 and bringing in a replacement. Any concern about an individual's health or safety is reported under BSP-04.
An employee who refuses to test, delays the test without a valid reason, or tampers with a specimen is treated as having a verified positive result.

The MRO contacts an employee whose result is positive and gives the employee a chance to explain it. The employee may, at the employee's own request, ask for retesting of the original specimen as permitted by the laboratory's procedures.

After a verified positive result, the Administrator meets with the employee, removes the employee from all duties involving individuals pending a decision, and decides on action under the agency's personnel policies, which may include termination. The Administrator may offer referral to an employee assistance or treatment resource, but referral does not require the agency to return the employee to direct support duties.
If the employee holds a license or certification that carries its own reporting duties, the Administrator determines whether a report to the licensing body is required and documents that decision.

The Testing Coordinator keeps all testing records (consent forms, chain-of-custody forms, notices, results, observation forms, and the testing log) in a locked or access-controlled confidential testing file, separate from the general personnel file. Only the Administrator, the Testing Coordinator, and persons authorized by law may see them.

Once a year the Testing Coordinator reports to the Administrator the number of pre-employment, random, and reasonable-suspicion tests performed and the number of verified positives and refusals, without employee names. The Administrator reviews the report as part of the Continuous Quality Improvement System (GOV-04).
The Administrator makes the testing records available to the Office of Licensing during inspections, with employee identifying information protected as the law requires.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, approves the testing vendor, makes the final decision on discipline after a verified positive result, and confirms that the testing standard matches N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5 at each annual review.
Schedules tests, conducts random selection, notifies employees, maintains the testing log and confidential file, and prepares the annual summary.
Gives the notice and consent form to applicants, holds job offers until pre-employment results are received, and keeps the personnel file free of test reports.
Documents signs of impairment, removes employees from duty when necessary, secures replacement coverage, and keeps individuals safe.
Report to work free from impairment, report prescribed medications that may affect safe performance to the supervisor in confidence, and take required tests promptly.

documentation: Annual manual review entry confirming the current testing requirements of N.J.S.A. 30:6D-9.5
Signed employee CDS testing notice and consent form
Pre-employment, random, and reasonable-suspicion test records, including chain-of-custody forms and MRO reports
Random selection record (date, method, witness)
Reasonable-suspicion observation forms
Testing log with dates and outcomes
Written disciplinary or employment decision after a verified positive result or refusal
Annual testing summary reviewed under the CQI system

policies.title: Emergency Coverage and On-Call Procedures
policies.applies_to: All residence staff, residence supervisors, the on-call administrator and designated on-call staff, and the Executive Director at every group home, supervised apartment, and supportive living site operated by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure someone qualified can be reached and can respond at all times, including nights, weekends, and holidays, and to meet the requirement in N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)7 for emergency coverage and on-call procedures, together with the staff coverage requirements of N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a written on-call system that is in effect 24 hours a day, every day of the year. At a group home or supervised apartment, staff are on site whenever any individual is present, in line with each individual's supervision needs (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(d)). When no individuals are present at a residence, staff need not be on site, but trained, paid agency staff who are familiar with the individuals are available for emergencies (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(c)). An on-call roster is published and posted so every staff member knows whom to call and how. Life-threatening medical emergencies are always handled by calling 9-1-1 first, never by waiting for the on-call person (see HW-04). Emergency coverage is arranged so that no individual is left without required supervision.

definitions.definition: A trained, paid employee of [AGENCY NAME] who is assigned for a scheduled period to be reachable by phone and able to respond, directly or by arranging coverage, to emergencies and staffing gaps.
A second trained, paid employee who takes the call if the primary on-call person does not answer within the response standard.
Replacement or additional staff sent to a residence, or available to be sent, when a staff member is absent, an emergency occurs, or additional supervision is needed.
The employee designated on the written schedule as responsible for the residence for a shift (see STF-01).

procedures: The Administrator designates on-call persons for each week, naming a primary and a back-up. Each person must be a paid employee who has finished orientation and is familiar with the individuals and residences they cover. The Administrator makes sure each on-call person has current training in medication administration (when the person may need to administer), first aid, CPR, and the specialized trainings relevant to the covered residences (see STF-09).

The Administrator publishes the on-call roster at least [NUMBER] days before the week begins. It shows each on-call person's full name, cell phone number, the dates and hours of coverage, and the back-up. The Administrator posts the roster in each residence's staff area and the administrative office, and gives a copy to every employee and to the in-charge employee of each shift.
The on-call phone number for the agency is [PHONE]. It is answered by a person, not only a voicemail. If the call goes to voicemail, the caller leaves a message and calls the back-up number.

The on-call person must answer or return a call within [NUMBER] minutes. If the person does not, the caller calls the back-up on-call person, and then the Administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) at [PHONE]. The on-call person must be able to reach any covered residence within a response time that fits the supervision needs of the individuals living there. The Administrator documents the response standard for each residence.

In any life-threatening emergency, staff on site call 9-1-1 first, then give first aid or CPR as trained, then call the on-call person (see HW-04). Waiting for the on-call person before calling 9-1-1 is never allowed.

If a staff member cannot work a scheduled shift, the staff member calls the in-charge employee and the on-call person as soon as the problem is known, and at least [NUMBER] hours before the shift when possible. The staff member does not leave a residence until relieved if doing so would leave an individual without required supervision.

The on-call person finds coverage by contacting qualified employees on the call-out list in order, then qualified per diem staff, then temporary agency staff under STF-10. The on-call person checks that replacement staff meet training requirements for the individuals at the residence, including the specialized training required for that shift (STF-09). The on-call person documents each call attempt and the outcome.

The on-call person may not designate a temporary agency employee as in-charge unless STF-10 is fully met. If no qualified in-charge replacement is available, the on-call person or the Residence Supervisor goes to the residence.

Where staff are on site while individuals are present, the on-call person must not allow staff to leave a residence below the staffing described in its program description and on the written schedule. If coverage cannot be arranged, the on-call person notifies the Administrator immediately, and the Administrator decides on further action, which may include assigning management staff to the shift.

When no individuals are present at a residence, the on-call person is the paid agency staff member available for emergencies at that residence, such as a fire alarm, a break-in, a utility failure, or a call from the individuals or a family member while they are away. The on-call person goes to the site or arranges for someone to go.

For a major emergency or evacuation (see HES-02), the in-charge employee follows the residence's emergency plan, notifies the on-call person, and the on-call person notifies the Administrator, who makes sure relocation, staffing, and notifications occur.

For utility or temperature emergencies (see HES-06), including indoor air below 68°F or above 82°F for four consecutive hours, the in-charge employee notifies the on-call person, who contacts the Administrator and arranges repairs or relocation as needed.

The on-call person notifies the Administrator of any incident that may be a reportable incident, alleged abuse, neglect or exploitation, a missing person, a serious injury, or a death, and helps the in-charge employee follow BSP-03, BSP-04, BSP-05, or HW-05 as applicable.

The on-call person completes an On-Call Log entry for every call, recording the date and time received, the caller, the nature of the problem, actions taken, who was sent to the residence and when they arrived, and the time resolved. The on-call person gives the log and any open issues to the next on-call person at handoff. The in-charge employee also records the event in the critical-information log (see PCS-07).

The Administrator reviews on-call logs monthly for response times, repeated coverage gaps, and unresolved problems, and brings the results to the Continuous Quality Improvement System (see GOV-04). Roster errors or missed calls are corrected through retraining or other action.

The Administrator tests the on-call system at least [QUARTERLY/SEMI-ANNUALLY] by an unannounced test call, records the response time, and corrects any problems found. The on-call roster and this policy are reviewed at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Designates on-call persons, publishes the roster, sets and monitors response standards, reviews logs, and acts when coverage cannot be arranged.
Remains reachable, responds within the standard, arranges qualified coverage, goes to the residence when needed, notifies the Administrator of serious events, and keeps the On-Call Log.
Keeps the posted roster current at the residence, trains staff on how to use the on-call system, and assists in finding coverage.
Calls 9-1-1 for life-threatening emergencies, calls the on-call person, stays at the residence until relieved, and records events in the critical-information log.
Know how to reach the on-call person, report absences promptly, and never leave an individual without required supervision.

documentation: On-call roster with names, phone numbers, dates and hours, including the back-up (kept on file for each week)
On-Call Log entries for each call
Call-out list for replacement staff
Record of qualifications and training of each on-call person
Critical-information log entries (see PCS-07)
Results of unannounced on-call tests and corrective actions
Monthly Administrator review of on-call activity

policies.title: Specialized Training and Qualified Trainers
policies.applies_to: All direct support professionals, residence supervisors, in-charge employees, on-call staff, and temporary agency staff assigned to a [AGENCY NAME] residence, and all persons who deliver training for the agency.
policies.purpose: To make sure staff are trained in the specific needs of the individuals they support, that each shift at each site includes at least one person with each required specialized training, and that policy training is delivered by a qualified trainer, in line with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 and 2.8(b).
policies.policy: Each direct support professional completes the specialized training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(d) within 90 days of employment. This includes feeding techniques (with feeding tube duties delegated to nursing), mobility devices and transport, seizure, physical and medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans, to the extent they apply to individuals supported. Specialized training identified by the Department, a placing agency, or [AGENCY NAME] is completed within the same 90 days. At least one person on each shift at each site has completed each specialized training required for that site (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(b)). Training in agency policies that is not covered in orientation is delivered by a qualified trainer (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(c) and (g)). Medication training and demonstrated competency come before staff administer any medication, and competency is demonstrated every year (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(b); see HW-01). [AGENCY NAME] may provide additional training beyond what is required without Division approval.

definitions.definition: Training in the specific needs of the individuals at a site, including feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure/physical/medical needs, mental health needs, and behavior support plans, and any further training identified by the Department, a placing agency, or [AGENCY NAME].

A person who meets the qualifications [AGENCY NAME] has documented for the subject taught, consistent with N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(g) and the Department's current requirements, and who has been approved in writing by the Administrator. The Administrator confirms the Department's current qualified-trainer standards at each annual manual review.
The written curriculum and schedule of the trainings the agency requires, who must take them, who may deliver them, and the due dates.
A chart for each residence showing each required specialized training, which staff hold it and when it was completed, and which staff on each shift cover each training.

procedures: At admission and whenever supports change, the Residence Supervisor and the nurse review each individual's plan (see PCS-02 and PCS-04) and list the specialized trainings needed at that site: feeding techniques, mobility devices and transport, seizure/physical/medical needs, mental health needs, behavior support plans, and anything else identified by the Department, the placing agency, or the agency. The Administrator confirms the list.

The Training Coordinator ([TRAINING COORDINATOR NAME]) keeps a written agency training plan and curriculum. It states for each training the content, the staff who must complete it, the due date, who may deliver it, and how competency is shown.

The Training Coordinator keeps a site training matrix for each residence. The matrix shows each employee's completion dates for each required specialized training and the Basic Training items in STF-03. The Residence Supervisor reviews it weekly.
On the first day of employment, the Training Coordinator enters each new employee into the matrix with a due date no later than 90 days after the hire date for every required specialized training.

The Administrator approves qualified trainers in writing. The approval records the trainer's relevant credentials or experience (for example, a registered nurse for health topics, a behavior analyst or clinician for behavior support plans, or a physical or occupational therapist for mobility devices), and the topics each trainer is approved to teach. Trainings that require a licensed professional (for example, tube-feeding delegated to nursing) are taught or delegated only by the licensed professional under the nurse's direction (see HW-02).

Individual-specific training is delivered by a person qualified under step 5, who explains the individual's plan and then demonstrates the technique. Where a technique involves a hands-on skill, the trainer watches the trainee perform the skill and records whether the trainee shows competency. Trainees who do not show competency are retrained and not left to perform the skill unsupervised.

Training in policies not covered in orientation, such as individual rights, grievances, reportable incidents, and emergency procedures, is delivered by a qualified trainer (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(c) and (g)). The trainer and trainee each sign and date the training record.
Medication training and demonstrated competency are completed before an employee administers any medication, and competency is re-shown every year. The nurse keeps the competency records (see HW-01).

The Training Coordinator makes sure every training record contains the curriculum or training plan reference, the training title and date, the printed names and dated signatures of the trainer and the trainee, and any results required by the Division. Records are kept in the administrative office (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(e)).

The Residence Supervisor builds each two-week schedule (see STF-01) so that on every shift at least one person has completed each specialized training required for that site, including nights, weekends, and holidays. The Supervisor checks the schedule against the site training matrix before it is posted.

If a shift cannot be covered with the required specialized trainings, the Residence Supervisor changes the assignment, uses the on-call process (STF-08), or has a person who holds the training come in. The shift is not worked short of the requirement. The Supervisor documents the problem and its resolution.

When temporary agency staff or on-call staff work at a residence, the Residence Supervisor checks that they hold the required trainings before they are counted toward the shift requirement (see STF-10).

Thirty days before an employee's 90-day deadline, the Training Coordinator notifies the employee and the supervisor of any trainings still due. An employee who has not completed a required training by the deadline is not counted as meeting the shift requirement for that training and is not assigned tasks that require it without direct supervision by a trained person. The Administrator is told, and a completion date is set.

When an individual's needs change, for example a new seizure disorder, a new mobility device, or a new behavior support plan, the Training Coordinator trains all staff who work with the individual before they carry out the change, or as quickly as possible while a trained staff member covers.
The Administrator may provide training beyond the required list at any time without Division approval. Such training is documented in the same way.

The Training Coordinator reports training completion rates and overdue trainings to the Administrator monthly and to the Continuous Quality Improvement System (see GOV-04). The training plan, trainer approvals, and matrix are reviewed at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the training plan and qualified trainers, confirms current Department requirements, and resolves overdue training.
Maintains the training plan, site matrices, and training records, schedules training, and sends deadline reminders.
Delivers the training within approved topics, checks competency, and signs and dates training records.
Trains and delegates health-related tasks (such as feeding tubes and medication) and keeps competency records.
Ensures at least one person on each shift holds each required specialized training and uses the matrix when scheduling.
Completes training by the due date and performs only tasks for which the DSP is trained.
