policies.title: Temporary Agency Staff and In-Charge Restrictions
policies.applies_to: All residence supervisors, schedulers, the Administrator, and any person who arranges or oversees staffing through a temporary employment agency at any [AGENCY NAME] residence.
policies.purpose: To control the use of temporary employment agency staff so individuals are supported by trained, qualified people, and to carry out N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.8(a), which bars the use of temporary agency staff as in-charge employees unless specific conditions are met.
policies.policy: Temporary employment agency staff are not designated or used as the in-charge employee on any shift unless all training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 has been completed and documented for that person. [AGENCY NAME] states in this policy that it assumes responsibility and liability for the actions of any temporary agency staff member it designates as in-charge. If these conditions are not met, the temporary agency staff member works only as additional staff under the direction of an in-charge employee who is an [AGENCY NAME] employee. Temporary agency staff are used only when needed to maintain required coverage, and not as the usual way of staffing a residence.

definitions.definition: A person employed by an outside staffing agency, not by [AGENCY NAME], who is sent to work at a residence.
The employee designated on the written schedule as responsible for the residence and the individuals during a shift (see STF-01).

All training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7, including Division basic training, medication training and competency before administering any medication, training in relevant policies, and specialized training, each documented as required.

procedures: Before using any temporary employment agency, the Administrator signs a written contract that requires the staffing agency to: send only staff with completed background checks, the Central Registry and Child Abuse Registry checks required for the position (see STF-02), and TB screening (see STF-04); provide copies of training certificates; and send the same staff whenever possible so they become familiar with the individuals.

The Residence Supervisor or scheduler requests temporary agency staff only after the on-call and call-out process in STF-08 has been used and has not produced enough qualified [AGENCY NAME] staff. The reason for the request is recorded.

Before a temporary agency staff member begins a first shift, the Residence Supervisor checks and keeps on file the staff member's identification, background and registry clearance confirmation, proof of Division basic training certificates (Shifting Expectations, abuse and neglect prevention, first aid, and CPR), and any specialized training certificates.

On the first shift, the Residence Supervisor or in-charge employee gives each temporary agency staff member an orientation to the residence: emergency and evacuation plans, location of the critical-information log, individual rights, reporting of abuse, neglect and exploitation, emergency contact numbers, and each individual's support needs, risks, and diets. The person signs an acknowledgment.

Temporary agency staff do not administer medication unless they have completed medication training and demonstrated competency as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7(b) and the nurse has verified it in writing (see HW-01). Otherwise they do not administer or assist with any medication.

Temporary agency staff do not perform tasks needing specialized training (for example, feeding techniques, use of mobility devices and transport, seizure response, or implementing a behavior support plan) unless the training is documented for that person, or a trained employee carries out the task.

The scheduler lists temporary agency staff on the two-week schedule by full name and marks them as agency staff. The scheduler does not list an agency staff member as in-charge unless every condition in steps 7 to 9 is met.

The Administrator, and no one else, may approve designating a temporary agency staff member as in-charge. Before approving, the Administrator verifies in writing that all training required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.7 is complete for that person, with valid certificates and competency records on file in the administrative office.

The Administrator confirms that the person knows the residence and the individuals, can use the emergency and reporting procedures, can reach the on-call person, and understands in-charge duties. The Administrator records approval on the Agency Staff In-Charge Authorization form.

By this policy, [AGENCY NAME] assumes responsibility and liability for the actions of any temporary agency staff member it designates as in-charge. The Administrator signs the policy as part of the manual, and the contract with each staffing agency states the same.

If any condition is not met, or the Administrator has not given written approval, an [AGENCY NAME] employee is designated in-charge. If no qualified employee is available, the on-call person or Residence Supervisor goes to the residence to serve as in-charge.

The Residence Supervisor observes each temporary agency staff member during early shifts, gives feedback, and tells the Administrator of any concern. A person who does not follow procedures, treats individuals disrespectfully, or is unfamiliar with the individuals is not used again, and the staffing agency is told.

Any abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury, medication error, or other incident involving agency staff is reported and investigated exactly as for [AGENCY NAME] employees (see BSP-03 and BSP-04), and the staffing agency is notified.

The Administrator keeps a log of every temporary agency shift, including the date, residence, staff name, reason, and whether the person served as in-charge, and reviews it monthly. Repeated use is reviewed in the Continuous Quality Improvement System (see GOV-04) and addressed through recruitment and retention steps.
The Administrator reviews this policy, the staffing contracts, and the agency staff file annually and at any change in the Department's requirements.

policies.title: Individual Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: All employees who create, use, store, or release records about individuals receiving services at any [AGENCY NAME] residence, including nurses, residence supervisors, direct support professionals, the Administrator, and administrative staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure a complete, accurate, secure, and available file exists for every individual served, as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9, and that records are kept for the required time and produced when the State, an individual, or a guardian is entitled to them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps an individual file for each individual receiving services (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(a)). For group home and supervised apartment residents, the file is kept at the residence (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9(b)). Each file contains at least the individual's full name, date of birth, and sex; Social Security and Medicaid/insurance numbers; and the dates of admission, readmission, transfer, or discharge, along with the other contents required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9 and listed in the Record Content Checklist kept by the Administrator. The individual's plan and monthly documentation of progress are kept in the record (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-4.3(b)). A written record of all financial arrangements and transactions involving the individual's entrusted funds is kept and made available to the individual and guardian on request, with copies provided on request (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10; see IR-06). The shift communication and critical-information log is kept separately from individual records (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)14). Records are kept for at least six years, or longer where another rule, a funding requirement, or a guardianship or legal matter calls for it. The Administrator confirms the current State retention requirement at each annual review and applies the longer period if the State period is longer. Records are protected under IR-05.

definitions.definition: The record, in paper or electronic form, that [AGENCY NAME] keeps for each individual, containing identifying information, plans, health, behavior, financial, and service documentation.
A checklist, approved by the Administrator, listing every item that must be in the file under N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9 and other policies in this manual, used at admission and at each audit.
The separate internal communication log kept for staff-to-staff communication (see PCS-07), which is not part of the individual file.
The written record of all financial arrangements and transactions involving an individual's personal funds (see IR-06).
The time a record must be kept after the date of discharge or the last entry, whichever is later.

procedures: At the time of admission, the Residence Supervisor opens an individual file at the residence and completes the Record Content Checklist with the Administrator. The file contains the individual's full name, date of birth, and sex; Social Security number; Medicaid and any other insurance numbers; and the date of admission.

The Residence Supervisor keeps the file at the residence in a locked cabinet or an access-controlled electronic system available to authorized staff at that residence. Files for group home and supervised apartment residents are not kept only at the main office.

The file holds the documents listed in the Record Content Checklist, which include identification and demographic data, guardianship or decision-making documents, the DDD plan and authorization, the Individual Habilitation Plan or service plan, physician orders, medication records, health and behavior plans, consents and rights notices, and discharge or transfer information. The Administrator updates the checklist whenever N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.9 or other rules require different contents.
The Residence Supervisor enters the dates of admission, readmission, transfer, or discharge within [NUMBER] business days of each event and notes the reason.

The IHP or service plan, and every revision, is placed in the file as soon as it is approved (see PCS-02). Monthly documentation of progress is written by the responsible staff member and filed by the end of the following month (see PCS-03).

The agency keeps entrusted funds records in accordance with IR-06 and N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.10. The Administrator keeps them where they can be reviewed with the file, ensures that the individual and guardian can view them on request, and gives copies when requested, without charge unless a charge is permitted by a documented policy.

Every entry in a file is dated, timed when appropriate, legible or electronically time-stamped, and signed or initialed by the author with full name and title. Corrections are made by one line through the error, with date and initials. Entries are never erased, covered, or removed.

Staff keep shift communications and critical information in the separate critical-information log (see PCS-07). They do not file the log in the individual's record. If information from the log is important to the individual's care, staff write it in the individual's file as a separate entry.

The Residence Supervisor checks each file monthly against the Record Content Checklist, notes anything missing or out of date, and corrects it. The nurse reviews the health sections. The Administrator audits a sample of files at each residence at least quarterly and reports results to the Continuous Quality Improvement System (see GOV-04).

Staff may see only the information they need to do their jobs. Release of information to anyone other than the individual, the guardian, the State, or an authorized provider requires a signed authorization or other legal basis (see IR-05). The staff member who releases information records the date, recipient, items released, and purpose in the file.

The individual and the guardian may review the individual's file on request. The Residence Supervisor makes the file available within [NUMBER] business days, stays with the person during review when appropriate, supports the person to understand the contents, and records the review. Requests are never refused without the Administrator's review and a written explanation.

On request, [AGENCY NAME] provides requested files, reports, or records to the Office of Licensing and DDD (see REC-02). The Administrator logs the request, the date provided, and the persons who provided the records. Electronic records are produced in a readable form.

When an individual transfers or is discharged, the Residence Supervisor copies the information needed for continuity of care to the receiving provider with proper authorization (see PCS-06), keeps the original, and updates the file with the transfer or discharge date and destination.

After discharge, the Administrator moves the file to secure archive storage, labels it with the discharge date and destruction-eligible date, and keeps it for the retention period. The retention period is at least six years from the date of discharge or the last entry, and longer when a longer period applies. If the individual was a minor, records are kept at least until six years after the individual reaches the age of majority, or longer as required.

Before any record is destroyed, the Administrator checks that no investigation, audit, litigation, billing review, or request for records is pending, then approves destruction in writing. Records are shredded or electronically erased so they cannot be read, and a destruction log is kept showing the individual's initials and file identifier, the date, the method, and who approved.

For electronic records, the agency uses unique user IDs, passwords, access limits by job role, audit trails, regular backups, and secure storage, and keeps its related security policies and procedures for the same period as other records (45 CFR 164.316(b)(2)). Records documenting services provided under the Medicaid program are kept in a way that allows full disclosure of the services and furnishing of information to the State on request (42 CFR 431.107).
The Administrator reviews this policy, the Record Content Checklist, and the retention schedule at least annually, and whenever the State changes a rule.

policies.title: Required Reports to the State
policies.applies_to: The Licensee/Executive Director, the Administrator, the finance and compliance staff, residence supervisors, and any employee who prepares, submits, or releases a report or record to the NJ DHS Office of Licensing, DDD, or another State agency.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] gives the State the reports, records, audits, and notices it requires, on time and accurately, so the agency stays licensed and approved as a DDD provider.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides files, reports, and records to the Department when requested, including during announced and unannounced inspections. Refusal to provide them is grounds for adverse action, and the agency does not refuse. The Office of Licensing may inspect without limitation and without notice (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(k)) and conducts annual on-site inspections (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(l)). Inspectors review staff files, schedules, credentials, background checks, physical plant, and insurance documents. Unusual incidents and each allegation of abuse, neglect, or exploitation are reported as required by N.J.A.C. 10:44A-2.2(b)8 (see BSP-03 and BSP-04). [AGENCY NAME] obtains an annual financial statement audit if it claims $350,000 or more in combined CCP and Supports Program reimbursement, and the audit follows generally accepted auditing standards (GAAS). The agency files its Fiscal Sustainability Report within 120 days after the state fiscal year ends (about October 30). The agency also notifies the State of changes affecting its application information, including changes in ownership, governance, agency head, and penalties or fines relevant to program safety. The Administrator confirms current notice requirements with the Office of Licensing and DDD at each annual review.

definitions.term: Combined CCP and Supports Program reimbursement
definitions.definition: The total amount [AGENCY NAME] claims from DDD under the Community Care Program and the Supports Program in a fiscal year.
An audit of the agency's financial statements by an independent CPA, performed under GAAS, required when combined CCP and Supports Program reimbursement is $350,000 or more.
The annual report to DDD, due 120 days after the end of the state fiscal year (about October 30), as published by DDD.
An event that the agency must report under its unusual incident reporting procedure, including each allegation of abuse, neglect, or exploitation (see BSP-04).
Any action by the Office of Licensing or DDD against the agency, such as a provisional license, non-renewal, denial, or other enforcement.

procedures: The Administrator keeps a Regulatory Reporting Calendar listing each recurring State report and notice, who prepares it, the due date, and when the Administrator reviews it. The calendar includes the Fiscal Sustainability Report, the annual audit, license renewal items, and any DDD reporting required by contract or notice.

When the Office of Licensing, DDD, or another State agency requests a file, report, or record, the person who receives the request logs it the same day with the date, the requester, what was requested, and the due date, and sends it to the Administrator. The Administrator assigns it and sets an internal due date at least [NUMBER] business days before the State deadline.

The Administrator sends the records requested in a complete and readable form by the due date, keeps a copy of exactly what was sent, and records the date and method of sending. Staff do not alter, back-date, or remove anything from a record before it is produced. A refusal or delay is never allowed without the Executive Director's written decision after consultation with the State agency.

During an announced or unannounced inspection, the in-charge employee greets the inspector, immediately calls the Administrator or on-call person, and makes records at the residence available. The Administrator makes available staff files, schedules, credentials, background check records, training records, and insurance and physical plant documents on request. Staff are told to be truthful and not to hide or delay anything. See GOV-07 for deficiencies and plans of correction.

Unusual incidents and each allegation of abuse, neglect, or exploitation are reported by the in-charge employee and the Administrator in the way and time set by BSP-03 and BSP-04. The Administrator keeps the report, the notification record, and the investigation file (see BSP-04).

By [DATE EACH YEAR], the Executive Director calculates the combined CCP and Supports Program reimbursement claimed in the fiscal year from billing records (see GOV-05). If the total is $350,000 or more, the Executive Director engages an independent CPA to perform an annual financial statement audit under GAAS.

The Executive Director confirms with the CPA the audit schedule and the documents needed, assigns a staff contact, and supplies the documents on time. The Executive Director reviews the draft audit and any management letter, and the Board or Licensee approves the final audit and a written response to any finding.

The Executive Director or finance lead prepares the Fiscal Sustainability Report using the current DDD form and instructions, has the Licensee review it, and submits it by the deadline of 120 days after the state fiscal year ends (about October 30). The submission confirmation is saved.

The Administrator keeps the audited financial statements, management letters, and Fiscal Sustainability Reports for the current and previous fiscal years in the administrative office, with the CPA examination of financial status and management letters for two fiscal years that were part of the licensing application (N.J.A.C. 10:44A-1.4(c)). They are available to State reviewers on request.

The Administrator and Licensee confirm at least once a year that the agency's application information is still accurate, including the table of organization, owners, governing body, agency head, and the history of penalties or fines related to program safety.

The Licensee or Administrator gives written notice to the Office of Licensing and DDD of any change in ownership, governance, or agency head, and of any new penalty or fine relevant to program safety. Notice is given before the change takes effect where possible and otherwise no later than five business days after the agency learns of it, or sooner if a State agency requires a shorter time. The agency also checks background clearance requirements before any new agency head is paid or contracted (see STF-02 and GOV-01).

Before any change to the residence or program that requires State approval or notice, including housing and capacity changes, the Administrator contacts the Office of Licensing and DDD in advance. Housing is cleared with DDD's Office of Housing and Resource Development before acquisition, as the Office of Licensing requires.

Electronic Visit Verification data and billing and service records submitted to the State are accurate and complete (see GOV-05 and GOV-06). The agency submits them through the State's approved systems, consistent with the federal requirement for Medicaid EVV (42 USC 1396b(l)). The Administrator reviews errors and exceptions monthly and corrects them promptly.

After a State report, notice, or audit identifies a deficiency, the Administrator prepares a written plan of correction by the due date in the notice and tracks completion (see GOV-07). The Administrator reviews each completed report to the State for accuracy and for any trend and includes the results in the Continuous Quality Improvement System (see GOV-04).

The Administrator keeps a copy of each report, notice, request, and confirmation of submission in a State Reports file for at least six years, or longer where required (see REC-01). The Administrator reviews this policy and the Reporting Calendar at least annually, and checks DDD and Office of Licensing notices for new reporting requirements.
